en: Preface to the Dhyānapāramitā.
Regarding the Dhyānapāramitā, the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Record) states that it was preached by the Great Master at Waguan Temple.
The *Dizhi chandimen mulu* (Catalogue of the Sequential Gate of Dhyāna) records that Dharmashen of Dazhuangyan Temple made a private record of it, and Zhiyi of Zhang’an received it.
The Chan Master compiled this into ten fascicles,
opening it into ten major chapters.
First, the general intent;
second, the explanation of the names;
third, the clarification of the gates.
Fourth, the sequential order;
fifth, the mind of phenomena;
sixth, the skillful means.
Seventh, cultivation and realization;
eighth, retribution;
ninth, the arising of the teaching.
Regarding the ten destinations,
they exist only in the stage of cultivation and realization;
the remaining three are essentially non-existent there.
Within the context of cultivation and realization,
four further distinctions are established:
first, worldly dhyāna.
The second is both mundane and supramundane;
the third is supramundane;
the fourth is neither mundane nor supramundane.
Among these four, only up to the third is supramundane.
This, in turn, is twofold:
first, the untainted (anāsrava) which serves as an antidote.
Second, those that take principle as their object are untainted;
they extend only to the stage of counteractive cultivation and are further divided into nine types.
That is to say: the nine perceptions,
the eight recollections, the ten perceptions,
the liberations, and the spheres of mastery.
The bases of mastery,
the nine successive attainments,
and the displays of supernormal power.
This transcends [conventional categories]. However, how could the characteristics of cultivation and realization be fully encompassed?
The Biography states:
Once, when the Great Master was seated upon the high throne, he said,
"If one were to speak of the gradual gate of dhyāna..."
It may be recited once a year.
If including the commentaries and sub-commentaries,
it would amount to fifty fascicles.
Now, the preliminary outline of the major sections is published for reference, so that students may not be ignorant of the beginning and the end.

Analysis of the Preliminary Expedients for the Dhyānapāramitā, Part One of Six. This section consists of three fascicles. Its commentary is as follows: Analysis of the Preliminary Expedients for the Dhyānapāramitā, Part Six, Section One. There are three fascicles in the explanation of this passage.
This present first fascicle correctly explains the external expedient means (*bāhyopāya*).
Within this, regarding the clarification of the subduing of the coarse mind of the desire realm,
there are those who seek shallow and proximate expedient means.

I suspect you may have doubts; however, since this discourse deals exclusively with matters that are shallow and mundane—explaining what is easy while practicing what is difficult—it cannot yet discuss the profound principles and various skillful means.
These will be addressed later, in the twelfth fascicle of the seventh major section, "Cultivation and Realization."

One should then follow the depth of the principles of meditative practice (*dhyāna*) prior to the stages of realization (*pramāṇa*), clarifying at each successive stage the characteristics of the skillful application of mind through the two types of practice:
the practice of conduct (*caryā-caryā*) and the practice of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*).
Since this text has not been widely circulated, I have recorded it here so that practitioners may know it. If a practitioner can master it,
they will understand the five types of characteristics of the dhyānas as previously explained.
Thus, internal faith is awakened.
If one wishes to settle the mind and engage in study,
one must skillfully understand the expedient means.
Now, to clarify the methods for practicing dhyāna,
they are broadly divided into two categories.
The first is the external method, which refers to the techniques for applying the mind outside of meditative concentration itself.
The second is internal skillful means (*adhyātma-upāya*), which is the method of applying the mind within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
These two are both termed "skillful means" (*upāya*);
this is a synonym for skillfully practicing and training.
Because the practitioner skillfully cultivates within the initial object of focus,
it is called "skillful means" (*upāya*).
If discussed in detail,
external skillful means also have internal application that involves meditative concentration,
and internal skillful means also have external application that results in attaining meditative concentration.
For now, we shall discuss this primarily from the perspective of the majority;
it should be analyzed as set forth above.
Regarding the clarification of external expedient means, there are five types.
First, one must possess the five conditions;
second, one must censure the five desires;
third, one must abandon the five hindrances.
The fourth consists of five methods for training;
the fifth consists of five methods for practice.
These five sets of five constitute twenty-five dharmas in total.
These are all the characteristics of the initial mental preparations for practice prior to attaining dhyāna. First,
regarding the possession of the five conditions:
First, purity of ethical discipline;
second, sufficiency of robes and food;
third, dwelling in a secluded and quiet place.
Fourth, ceasing all distracting affairs;
fifth, obtaining virtuous friends.
These are the five conditions for practicing dhyāna.
Regarding the first point, the purity of upholding the precepts,
it is divided into three aspects.
The first clarifies the presence or absence of the precepts.
Second, the explanation of observing and violating the precepts;
third, the explanation of repentance.
First, the explanation of those who possess the precepts and those who do not.
Because one has received and attained the prohibitive precepts upon leaving the household life, they are said to possess the precepts; this constitutes three points.
First, to clarify that the conditions for the arousal of the precepts differ from those of ordinary people, there are ten types.
What are the ten?
First is the one who naturally attains the precepts; the Buddha is such a person.
He spontaneously generated them without a teacher.
The second is attaining the precepts through self-vow, namely Kāśyapa;
he was originally of the nature of a pratyekabuddha,
but having encountered the appearance of a Buddha in the world, he fell among the ranks of the śrāvakas.
He replied to the Buddha, saying,
"The Buddha is my teacher;
I am the Buddha's disciple."
Having spoken these words, they immediately received the precepts.
Third, those who obtain the precepts through the realization of the truths are the five, including Kauṇḍinya;
for them, the Buddha turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Truths.
He immediately realized the cause of the first fruit (*srotāpatti-phala*) and gave rise to the precepts.
Fourth is receiving the precepts through the Three Refuges;
at that time, the formal ritual of ordination (*karmavācanā*) did not yet exist.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s threefold proclamation, they immediately gave rise to the categories of precepts;
because their faculties were sharp,
they obtained the five and eight respectful precepts.
She was the Buddha’s maternal aunt.
The Buddha did not wish to allow women to leave the household life and become ordained,
but his aunt earnestly entreated him.
Sixth is obtaining the precepts through formal debate. This refers to cases where one receives the Eight Respectful Precepts from afar and immediately generates the full precepts.
Then the śrāmaṇera Śuddhika engaged in a discussion on the principles with the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned him regarding such matters as impermanence,
and he was able to answer every point.
Later, the Buddha asked, "Where is your home?
He replied to the Buddha,
"The Triple World is entirely empty, World-Honored One."
"Why do you ask for the location of my home?
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Take him back to the midst of the Saṃgha."
He received full ordination;
at that time he was seven years of age. Regarding the number seven:
he attained the precepts by the "Come hither" (ehi-bhikṣu) formula.
When the conditions for the Way were ripe, the Buddha called out,
"Welcome," and he immediately attained the precepts.
Eighth is attainment of the precepts through being sent by another.
She was the daughter of the King of Kāśī;
she possessed a most excellent and beautiful countenance,
capable of captivating the hearts of men throughout the entire kingdom of Kāśī.
Therefore, it was permitted to dispatch a messenger from among the monks to receive the precepts on one's behalf;
subsequently, upon returning to the nunnery, the precepts would be conferred upon them.
Ninth, in frontier regions where the Dharma is practiced but practitioners are few...
It is permitted for five people to receive the precepts.
Tenth, because there are many people in the central lands,
ten people may receive full ordination.
These are the ten types of characteristics for obtaining the precepts.
In the present age, the precepts are most commonly obtained through the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) of ten persons.
This explains the characteristics of possessing the precepts.
Second, to clearly elucidate the essential nature and characteristics of the precepts,
there are two different types of doctrinal gates.
As for the teachings of the Hīnayāna:
It is explained that the precepts are unmanifest wholesome dharmas;
when the causes and conditions for receiving the precepts are complete,
one brings forth and attains the unmanifest precepts.
Thereafter, when falling asleep or entering meditative absorption,
this goodness arises spontaneously and naturally,
without the need for any deliberate effort of body, speech, or mind.
Taking non-action (avijñapti) as the true essence of the precepts;
this is how the Sarvāstivādins understand the precept of non-action.
This unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa) is invisible and non-obstructive;
this is how the Dharmaguptakas clarify the precept of non-action (avijñapti-śīla).
This third category consists of dharmas that are neither form nor mind;
since the various schools differ on this point,
one should not adhere dogmatically to any single view.
According to the teachings of the Hīnayāna,
the precept-body ultimately consists of non-action;
this principle is unerring.
If, within the Mahāyāna teachings,
it is said that precepts arise from the mind,
then one takes the virtuous mind itself as the essence of the precepts.
This meaning is as explained in the *Sragdharā-sūtra*.
Some masters say:
"The people of the Mahāsāṃghika school state..."
The unmanifest precept (avijñapti-śīla) is a mental dharma (citta-dharma).
Third, it clarifies that there are differences in the characteristics of the precepts;
this involves two points.
First, if categorized according to the Hīnayāna,
there are seven classes of practitioners who generate the resolve;
this is because the ritual procedures for receiving the precepts differ for each.
The attainment of precepts also has degrees of excellence or inferiority.
For example, for laymen (upāsaka) and laywomen (upāsikā),
there are the five precepts as their characteristic form while remaining at home.
If men or women who have not yet entered the Buddha-dharma do not kill their fathers or harm their mothers,
and do not commit the heinous crimes of immediate retribution, they may encounter a good and virtuous teacher who instructs them.
He took refuge in the Triple Gem and received the five precepts;
the ritual was thus successfully accomplished.
Immediately, the non-informative action (avijñapti) of the five precepts arises;
this is called "attaining the five precepts.
From this point on, one is named a lay follower (upāsaka or upāsikā).
Furthermore, regarding the śrāmaṇera,
there are ten precepts.
If the upādhyāya...
The ācārya and the two masters receive the person according to the Dharma;
he is pure and takes refuge in the Triple Gem.
Following the Buddha, they leave the household life;
if the two masters perform the ritual correctly,
the unmanifest karma (avijñapti) is immediately produced.
This is called attaining the śrāmaṇera precepts.
Next, the characteristics of the precepts for the great saṃgha are explained.
If one acts as a śrāmaṇera at that time:
Without committing a grave offense,
the ten pure masters— the Upādhyāya and Ācāryas— perform the *karmavācanā*,
whereby it is accomplished in accordance with the Dharma.
This is called attaining the full ordination of a great bhikṣu.
[The same applies to] a śrāmaṇerī or a śikṣamāṇā.
The same applies to *bhikṣuṇīs* who possess the marks of the precepts.
Even if these seven persons have originally committed a grave offense,
if they encounter a favorable condition (*kalyāṇamitra*), [they may be restored].
This refers to performing the Mahāyāna Vaipulya repentance;
after attaining the accomplishment of the signs, one receives the precepts and also achieves the arising of non-informative virtue (*avijñapti-kuśala*).
This is distinct from the terminology explained above.
Not obtaining the precepts is also called being without precepts.
Second, if a bodhisattva practitioner possesses the precepts, they are "with precepts"; if they do not possess the precepts, they are "without precepts."
This cannot be known. Why is this?
Because from lifetime to lifetime since the Bodhisattva first appeared in the world, [he has practiced].
Alternatively, at the time of first generating the resolve for enlightenment,
one may encounter a favorable condition and receive the precepts.
The second section clarifies the observance and violation of precepts, which contains three points:
first, a brief explanation of observance and violation;
second, a detailed and systematic explanation of observance and violation.
The three types of knowledge (*vidyā*) are now revealed.
Regarding the first [section], there are two general explanations of observance (*dhāraṇa*) and transgression (*aticāra*).
The first is the characteristic of observance.
Second, the characteristics of transgression.
Regarding the first, the characteristic of upholding:
"upholding" means guarding and maintaining.
As stated above,
these seven types of persons receive the prohibitory precepts of the Buddha.
For the sake of ten benefits,
one should protect and uphold [the precepts] without transgression. As for these ten benefits,
they are as explained in the Vinaya.
First, for the sake of unifying the Saṃgha;
second, for the sake of excellent unification;
third, for the sake of the Saṃgha dwelling in peace and happiness.
Fourth, to subdue those with haughty minds;
fifth, so that those with a sense of shame may dwell in peace and happiness;
sixth, to cause those who lack faith to gain faith.
Seventh, because it increases faith in those who have already gained faith;
eighth, because it prevents outflows in the present life;
ninth, because it severs evil in future lives.
Tenth, it causes those who practice the holy life to dwell for a long time;
thus, practitioners remain single-mindedly reverent and cautious,
not daring to violate or defile [the precepts].
It is like protecting a life-preserving bag;
because not even a speck of dust is discarded, it is called "guarding and maintaining" (護持),
and it is also called "upholding" (秉持).
This is called the characteristic of maintaining [the precepts], as illustrated by the analogy of holding a bowl of oil.
Second, to clarify the characteristic of transgression:
To commit an offense is called a transgression.
One originally received the Buddha’s precepts with the desire to transcend birth and death.
I seek liberation;
yet now encountering adverse conditions,
I am unable to restrain my own mind.
To turn back midway,
whether the act be grave or light,
is therefore termed a transgression.
Furthermore, "offense" (āpatti) means "contact through transgression.
It is like taking medicine while disregarding dietary prohibitions and failing to follow the physician's instructions;
by consuming unwholesome food, one comes into contact with and violates the potency of the medicine.
Not only can it not cure the illness, but on the contrary,
it causes it to increase further,
or at times even leads to death.
The characteristics of violating the precepts are likewise thus;
therefore, it is called "violation.
Second, the detailed explanation of upholding and violating [the precepts]:
From the initial resolve to the fruit of Buddhahood,
there are ten types of clarity regarding the observance and violation of precepts.
First is the precept of non-deficiency.
This means: first, maintaining the four grave offenses without transgression;
second, maintaining the precepts without breach, which refers to not transgressing regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.
Third, maintaining the precepts without breach,
meaning not committing offenses against the first three categories [of the *Prātimokṣa*].
Fourth, maintaining the precepts without flaw.
It is also called the "unadulterated precept," meaning that one does not give rise to a deceitful mind or various afflictive discursive thoughts and mental explorations.
It is also called the "precept co-existent with meditative concentration."
The fifth is maintaining the precepts that accord with the Path;
this consists of the mental cultivation of the sixteen aspects of contemplation,
which gives rise to the wisdom of the patience regarding suffering.
It is also called the precept concomitant with the Path (mārga-sahagata-śīla).
The sixth is the upholder of the precept of non-attachment (anāsakta-śīla),
namely the person who has attained the stage of Anāgāmin.
If one exhausts the nine grades of discursive thought (*vitarka*) of the desire realm,
it is called the restraint of the morality of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃvaraśīla*);
this extends even to the attachment of the form realm and the attachment of the formless realm.
The exhaustion of all fetters and proclivities is called the precept of non-attachment;
it is the seventh, the precept praised by those who possess wisdom.
Having resolved upon bodhicitta,
one observes the precepts in order to enable all sentient beings to attain nirvana.
Maintaining the precepts in this manner is praised by the wise;
it may also be described as upholding the Bodhisattva’s ten grave and forty-eight light precepts.
Because this precept can lead to the fruit of Buddhahood, it is praised by the wise.
It is the eighth: the precept of mastery over maintenance.
The Bodhisattva maintains the precepts and attains mastery amidst various conditions that lead to the breaking of them.
It may also be said that because a bodhisattva knows that both transgression and non-transgression are unapprehendable,
they maintain the mind of upholding the precepts solely for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
Because there is no grasping,
it is called the precept of mastery.
Ninth is the fulfillment of the upholding precepts.
The Bodhisattva is able to fully possess the precepts of all sentient beings,
as well as the precepts of the higher stages and the ten types of precepts that follow meditative concentration.
Without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation, they manifest various dignified conducts and precepts to deliver sentient beings;
these first four constitute the purity of mundane precepts.
One also attains supramundane precepts;
their meaning is fully explained as previously stated in the *Suvibhakta* (The Well-Differentiated).
The second is the purity of supramundane precepts.
The latter four are the purity of the supreme-supramundane precepts.
If one can receive and uphold them as described above, [one will attain these purities].
This is the characteristic of upholding the precepts;
anything different from what has been described above is the characteristic of transgression.
This is called the discussion on the depth and shallowness of observing the precepts from the initial resolve up to the fruit of Buddhahood,
as well as the characteristics of violating them;
thus the Sūtra says that only the Buddha alone possesses pure precepts.
All others are called those who have broken the precepts.
Furthermore, it is now clarified that one who upholds the precepts merely practices according to their own capacity and strength.
This causes them to progress and gradually become purified;
if it were not so, one would be unable to give rise to the various meditative absorptions (dhyāna-samādhi).
Furthermore, a bodhisattva who practices through sudden realization is able,

Second, regarding the determination and exclusion of what is concealed and subsequently manifested:

One should apply a fourfold analytical distinction (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Fourth, there are those who do not give rise [to offenses] because they possess both the precepts and their transgressions;
first, there are those who are individuals who have committed a violation of the precepts but who give rise [to them] while practicing meditative concentration.

because their roots of goodness are profound and deep,

Because the power of past roots of goodness is strong,

The three cases where they arise together and the four cases where they do not arise together can all be explained by analogy.

if one traces their source,

Violating the precepts ultimately constitutes an obstruction.

One immediately knows that because one formerly maintained the precepts and gave rise to meditative concentration in the past,
these have become the habitual causes for the present life;
furthermore, in this life, one takes shame, remorse, and purification through repentance as the conditions.
Therefore, one is able to arouse the roots of goodness from past lives.
In the third section, which clarifies repentance, there are two internal intentions.
The first is to first clarify the cultivation of the mind of repentance.
The second part clearly explains the method of repentance.
First, what is meant by "generating the mind of repentance"?

Then there would be no transgression to repent for.
Since practitioners are unable to maintain the precepts with absolute determination,

Even if it is broken,

"If these transgressions of mine can now be extinguished..."
In the future,
I would rather lose my body and life than ever again create such karma of suffering.

Such instances are numerous and will not be explained in detail here;
to state the essentials: [the text continues].
If one can know that phenomena are illusory,
evil karma will cease forever,
and one will practice the path of goodness.
This is called repentance (*pratikramaṇa*).
Second, the method of repentance is clarified through three points.

First, the primary clarification of the different methods of repentance.
The causes for the extinction of offenses each have their respective methods,
just as the stains and grease on clothing do.
If one merely washes it with water,
it can never be removed;
[it requires] the alkaline lye of soapberry pods.

The method for extinguishing transgressions is likewise so.
Now, to clarify the methods of repentance:
the teachings of the gateways are indeed numerous;
yet, taking the essentials as our focus, we shall discuss them.
There are, however, three types.
The first is the ritual repentance (*vidhi-pratikramaṇa*),
which supports the Vinaya.
First is the repentance through clarity;

which supports the methods of meditative concentration.
The first is the repentance through clarity;

This clarifies the method of repentance.

First, the repentance through ritual performance (*vidhi-pratikramaṇa*) is explained.
Because one turns away from evil deeds by performing virtuous deeds,

As stated in the *Vinaya*:
One should exclusively employ this method to extinguish transgressions.

Why is this? Because, as in the case of confessing a second-grade offense, the ritual procedures for performing *parivāsa*, *mānāpya*, and the removal of the offense (*āpattivyutthāna*) are successfully accomplished through the formal act (*karmavācanā*).

Therefore, it is known that these are merely ritual acts of repentance (*karmavācanā*).

This matter is easy to understand;

One should know that although this is not explicitly set forth in the Vinaya,

With focused attention,

If you wish to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true nature of reality.

It is simply because sentient beings engage in unwholesome reflection that they falsely cling to conditioned phenomena, thereby giving rise to ignorance, craving, and hatred.
From these three poisons,

If you wish to eliminate it, you should simply reflect inwardly: from where does such a mind arise?
If it were in the past, [it would have already ceased].
The past has already ceased.
That which has ceased is non-existent.
A dharma that is non-existent...
It cannot be called "mind.
If it were in the future,
the future has not yet arrived.
The dharmas that have not yet arrived are dharmas that neither exist nor do not exist;

Within the present, there is not a single moment of abiding; within this state of non-abiding,

The mind cannot be apprehended.

If you say it exists externally,

How could there be a mind?

observe it in this way.

From what do offenses arise?
Furthermore, all phenomena without exception belong to the mind.

Non-abiding and non-destruction—

severing all social interaction with them,

cultivating the same path and mutually encouraging one another.
Third, the spiritual friend who provides instruction by means of internal and external skillful methods and the dharma-gates of meditative concentration.
He instructs, exhorts, benefits, and gladdens them.
This briefly clarifies the fulfillment of the five conditions.
Second, regarding the censure of the five desires and the abandonment of the five hindrances:
The Sūtra says: "Having departed from sensual desires and unwholesome states, there is applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra).
As for 'departing from sensual desires'..."
This is precisely the censure of the five desires;
"evil dharmas" refers to the abandonment of the five hindrances.
As for the "five desires," they refer to the superior and exquisite forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tactile objects of the world,
which constantly deceive and delude all ordinary beings.
It destroys wholesome deeds.
If one does not clearly recognize transgressions and offenses, and does not censure them with a sense of weary detachment,
then all dhyānas and samādhis—
There is no way to obtain even one.
Those who revile sensual desire are men and women.
His physical appearance was dignified and majestic;
his eyes were long and his eyebrows high,
with lips as crimson as vermillion and teeth as white as jade.
As well as worldly treasures of blue,
yellow, red, white,
crimson, purple, pale green, and emerald.
These various exquisite forms can cause fools,
upon seeing them, to immediately give rise to craving and commit all manner of evil deeds.
For example, King Bimbisāra,
on account of sensual desire,
entered the enemy kingdom with his own body.
He was staying alone in the chamber of the courtesan Āmrapālī.
Because King Udayana was stained by lustful passion,
he cut off the hands and feet of five hundred rishis.
Through such various causes and conditions as these,
one understands the faults and transgressions of form,
as explained in detail within the Mahāyāna.
Second, those who desire the sound of music refers to the lute,
the zither, and the flute; the stringed,
the bamboo, the metal, and the stone instruments.
The sounds of music,
as well as the voices of men and women singing hymns and offering praises,
are able to cause ordinary beings to...
Upon hearing it, they immediately become stained by attachment and give rise to various evil karmas.
For example, five hundred rishis dwelling in the Snowy Mountains heard the singing voice of the maiden Kanchanā.
One immediately loses meditative concentration;
the mind becomes intoxicated and deranged— through various causes and conditions such as these,
one comes to know the faults and transgressions of sound.
As explained in detail in the Mahāyāna,
the three fragrances of desire are the bodily fragrances of men and women.
Regarding the fragrant scents of worldly food and drink,
as well as all types of incense and perfumes,
the foolish person does not understand the true nature of fragrance.
Upon hearing it, one immediately becomes attached to it,
opening the gateway to the fetters and latent tendencies.
It is like a bhikṣu who was by the side of a lotus pond.
Upon smelling the fragrance of the flowers,
a heart of attachment and delight arose;
the deity of the pond immediately rebuked him severely.
"Why do you steal my fragrance?
Because of your attachment to this scent,
you cause all the latent defilements (*anuśaya*) that were lying dormant to arise."
They all give rise to these various causes and conditions to know the faults and evils of fragrance,
as explained in detail in the Mahāyāna.
The fourth is the reproving of the desire for flavors,
which refers to various foods and delicacies with delicious tastes, such as bitter, sour, sweet, pungent, salty, and bland.
It can cause the minds of ordinary persons to give rise to defiled attachment and initiate unwholesome karma,
just as a certain śrāmaṇera became attached to the taste of curd.
After his life ends, he is immediately reborn within curd and receives the body of an insect.
In this way, one should recognize the various faults and transgressions associated with the sense of taste.
As explained at length in the Mahāyāna,
the five types of contact with sensual desire refer to the physical parts of men and women.
It is soft, supple, and smooth;
in cold weather the body is warm,
and in hot weather the body is cool.
And as for pleasant tactile sensations,
the foolish person, lacking wisdom,
becomes submerged by them.
They give rise to karma that obstructs the path,
just as the Unicorn Sage did because of contact with sensual desire.
He fell away from his supernormal powers and was even mounted on the neck by a courtesan;
such were the various faults and transgressions resulting from the touch of sensual desire.
As explained in detail in the Mahāyāna,
it is asked:
How does one censure the five desires?
The answer is:
The method for censuring desire is as it is presented in the Mahāyāna.
Alas for sentient beings!
Constantly tormented by the five desires,
they nevertheless seek them without ceasing.
These five desires, once obtained,
only become more intense,
like fire fed with fuel.
The flames blaze ever more fiercely;
the five desires are of no benefit,
like a dog gnawing on a dry bone.
The five desires increase contention,
like birds competing for meat;
the five desires burn people.
Like holding a torch against the wind,
the five desires harm a person;
they are like treading upon a venomous snake.
The five desires are without reality,
like what is obtained in a dream;
the five desires do not endure for long.
It is also like a temporary loan for a brief moment;
worldly people, deluded and ignorant,
greedily cling to the five desires.
They do not abandon them even unto death,
thereby undergoing immeasurable suffering in future lives.
These five desires are shared by all sentient beings.
All sentient beings are constantly driven by the five desires;
they are called slaves to desire.
Sitting here, I am about to fall into the three miserable realms due to these wretched desires;
now that I practice dhyāna,
they again act as obstacles and hindrances.
This is a great thief;
one should quickly distance oneself from it.
As stated in a verse within the *Dhyāna-sūtra*:
Birth and death are never severed; because of craving for the taste of desire, one nourishes an enemy and enters the burial mounds.
One undergoes manifold sufferings at great length;
the body stinks like a corpse, with impurities flowing from its nine orifices.
Just as a worm in a latrine delights in filth, the fool’s craving for the body is no different.
The wise should contemplate the body;
being free from attachment to the world, without burdens and without desires—this is called true nirvāṇa.
As the Buddhas have taught: practicing with a single mind and focused intent on counting the breaths while in meditative concentration—this is called practicing the dhūtas.
Such are the various causes and conditions.
Knowing the faults and transgressions of the five desires,
the mind does not draw near to them;
because it has distanced itself from them, it is like avoiding a hostile thief.
The mind is free from feverish affliction,
and sensual thoughts do not arise;
this is the essential method for practicing dhyāna.
One censures the characteristics of the five desires as extensively explained in the Mahāyāna.
Third, one abandons the five hindrances.
First is the hindrance of sensual desire;
second is the hindrance of ill will;
third is the hindrance of sloth and torpor.
The four hindrances of restlessness and remorse,
and the fifth hindrance of doubt.
Regarding the first, the abandonment of sensual desire:
Previously, it was explained that desire arises from the five external sense objects;
now, it is explained that desire arises from the internal faculty of mind (*manas*).
That is to say, the practitioner sits upright and practices meditation.
A sensual thought arises in the mind,
continuing from moment to moment,
obscuring the wholesome mind.
One should prevent them from arising;
having recognized them, one should abandon them. Why is this so?
Just as when the fire of a magic spell (*yoginī-mantra*) blazes within,
it is still able to burn the body.
How much more so when the fire of desire arises in the mind and burns away all wholesome dharmas?
Furthermore, a person possessed by craving is very far from the Path. Why is this?
Desires are manifold and disturb one's dwelling;
if the mind is attached to desire, [it is disturbed].
There is no way to approach the Path.
As stated in the *Nīvaraṇa-vigama-gāthā*:
"One who enters the Path with a sense of shame and modesty, holding the alms-bowl, brings blessings to sentient beings."
How can one who has cast off sensual desires and abandoned the five objects of the senses, having already sunk through them,
now wish to regain them? It is like a fool who eats his own vomit.
All desires are suffering when sought; they bring much fear when obtained;
and one harbors grief and distress when they are lost. There is not a single place of happiness among them.
Such are the afflictions of desire; having thus rebuked them, one should abandon them.
One who attains the bliss of meritorious meditative concentration will not be deceived;
for such various reasons as these,
he censures the hindrance of sensual desire.
As stated in the verses on the condemnation of desire within the Mahāyāna,
the second [step] is to abandon the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*).
Ill-will is the root from which all unwholesome dharmas arise.
It is the causal condition for falling into the various evil realms,
the enemy of the joy of the Dharma,
and the great thief of the virtuous mind.
It is a repository of various kinds of harsh speech.
Furthermore, while seated in meditation, the practitioner reflects:
"This person has harmed me and harmed my kin."
To praise my enemy;
to contemplate the past and the future—
these are also like this.
These are the nine grounds for resentment.
Because of resentment, anger arises;
because of anger, hatred arises.
From resentment, enmity arises;
from enmity, one desires to inflict retaliatory harm.
His mind is then shrouded by these perceptions and discursive thoughts of anger, resentment, enmity, and affliction.
Therefore they are called "hindrances.
One should abandon them with urgency,
lest they increase.
As Śakra Devānām-Indra asked the Buddha in verse:
"What is it that, when killed, brings peace? What is it that, when killed, leaves no sorrow?
What is the root of poison That swallows up all goodness?"
The Buddha replied:
"By slaying anger one attains peace; by slaying anger one is free from sorrow.
Anger is the root of poison; when anger is extinguished, all that is wholesome flourishes."
Having understood this,
one should cultivate loving-kindness and patience to eliminate them.
This causes the mind to become pure.
As it is said in the Mahāyāna, in the verses on rebuking anger for the disciples of the Buddha;
this should be explained in detail therein.
Third, regarding the refutation of the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor:
mental dullness and obscurity are termed "sleep."
When the limbs and joints are relaxed and one lies prostrate with the body fully extended,
it is called sleep.
Furthermore, when the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is clouded and darkened, it is called "spittle"; when the five sense organs are obscured and muddled, it is called "sleep.
For these reasons:
It is called the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor (*styāna-middha*).
In the Abhidharma, it is explained as a factor that increases mental states (*caitasika-dharma*) and is capable of destroying three matters in this present life.
That is to say, it is the pursuit of pleasure, benefit, and merit;
yet it is an evil dharma that can destroy the true happiness of both this life and future lives.
This is the most unwholesome.
Why? Because other hindrances and mental afflictions can be removed.
Sleeping is like being a dead person;
there is no perception or cognition. Because of this lack of awareness, [one does not perceive].
It is difficult to eradicate.
For instance, there is a bodhisattva who instructs his sleeping disciple, saying:
"Arise! Do not lie down embracing a corpse—a mere collection of various impurities falsely called a 'person'."
As if afflicted by a grave illness with an arrow piercing the body, amidst a mass of all manner of agonies, how can one sleep?
Like a person bound and led away to execution, with disaster hanging over them, how can one sleep?
The bandits of the fetters have not yet been destroyed and the harm has not yet been removed; it is like dwelling in the same room as a venomous snake.
It is also like standing on the edge of a battle amidst white blades; how could one sleep at such a time?
Sleep is a great darkness in which nothing is seen; day after day it deceives and robs one of clarity.
When the mind is shrouded by sleep and sees nothing, such a great loss—how can one sleep?
In these and various other ways, he censures the hindrance of drowsiness,
arouses awareness of impermanence,
and eliminates the damage caused by sleep.
To ensure that there is no obscuration by drowsiness: if the mind is overcome by sleep,
one should vigorously employ meditation cushions, meditation staffs, and the like to dispel it.
Fourth, regarding the abandonment of restlessness and remorse:
there are three types of restlessness—first, of the body;
second, of speech; and third, of the mind.
Regarding bodily restlessness:
it is when the body delights in wandering about and various forms of frivolous play.
He cannot sit still for even a moment;
his mouth flutters as he delights in chanting and versifying,
and he quarrels over right and wrong.
Regarding frivolous talk,
worldly conversation, and the like,
as well as mental restlessness:
The mind becomes dissolute and unrestrained, wandering among objects of attachment;
it dwells upon literature, arts, worldly skills,
and various unwholesome thoughts and reflections.
This is called mental restlessness.
Restlessness is a state that destroys the mind of one who has gone forth.
If a person cannot attain concentration even when gathering the mind,
how much less so when it is distracted and agitated?
A person who is restless and distracted is like a hookless elephant in rut or a camel with its nose pierced; they cannot be restrained, as it is said in verse:
"You have shaved your head and donned the dyed robes; holding an earthen bowl, you go forth to beg for food."
Why do you delight in and cling to frivolity and agitation? Through negligence and indulgence of the passions, you lose the benefits of the Dharma;
having lost the benefits of the Dharma, you further lose worldly happiness.
Having recognized its fault,
one should quickly abandon it;
for remorse is like agitation.
If there is no remorse, it does not constitute an obscuration. Why is this?
Because at the time of agitation, one is not yet within the object of focus.
Later, when one wishes to enter meditative concentration,
one deeply regrets what was previously done;
because the mind is shrouded by anxiety and distress, these are called "hindrances" (nīvaraṇa).
Furthermore, there are two kinds of regret.
The first is that which arises subsequent to restlessness,
as previously explained.
Second, they are like those who have committed grave offenses,
constantly harboring fear,
with the arrow of remorse piercing their hearts.
It is firm and cannot be uprooted.
As it is said in verse:
"One does what should not be done, and fails to do what should be done."
Burning with the fire of afflictions, one falls into evil realms in future lives.
If a person can repent for their transgressions, having repented, they need no longer grieve.
Thus the mind is peaceful and happy; one should not dwell constantly on them.
If there are two kinds of regret— regretting what should have been done was not done,
and regretting what should not have been done was done— these are merely the marks of a fool;
for by means of mental regret, one does not fail to do what should be done.
"Once various evil deeds have been committed, one cannot make them not have been done"—
through such various causes and conditions,
he rebukes the hindrance of restlessness and remorse.
The mind and spirit are pure and clear;
there is no obscuration,
and one always abides in a virtuous state of mind.
Then one becomes tranquil and at ease;
by these causes and conditions,
the mind attains the joy of the Dharma.
Fifth, regarding the abandonment of the hindrance of doubt:
because one is shrouded by doubt,
one cannot attain a concentrated mind amidst all phenomena.
Because they lack a concentrated mind,
they obtain nothing at all within the Buddha-dharma,
just as if a person were to enter a mountain of jewels.
If one has no hands, there is nothing that can be grasped.
Furthermore, pervasive doubt is very common,
yet it does not necessarily obstruct meditative concentration.
Now, that which specifically obstructs meditative concentration through doubt refers to three kinds of doubt.
The first is doubt regarding oneself.
Second, doubting the teacher;
third, doubting the Dharma;
and doubting oneself.
If a person thinks to themselves:
"My faculties are dull and dark;
my karmic defilements are deep and heavy."
"Is he not a worthy vessel?
Having harbored such self-doubt, his fixed conviction will never arise.
Those who wish to remove this [doubt]..."
Do not disparage yourself, for the roots of goodness from past lives are difficult to fathom.
Second, regarding doubting the teacher:
this refers to the person’s deportment and physical appearance.
"Since he himself does not yet possess the Way,
how can he teach me?
Thinking thus, he harbored doubts and arrogance.
This immediately constitutes an obstacle to meditative concentration.
The method for removing it is as explained in the Mahāyāna.
It is like gold within a stinking leather bag;
because of the desire for the gold, one cannot discard the stinking leather bag.
The practitioner is likewise.
Even if the teacher is not pure,
one should still conceive of them as a Buddha;
this matter is as explained in the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the explanation of Sadāprarudita seeking a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) with full clarity,
this should be explained in detail herein.
Regarding the third method for dispelling doubt:
worldly people generally cling to their own original minds regarding the teachings they have received.
One cannot believe it immediately;
therefore, if one does not receive and practice it with a respectful mind, or if doubt arises in the mind,
then the Dharma will not permeate the spirit.
Why is this? As it is said in the *Vigrahavyāvartanī* verse:
"Like a person at a forked road, who is filled with doubt and takes nothing."
Within the true reality of all phenomena, doubt is likewise thus;
because of doubt, one does not diligently seek the true reality of all phenomena.
This doubt arises from delusion, and it is the most evil among evils.
Within the phenomena of good and evil, birth-and-death, and nirvana, there exists a definitive, real, and true dharma; do not give rise to doubt therein.
If you harbor suspicion or confusion, the jailers of death and rebirth will bind you.
As a lion seizes a deer, one cannot escape;
though there may be doubt while in the world, one should follow the sublime and wholesome Dharma.
Just as when observing a forked road, one should pursue that which is beneficial and excellent.
Furthermore, within the Buddha-dharma,
faith is that which enables entry.
If one lacks faith, [one cannot enter].
Even though they are within the Buddha-dharma,
they ultimately gain nothing.
For various reasons such as these...
One should recognize the fault of doubt and abandon it immediately.
It is asked:
The objects of unwholesome dharmas are immeasurable;
for what reason, then,
does one discard only five dharmas?
The answer is:
Within these five hindrances, the three poisons exist,
with their equal distribution as the fundamental basis.
It also encompasses the eighty-four thousand gates of affliction.
Why is this? The hindrance of sensual desire is itself the poison of greed.
The hindrance of ill will is the poison of hatred;
sleep and doubt—
these two hindrances together constitute the poison of delusion.
It should be understood that the three poisons, restlessness, and the hindrance of remorse arise collectively from the three poisons;
they are thus subsumed within the category of equal proportions (*sabhāga*),
forming together four divisions of afflictions.
Within one [set] there are twenty-one thousand;
within the four [sets], there are a total of eighty-four thousand.
Therefore, one eliminates these five hindrances.
This is precisely the removal of all unwholesome dharmas.
Through such various causes and conditions as these,
the practitioner abandons the five hindrances.
It is like being released from debt,
like recovering from a grave illness,
or like a person suffering from famine reaching a land of plenty.
Just as one who escapes from among enemies and robbers attains personal deliverance, peace, and freedom from affliction,
so it is with the practitioner who eliminates these five hindrances.
Their minds are peaceful, secure,
pure, and blissful.
It is like the sun and moon being obscured by five things.
Just as smoke, clouds, dust, mist, or the hand of the asura Rāhu can obstruct [the sun] so that it cannot shine,
so too is it with people regarding the fourth method for harmonizing the five dharmas.
First, regulating food and drink;
second, regulating sleep;
third, regulating the body.
Fourth is regulating the breath;
fifth is regulating the mind. Why is this so?
Now, let us employ a proximate analogy to illustrate this Dharma.
It is like a worldly potter who,
wishing to fashion various vessels, [prepares his clay].
First, one must skillfully prepare the clay so that it is neither too hard nor too soft;
thereafter, one may proceed to the wheel and cord, just as when playing a lute.
First, one should tune the strings so that they are neither too loose nor too tight;
only then may one proceed to the performance.
It produces various exquisite melodies.
The practitioner’s cultivation of the mind is likewise:
they skillfully harmonize the five matters.
If one ensures that [the body] is harmonious and appropriate,
then samādhi will arise easily;
if there is anything that is not adjusted, [samādhi will not arise].
There are many obstacles and difficulties;
it is hard for roots of goodness to arise.
First, regarding the regulation of food:
Now, the principle of eating is fundamentally intended to sustain the body and advance the Way.
If one eats to excess,
the breath becomes labored and the body feels distended.
If the hundred vessels are not unobstructed,
it will cause the mind to become congested, such that one’s seated meditation is uneasy.
This also occurs if one eats too little.
Consequently, the body becomes emaciated and the mind remains in a state of anxious suspension;
one's mental faculties lack stability.
None of these constitute the way to attain meditative concentration.
Furthermore, if one consumes impure or turbid substances,
it causes the human consciousness to become clouded and deluded; likewise,
if one consumes things that are unsuitable for the body.
Consequently, it will stir up chronic ailments and cause the four elements to fall into disharmony.
This is the very beginning of practicing meditative concentration;
one must be profoundly cautious regarding this.
Therefore it is said: "When the body is at ease, the Way flourishes.
As the Sūtra says:
"In eating and drinking, know moderation."
Always delighting in secluded places,
with a tranquil mind rejoicing in diligence—
this is called the teaching of all Buddhas.
Second, regarding the regulation of sleep:
sleep is a state of being shrouded by the delusion of ignorance;
therefore, although it should not be indulged in recklessly, [it must be regulated].
If one does not sleep at all, the mind and spirit will become vacant and dazed;
if one sleeps too much,
it not only hinders the cultivation of the holy Dharma but also causes one's efforts to be wasted in vain.
It causes the mind to become darkened and the roots of goodness to sink;
one should awaken to impermanence, subdue sloth,
and keep the divine path pure and bright.
When the mind of mindfulness is luminous and pure,
one can thus settle the mind within the sacred realm,
and samādhi will manifest before one.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"During the first watch of the night and the last watch of the night,
do not allow for any neglect."
Do not allow your entire life to pass in vain and yield no attainment on account of sleep;
you should constantly reflect that the fire of impermanence consumes all worlds.
Seek early to deliver yourself;
do not succumb to sleep.
Third, the regulation of the body.
The fourth is the regulation of the breath;
the fifth is the regulation of the mind.
These two should be applied in conjunction.
It cannot be explained separately;
there are merely differences in the methods of the beginning, middle, and end.
Thus, there are distinct characteristics for entering, abiding, and emerging.
Regarding the first point, entering dhyāna to harmonize the three matters:
when a practitioner wishes to enter samādhi,
they must appropriately harmonize the body.
If one is outside of meditative concentration,
whether walking, standing, advancing, or halting, moving,
remaining still, or engaging in activity.
One must examine all things with thorough scrutiny.
If one's actions are coarse and violent,
then the breath will follow suit and become coarse.
Because the vital energy (prāṇa) is coarse,
the mind becomes distracted and difficult to collect;
furthermore, while sitting, it remains agitated and turbid.
The mind will not be at ease; therefore,
even when outside of formal meditative concentration,
one must still apply the mind to proactively cultivate skillful means.
When entering meditation later on,
one must properly settle the body in its appropriate place;
first, upon reaching the meditation seat.
One should remain seated exactly where one sat before,
ensuring at all times that one is secure and comfortable for a long duration without hindrance.
Next, one should properly position the feet.
If sitting in the half-lotus posture, place the left foot upon the right thigh,
drawing it close to the body so that the toes of the left foot are level with the right thigh.
The right toes should be level with the left thigh.
If one wishes to sit in the full lotus posture,
one should then place the right foot, both top and bottom, upon the left foot.
Next, loosen your waistband so that it remains secure and does not slip off while sitting.
Next, you should place your hands [in their proper position].
Place the left palm upon the right hand,
stacking the hands together with palms facing each other,
and rest them firmly upon the left foot.
Drawing [the body] close to oneself,
one should settle the body upright with the mind at its center.
First, one should extend and move the body along with all its limbs and joints.
Perform this seven or eight times,
according to the method for self-massage;
do not cause any injury or strain to the hands or feet.
Having finished, one should straighten the body and keep it upright,
ensuring the spine is aligned;
neither slouching nor stiffening.
Next, straighten the head and neck so that the nose is aligned directly with the navel,
neither leaning to one side nor crooked.
Neither lowering nor raising [the head],
remain balanced and upright.
Next, open the mouth and expel the foul air from within the chest.
Regarding the method of exhaling: open the mouth and release the breath freely.
Visualize that all locations within the body where the hundred vessels are obstructed are completely cleared as they follow the breath outward until exhausted.
Close the mouth and draw the pure breath inward through the nostrils;
do this three times.
If the body and breath become harmonized, [proceed].
A single [breath] is sufficient.
Next, one should close the mouth,
with the lips and teeth merely touching.
Turn the tongue upward toward the palate.
Next, you should close your eyes,
merely enough to cut off external light.
One should sit upright with the body straight,
like a set stone; one must not allow the body,
head, or four limbs to move about or scratch restlessly.
This is the method for initially entering meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to harmonize the body.
To state the essentials:
it is neither too relaxed nor too tense.
This is the sign of bodily composure.
Second, regarding the method for initially entering dhyāna through the regulation of the breath:
there are generally four signs of regulated breathing.
First is wind, second is panting, third is breath, and fourth is respiration.
The first three are signs of lack of regulation;
the last one is the sign of regulation.
What is the characteristic of wind?
When sitting, one perceives a sound as the breath enters and exits through the nostrils.
What is the characteristic of panting?
Although there is no sound while sitting, the inhalation and exhalation are obstructed and do not flow freely;
this is the characteristic of panting.
What are the characteristics of the wind-element?
Although there is no sound when sitting,
it is neither constricted nor obstructed.
Yet their movement in and out is not subtle.
This is called the characteristic of breath (*āśvāsa*). As for the characteristic of respiration (*praśvāsa*):
Without sound, without entanglement, and without coarseness;
his inhalations and exhalations are subtle and continuous, as if present and yet as if absent,
sustaining the spirit in peaceful stability.
The mind feels joyful and content;
this is the sign of cessation.
If one holds onto the breath, it will scatter.
To fixate on the panting leads to entanglement;
to fixate on the vital energy leads to exhaustion;
to fixate on the breath leads to stability.
Furthermore, when sitting, there are three signs such as wind-disorders and so forth;
these are called "lack of composure.
One who applies the mind [should recognize them].
This leads to affliction;
the mind is likewise difficult to stabilize.
If one wishes to harmonize it, [one must apply effort].
One should rely on three methods:
first, settle the mind by lowering it;
second, relax the body.
Third, one visualizes the breath pervading all the pores;
its entry and exit are equally unimpeded.
If one refines the mind, it becomes subtle.
Cause the breath to become subtle and faint.
When the breath is regulated, various afflictions do not arise,
and the mind is easily concentrated.
This is called the method for regulating the breath when a practitioner first enters meditative concentration.
To state the essentials:
it should be neither constricted nor slippery.
This is the characteristic of the breath being regulated.
Regarding the third point, "initially entering meditative absorption to regulate the mind," there are two meanings to regulating the mind.
First, one should subdue distracted thoughts so that they do not wander astray.
Second, one should ensure that sinking and floating, as well as laxity and tension, are brought into their proper balance.
What are the signs of sinking?
If, while sitting, the mind becomes dark and obscured,
one is unable to maintain mindfulness,
and the head tends to droop low.
This is the sign of sinking.
At that time, one should fix the mindfulness on the tip of the nose,
causing the mind to abide within its object.
Do not allow the mind to be distracted;
this can remedy sinking.
What are the signs of floating?
If, while sitting, the mind and spirit wander and fluctuate,
the body will likewise be restless,
and mindfulness will dwell upon external objects.
This is a floating state;
at such a time, one should settle the mind and direct the object of focus downward.
By restraining all distracted thoughts,
the mind becomes settled;
thus, the mind is easily brought to tranquility.
To state the essentials:
neither sinking nor floating is the characteristic of a balanced mind.
Question: Can the mind possess the characteristics of being either expansive or constricted?
Answer: Yes.
There is indeed such a thing.
Regarding those whose minds are agitated,
they seek to attain [concentration] by grasping the mind while seated and employing mindfulness.
Because he entered meditative absorption for this reason,
his breath rose upward,
and his chest was constricted with acute pain.
One should relax the mind and imagine the breath flowing downward;
the ailment will naturally subside.
If the mind has the characteristic of expansiveness, one perceives that the mental will is wandering and dissipated,
and the body feels like a withered snake.
If saliva flows from the mouth or if one becomes darkened by fainting,
at that time one should withdraw the body and apply urgent mindfulness.
One causes the mind to abide within its object,
maintaining the body in a state of composure;
this serves as the remedy.
The mind possesses the characteristics of roughness and smoothness,
which can be understood through investigation.
This constitutes the method for regulating the mind when first entering meditative concentration.
When entering meditative concentration,
one originally proceeds from the coarse to the subtle;
therefore, since the body is already coarse, [one must first master it].
The breath dwells within it;
the mind is the most subtle.
By means of skillful means, one [should practice].
By regulating the coarse and proceeding toward the subtle,
one causes the mind to become tranquil;
this is the initial expedient for entering meditative concentration.
Regarding the second point, the regulation of three matters while seated:
during a single sitting session, regardless of its duration,
one should [regulate these three].
Gathering the mind and applying focused attention,
one should therein skillfully recognize the signs of whether the three factors— the body, the breath, and the mind—
are balanced or unbalanced. Even if, while sitting, the body and mind are initially balanced, [one must remain vigilant].
If the body becomes too loose, too tight, uneven, or crooked, such that its various parts do not rise and fall together,
one should become aware of this and adjust it accordingly to achieve correctness.
One should always remain in a state of tranquility, neither too relaxed nor too strained,
abiding in a state that is level,
straight, and upright. Furthermore, while seated:
Although the body is harmonized,
the vital energies may not be;
as for the signs of their lack of harmony:
As described above,
there may be wheezing or shortness of breath,
and the body feels distended and full.
One should treat it according to the aforementioned methods,
ensuring that the flow of the breath is always subtle and continuous,
as if it were both present and absent.
Furthermore, during a single sitting,
although the body and breath may be regulated,
the mind may at times sink or at times float.
Laxity and urgency cannot coexist.
At that time, if you become aware [of this],
you should employ the previous method to adjust it until it becomes balanced and appropriate.
Regarding these three matters,
one should bring them to proper adjustment according to whatever is untamed, whether before or after.
Within a single sitting,
may the three factors of body, breath, and mind be harmoniously adjusted,
without any mutual discord or deviation.
Harmonious and non-dual;
this can eliminate latent afflictions so that obstacles do not arise.
The path of meditative concentration can be mastered.
Third, when one is about to conclude a session of seated meditation and wishes to emerge from samādhi:
One should first relax the mind from external objects, open the mouth to release the breath,
and imagine the breath dispersing through the hundred vessels according to one's will;
thereafter, move the body very subtly.
Next, move the shoulder blades, as well as the head and neck;
next, move both feet until they are entirely supple.
Thereafter, rub all the pores thoroughly with the hands.
Next, rub the hands together to warm them and cover both eyes;
then, remove the hands and open the eyes.
Only when the heat of the body and the perspiration have somewhat subsided may one enter or exit at will;
if it is not so, [one must remain].
Alternatively, one may attain stability of mind;
since the emergence [of the breath] is already brief and rapid,
the subtle phenomena have not yet dispersed.
Residing within the body,
it causes headaches and stiffens the hundred joints.
It was like the exhaustion from the wind;
later, while sitting,
he became restless and uneasy.
For this reason, the mind does not wish to sit;
one must always be mindful of this.
This is the method for adjusting the body and calming the mind upon emerging from meditative absorption.
Because one emerges from the subtle into the coarse,
this is called skillfully entering, emerging,
and abiding. As a verse says:
In advancing and halting there is a sequence; the coarse and the subtle do not conflict.
It is like a well-trained horse that wishes to go and wishes to stay.
The fifth practice consists of five factors: first, desire; second, diligence; third, mindfulness; fourth, skillful wisdom; and fifth, one-pointed concentration.
Regarding "desire":
when a practitioner first cultivates dhyāna,
they desire to emerge from the realm of desire (kāmadhātu).
Because one desires to attain the first dhyāna,
it is also called "aspiration" (chanda) and also called "vow" (praṇidhāna).
It is also called "joy" because such a person’s inner mind and aspirations take pleasure in various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).
Question:
Does the arising of a longing in the mind occur during the practice of meditation?
This constitutes an obstacle.
How, then, can this be considered a skillful means? The answer is:
as for desire—
It is simply the mind that aspires to and delights in the fulfillment of great vows;
therefore, it is called "desire.
One should not [confuse this] with the time of mental application.
One gives rise to thoughts of longing and conceptualization.
If a longing mind arises,
then it is not serene and still.
If the mind is not serene and still,
then the various samādhis cannot possibly arise.
Second is diligence.
There are two kinds:
first, physical diligence;
second, mental diligence.
If a practitioner can cultivate the twelve dhūtas,
they are fully endowed with physical and mental diligence,
as the Buddha told Kāśyapa:
The araṇya bhikṣu remains detached from the two attachments;
his body and mind are pure, and he practices the dhūtas.
There are twelve matters regarding these dhūtas.
First, dwelling in an araṇya;
second, constantly practicing alms-gathering;
third, practicing sequential alms-gathering.
Fourth, the practice of eating only one meal a day;
fifth, moderation in the quantity of food;
sixth, not drinking liquids after midday.
Seventh, wearing tattered robes;
eighth, possessing only the three robes;
ninth, dwelling among burial mounds.
10. Dwelling under a tree;
11. Sitting in the open air;
12. Constantly sitting without lying down.
These are called the twelve dhūtas,
as clarified in the Dhūta Sūtra. Herein,
the dhūtas should be explained in detail.
It is called "shaking off" (*vidhūnana*),
because it shakes off all unwholesome dharmas of body and mind when practicing dhyāna.
To practice these dharmas is called the practice of heedfulness;
it is to be fully endowed with physical and mental diligence.
One should know that such a person is able to attain the noble fruits of the three vehicles,
let alone worldly meditative concentrations.
Furthermore, for the sake of practicing dhyāna, the practitioner...
Maintaining pure ethical discipline,
he abandons the five hindrances;
during the first and last watches of the night, he applies himself with diligent effort without ceasing.
For example, it is like drilling for fire: one does not stop until it is kindled.
This is called diligence.
As the Buddha told Ānanda:
Because all Buddhas attained supreme enlightenment through single-minded and diligent exertion,
how much more so for other dharmas of the wholesome path?
Regarding the three recollections:
as it is taught in the Mahāyāna,
one recollects the impurity of the desire realm.
Deception is contemptible;
one should regard the first dhyāna as honorable and precious.
This is the same as the sixfold mental application.
It is merely that the names established differ.
Regarding the contemplation of the six aspects:
first, regarding the aversion to the lower realms, suffering, coarseness, and hindrance, these constitute three [aspects].
That is to say, one contemplates desire as impure, deceptive, and contemptible;
and one contemplates the higher, superior, and sublime emergence as threefold— namely,
one contemplates the first dhyāna as honorable and precious.
Now, the explanation of these six dharmas can be understood through two perspectives.
The first is by way of clarifying them in terms of their results.
Second, regarding the explanation by way of cause and effect:
first, explaining by way of the effects in the desire realm,
it says, "to become weary of the suffering, coarseness, and hindrances of the lower [realms]."
Because they feel weary of and loathe the coarse and heavy nature of the inferior form and mind within the desire realm,
the practitioner contemplates:
"I am now experiencing the resultant body of the desire realm."
It is called suffering because one is oppressed by various conditions such as hunger, thirst, cold, heat, illness, pain, knives, and staves.
"Coarse" means that this body is composed of thirty-six impure substances, such as excrement and urine, and is foul-smelling and filthy; therefore, it is called coarse.
It is also called coarse because it is ugly and repulsive.

Regarding "obstruction" (āvaraṇa): this refers to the physical body's material resistance, whereby it lacks autonomy because it is blocked and hindered by mountains, rivers, rocks, and walls; therefore, it is called an obstruction.
Next, this is explained in terms of the fruits of the form realm (rūpadhātu).
Climbing toward victory,
the practitioner contemplates and knows that the bliss of the form realm is supreme.
Just as the pleasure of the desire realm is considered suffering,
the pleasure of the form realm is superior;
because one attains a pleasure that surpasses suffering, it is called "superior excellence."
Those of superior capacity receive a body in the form realm;
like a reflection in a mirror,
although it possesses form and color, [it lacks substantiality].
It is called "sublime" because it is without material obstruction.
As for "emergence," it refers to the attainment of the five supernormal powers.
It penetrates and perceives things beyond obstructions;
because mountains and walls do not hinder it, it is called "emerging.
Second, regarding the six practices within the causal stage:
First, regarding the causes of the desire realm,
to clarify the aversion toward the suffering, coarseness, and hindrances of the lower [realms],
the practitioner contemplates as follows:
If the mental factors arising within the *saṃbhogakāya* take desire as their object,
one will be unable to achieve liberation.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"All sentient beings are called suffering because they are slaves to craving.
As for the coarse [suffering]:
Because they take the five sensory objects of the desire realm as their object and give rise to distraction and evil, they are called "coarse.
As for "obstructing":
Because they are covered by the hindrances of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*), they are called "obstructions.
Next, with respect to the causes of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
it clarifies those who ascend to and emerge from the superior and sublime [states].
The practitioner reflects:
"The superior bliss of the first dhyāna is called 'superior' because it arises from within;
the bliss of sensual desire arises from the external five sense objects."
Afflicted by feverish resentment and enmity,
they regard themselves as inferior and think they are not equal to those who are sublime.
The bliss of meditative concentration is called "sublime" because the mind is settled and unmoving, and the accomplishment of the Dharma brings joy.
As for the bliss of sensual desire:
Because the mind is distracted and agitated, it is called "coarse.
As for "emergence," it means the mind attains liberation from hindrances and obstacles.
Because one reaches the first dhyāna, it is called "emergence.
It is like a spring in a rock that does not come from without,
but wells up spontaneously from within.
Now, based on these six aspects, the meaning of mindfulness (smṛti) is explained;
its intent is evident.
It is asked:
Now, it is said that the disciples of the Buddha practice dhyāna.
Why, then, is the method of the sixfold contemplation for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) explained?
The answer is:
Since it has been explained that the three realms share the same meditative absorption (dhyāna),
one should also understand the causes for their respective practices,
if one is a disciple of the Buddha.
Employing the eight noble lineages,
one gives rise to the contemplation of the sixteen aspects to become free from desire,
and through mindfulness enters the first dhyāna.
Thus, there is no fault.
This shall be explained in detail below in the section clarifying the untainted dhyānas (*anāsrava-dhyāna*).
The four types of skillful wisdom consist in weighing the pleasure of the desire realm against the pleasure of the first dhyāna,
as well as the characteristics of their respective gains, losses, and relative weight.
Now, I shall provide two alternative interpretations.
As for the term "deliberation" (chou-liang),
it is a name for employing wisdom to contemplate and evaluate.
Regarding gain and loss:
the pleasure of the desire realm is loss;
the pleasure of the first dhyāna is gain.
The bliss of the first dhyāna is considered an attainment because it is free from faults;
the bliss of the desire realm is called a loss because it possesses faults.
Alternatively, one may also say that the first dhyāna constitutes a loss [in comparison to higher states].
Regarding the claim that the pleasure of the desire realm is what is attained:
because the pleasure of the desire realm is coarse,
it is reckoned as being real.
Having given rise to a profound state of mind,
one regards the first dhyāna as a loss; thus,
one perceives the body as empty and quiescent.
Because one experiences subtle pleasure as if it were non-existent,
it cannot be definitively grasped.
It is called "loss" because the characteristics of pleasure have been lost.
Regarding "light and heavy," the desire realm is considered light.
The first dhyāna is heavy;
that which belongs to the desire realm is light.
This is because the pleasure obtained through association with the five consciousnesses is rapid and shallow, and is therefore considered light.
The bliss obtained in the first dhyāna is "heavy.
It is called heavy because it is associated with the mental consciousness, persists for a long duration, and has a profound object of focus.
As for "heavy":
It may be considered precious and weighty;
likewise, one may say that the desire realm is heavy while the first dhyāna is light.
The pleasure of the desire realm is called "heavy" because it is accompanied by afflictions and the mind is burdened;
the pleasure of the first dhyāna is called "light" because the burden on the mind is slight.
Next, there is a teacher who speaks of skillful wisdom:
when a practitioner first cultivates dhyāna,
they skillfully recognize the internal and external expedient means.
If one employs it skillfully,
one will not lose what is appropriate; thus,
one quickly attains meditative concentration (dhyāna).
This is called "skillful wisdom.
First, regarding "single-mindedness":
the practitioner has already become well-versed in skillful wisdom.
When one deliberates with focused attention, there is no error;
now, one should simply practice by concentrating the mind on a single object, which is therefore called "one-pointedness of mind" (*ekāgratā*).
It is like a person who wishes to travel.
One must skillfully recognize the signs of whether the road is passable or obstructed;
having gained certain knowledge,
one then proceeds with single-minded focus.
It is said that where there is no wisdom, there is no dhyāna; where there is no dhyāna, there is no wisdom.
This is the meaning [of this teaching].
