In the *Disciple’s Consecration for Re-examining the Preparatory Practices of the Dhyānapāramitā*, Part Six, Section Four: "Internal Preparatory Practices, Lower Section: Clearly Verifying the Nature of Evil Roots," specifically within the section "Verifying the Nature of Evil Roots."
There are four points:
first, clarifying the number of afflictions;
second, clarifying the arousal of the nature of the evil roots.
Third, the presentation of the methods of counteraction;
fourth, the conclusion establishing the *siddhānta* as the comprehensive inclusion of all Buddha-dharma.
Now, I shall explain the first [section]: the quantity of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding "afflictions" (*kleśa*):
the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states,
"Afflictions are precisely unwholesome dharmas."
If one were to discuss unwholesome dharmas exhaustively,
their names and categories would be numerous;
for now, I shall briefly summarize them according to five kinds of unwholesome and evil dharmas.
The opening and closing [of the gates] serve to distinguish quantity.
As for the five kinds of unwholesome dharmas:
the first is unwholesome dharmas consisting of vitarka and vicāra.
1. Unwholesome states of sensual desire; 2.
Unwholesome states of ill will; 3.
Unwholesome states of delusion.
The five evil karmas and unwholesome dharmas,
when expanded, amount to eighty-four thousand; yet,
regarding their roots, they do not exceed the three poisons and the equal portion [of the four afflictions].
If the five unwholesome dharmas are combined and categorized as four divisions of afflictions,
then the three poisons remain their fundamental basis.
These are further divided into three parts,
all of which belong to the causes of habituation— namely, vitarka and vicāra—
and constitute evil karma that obstructs the Path.
These two unwholesome [factors] are combined into one category. Why is this so?
Vitarka and vicāra arise accompanied by the three types of afflictions;
they may also be described as the causes of habituation and the category of equal parts.
Evil karma obstructs the Path.
They belong to the category of retributive causes (vipāka-hetu) and their corresponding factors (sabhāga).
Since the combined discussion of practice and retribution speaks of only one type of corresponding factor,
there are five kinds of unwholesome dharmas.
If one were to speak of them in a general synthesis,
there would be only four parts;
yet, when analyzed in detail, they become eighty-four thousand.
As clarified in the Mahāyāna-śāstra,
the affliction of sensual desire comprises twenty-one thousand varieties.
There are twenty-one thousand afflictions of anger;
there are twenty-one thousand afflictions of delusion.
The afflictions of equal proportion (samabhāga) number twenty-one thousand; the afflictions of the four parts (caturbhāga) likewise number twenty-one thousand.
In total, eighty-four thousand afflictions arise;
the Buddha, in response to these, taught eighty-four thousand Dharma gates.
To treat them, he clarified the Middle Way.
Therefore, we shall distinguish the characteristics of the arising of the nature of the unwholesome roots by means of only five kinds of unwholesome and evil dharmas. Why is this so?
The preceding section clarified the arising of the nature of wholesome roots through fivefold distinctions;
now, the arising of the nature of unwholesome roots is explained.
Is it not the case that this is distinguished not merely by relying on the five unwholesome dharmas?
Herein, medicine and disease correspond to one another,
and their respective characteristics are perfectly balanced.
A practitioner who wishes to cultivate meditative concentration must skillfully discern it.
Second, the clarification of those in whom the nature of the evil roots arises.
When there are practitioners who cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*),
their afflictions and karmic defilements are deep and heavy; thus,
although they may bring the mind to rest and abide in stillness, [they cannot remain long].
As stated above, among all the wholesome dharmas, both internal and external,
not a single thing is brought forth.
It is only through the arousal of afflictions that awakening occurs;
therefore, the nature of the arousal of the unwholesome roots is explained next.
Now, regarding the arousal of unwholesome dharmas:
This is further analyzed by way of five kinds of unwholesome states;
within each of these unwholesome dharmas,
there are three categories respectively.
The thirty-five [factors] constitute fifteen unwholesome dharmas; however,
when discussing the moments when a practitioner gives rise to unwholesomeness,
there is no fixed sequence.
Now, according to the gate of the teachings,
they shall be distinguished in sequence,
as fully detailed in the preceding list.
First, the characteristics of the arousal of vitarka and vicāra are clarified;
these consist of three types.
The first is vitarka and vicāra within a mind that is clear and sharp.
Second, vitarka and vicāra within a mind that is half-awake and half-obscured;
third, vitarka and vicāra within a mind that is entirely deluded and obscured.
Regarding the arising of vitarka and vicāra within a clear and sharp mind:
If a practitioner has not deeply planted roots of goodness in the past,
they will not give rise to any kind of wholesome dharmas at all when practicing meditative concentration.
There are merely vitarka and vicāra that take objects as their focus;
from moment to moment they do not abide within the three poisons,
nor do they have any specific object.
At times it takes greed as its object;
at times it takes hatred as its object;
at times it takes delusion as its object.
Yet the object of focus remains distinct and clearly manifest;
thus it continues even as years and months pass.
Yet one does not give rise to the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
This is the manifestation of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) within a mind that is clear and sharp.
As for the applied and sustained thought within a mind that is half-illuminated and half-obscured:
If, at the time of gathering the mind in mindfulness,
one perceives that the afflictions of vitarka and vicāra do not abide for even a single moment.
However, at the time of following an object of focus,
it may be either clear or dim;
when clear, there is the grasping of applied and sustained thought.
Thought does not abide. When obscured,
it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), vacant and dull,
with nothing perceived or understood.
This is called the sign of the arising of vitarka and vicāra when half-awake and half-obscured.
Third, regarding vitarka and vicāra within a mind that is consistently sunken and obscured:
if a practitioner, at the time of practicing meditative concentration...
Although the mind is darkened as if in sleep,
within that state of profound obscurity,
it still intensely clings to its objects of perception.
When applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) do not abide,
this is called the manifestation of the afflictions of applied and sustained thought within a sunken and obscured mind.
Second, regarding greed and desire:
There are three kinds of signs of arousal:
first, external desire;
second, internal-external desire.
Third, there is greed that pervades all places.
First, regarding the arousal of external greed-afflictions:
when a practitioner is practicing meditative concentration, [if such greed arises...]
A mind of desire arises; if it is a man,
he then takes a woman as his object.
If it is a woman,
she then takes as her object a man,
grasping at his physical appearance and features.
From deportment and speech,
the fetters arise in the mind;
they do not abide for even a single thought-moment.
This is precisely the manifestation of the fetter of external lustful desire.
Second, regarding the manifestation of internal and external afflictions of lustful desire:
if a practitioner, at the time of practicing meditative concentration...
The mind of desire is stirred;
either by taking as its object the physical forms, complexions, postures, and demeanors of external men or women,
it gives rise to greedy attachment.
Or again, they may take as their object their own physical form and appearance,
and by stroking their heads and wiping their necks, they become stained with attachment moment after moment,
giving rise to various forms of craving and lust.
Therefore, it obstructs all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
This is precisely the manifestation of internal and external craving and afflictions (*rāga-kleśa*).
Third, as for the arising of craving and afflictions that pervade all places:
This person is attached to internal and external things as previously described;
furthermore, they give rise to craving and attachment toward all objects of the five sensory realms, material requisites, and possessions.
Or they may crave fields, gardens, houses,
clothing, and drink in all circumstances.
The signs of the arousal of greed;
third, the signs of the arousal of hatred,
which are of three kinds.
First, irrational anger;
second, anger that accords with reason;
third, anger arising from contentious debate.
First, regarding that which arises from anger contrary to reason:
if, while the practitioner is engaged in the cultivation of meditative concentration,
a thought of anger suddenly arises.
Without inquiring whether it is right or wrong,
or whether another has committed an offense or not,
one becomes angry without cause.
This is the manifestation of irrational, perverse anger.
Second, regarding the manifestation of rational, correct anger:
if, at the time of practicing meditative concentration...
An external person actually comes to provoke and disturb one;
with this as a condition, a perception of anger arises and continues without ceasing.
It is also like a person who upholds the precepts seeing one who acts contrary to the Dharma and consequently giving rise to anger; therefore,
it is said in the Mahāyāna:
Within a pure buddha-field,
although there are no perverted three poisons,
there are the three right poisons.
The one currently described as being "rightly angry in accordance with principle" is precisely that person.
As for the anger arising from the three types of disputes:
When a practitioner is practicing meditation,
they become attached to the teachings they themselves understand as being correct,
while regarding what others practice and what they say as being wrong.
They all considered it incorrect;
since it was the teaching of outsiders,
it did not accord with their own sentiments.
Thereupon, a mind of vexation arises.
In the world, there are people who,
even when their wealth and silks are encroached upon, [do not become resentful].
Even if one can endure a small amount of contentious reasoning,
one immediately gives rise to great resentment.
When wind and horse do not meet,
this is called the manifestation of anger arising from contentious debate.
Fourth, the manifestation of delusion arising.
There are three types:
first, reckoning [things] as eternal or annihilated;
second, reckoning [them] as existent or non-existent.
Third, calculating the nature of the world.
These three are all attachments to various false views;
they do not lead out of birth and death.
Therefore, they are collectively termed "delusion.
First, regarding the delusion that calculates [the self] as either annihilated or eternal:
while the practitioner is engaged in the cultivation of meditative concentration...
Suddenly, he gave rise to a wrong thought and,
with a calculating mind, discriminated:
"Did my past self and all phenomena cease to exist so that my present self and all phenomena now come to be?"
Thinking that it must exist because it does not cease,
he reflects on this and,
upon seeing the mind, immediately begins to investigate the three periods of time.
If one claims that cessation is equivalent to falling into annihilationism,
or if one claims that non-cessation is equivalent to falling into eternalism—
such is deluded cognition.
Moment by moment they do not abide;
therefore, their sharp intelligence is swift and agile,
and their eloquence is unimpeded, free from contention, rivalry, and frivolous proliferation.
Committing various evil deeds that can obstruct the supramundane Dharma of right concentration—
this is the manifestation arising from the delusion of reckoning things as either annihilated or eternal.
Second, regarding those whose delusion arises from calculating existence and non-existence:
while practicing meditative concentration,
they suddenly engage in conceptual discrimination.
One contemplates vitarka and vicāra, thinking:
"Are the self, the aggregates, and all other phenomena definitively existent?
Or are they definitively non-existent?"
"Even up to [the view that it is] neither existent nor non-existent.
As one investigates in this manner, the mind immediately arises;
following that perception, attachment is produced.
He considers this to be a fixed, real, and false awakening that does not abide for even a single moment;
because of this, his wisdom becomes sharp and swift.
Through frivolous discourse and contentious strife,
they give rise to various wrong practices,
which obstruct right concentration.
One must not give rise to [such views].
This is the mark of the delusion that gives rise to the calculation of existence and non-existence.
Third, the delusion that gives rise to the calculation of the nature of the world:
Furthermore, while practicing meditative concentration,
he suddenly had this thought:
"Because there are subtle particles, there must consequently be real dharmas."
Because there are real dharmas,
the four great elements exist;
because the four great elements exist, [the body exists].
Yet there are conventional designations for sentient beings and various worlds.
Reflecting in this way,
the vision of the mind immediately arises.
Moment by moment they do not abide;
by means of this sharp intelligence and eloquence,
they are able to question and to explain.
Arrogant in mind and self-exalting,
they engage in disputes over right and wrong and practice exclusively in deviant ways.
It departs from the true path;
even the conceptualization and discrimination of a single moment of mind is likewise so.
For these reasons,
they are unable to give rise to various meditative absorptions; even if they were to give rise to meditative absorptions, [they would not abide in them].
Falling into the group of those fixed in error;
this is the sign of the arising of delusion regarding the nature of the world.
The five types of ignorance and evil karma are the signs of the arising of obstacles to the Path.
There are also three kinds:
first, the hindrance of dullness, torpor, and obscuration;
second, the hindrance of evil thoughts and reflections.
Third is the obstacle of oppressive sensory objects.
First, regarding the obstacle of dullness, torpor, and obscuration:
when a practitioner is engaged in the cultivation of meditative concentration...
When one attempts to apply the mind,
it immediately becomes sunken, dull, and obscured by sleep;
it remains in a state of indeterminate mental blankness and vacant staring.
There is no distinct cognition;
it obstructs all meditative concentrations,
preventing them from being developed.
This is the sign of the hindrance of being submerged in darkness and obscured by ignorance.
Second is the hindrance of evil thoughts and reflections:
when a practitioner wishes to cultivate meditative concentration, [if...]
Although one is not sunk in dullness,
darkness, or sleep, evil thoughts arise in the mind;
one may think of committing the ten unwholesome deeds, the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, violating the prohibitions, or returning to secular life.
Without ceasing for even a moment,
they thereby obstruct all meditative concentrations (dhyāna-samādhi),
preventing them from being developed.
This is the sign of the obstruction caused by the arousal of evil thoughts and reflections. Regarding the third, the obstruction of being oppressed by external objects:
if a practitioner, at the time of cultivating meditative concentration, [encounters] even though there is no superior matter...
Yet at times the body may suddenly experience pain,
feeling as though it is being oppressed,
and perceiving various external objects.
Some see themselves headless, lacking hands, feet, or eyes;
some see their clothing torn and ruined;
others see themselves sinking into the earth.
Alternatively, fire may come and burn their bodies;
or they may see high cliffs from which they fall;
or they may be obstructed by two mountains standing apart.
Rākṣasas, tigers, and wolves,
or perhaps one may see various evil omens in dreams;
such matters are all the arising of obstacles and transgressions that oppress the practitioner.
Or they cause them to be terrified,
or at times to suffer distress;
such are these various kinds [of experiences].
It cannot be fully explained.
This is called the sign of the arousal of obstacles through the pressure of the objective sphere (*ālambana*).
Now, based on these five unwholesome factors:
These are combined to form the three obstacles. The aforementioned three poisons constitute the habitual causes;

among the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the equal-parts obstacles (*vibhāga-āvaraṇa*), they are the factors of discursive thought and investigation (*vitarka-vicāra*) that cause distraction.
Because these are the coarse four aggregates,
they are called "obstructions of retribution.
These are the three types of obstructions to the Path.
This constitutes a karmic obstruction.
How is this known?
It is because of the evil deeds committed in the past.
One will subsequently have to undergo an evil retribution;
thus, one maintains this evil through karma.
If a practitioner, during the interval before that retribution has been received, [encounters such circumstances...]
However, for one who cultivates goodness,
good and evil are at odds;
thus, karma arises in support of evil.
Because they come to obstruct what is wholesome,
it is known that these are precisely karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*).
Such are the three obstructions.
They obstruct the meditative concentration and wisdom of all practitioners,
preventing them from being developed;
therefore, they are called "obstructions."
Third, explaining the method of the antidote:
"antidote" (pratipakṣa) refers to that which opposes;
it is called an antidote because it counteracts [the afflictions].
Just as the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) is called "antidote" because it primarily treats lustful desire,
so it is likewise for everything up to the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti), meditative concentration (samādhi), and so forth.
This primarily treats the obstruction of the path caused by evil karma.
Now, within the explanation of its remedies,
there are six distinct points of meaning.
First is counteractive treatment;
second is transformative treatment;
third is non-transformative treatment.
Fourth is simultaneous treatment;
fifth is simultaneous transformation;
and sixth is simultaneous non-transformation treatment.
Sixth is "non-confrontation.
Regarding the statement that it is neither transformative nor comprehensive, but rather clarifies a single confrontation:
among the aforementioned natures of the roots of goodness and evil that arise, [this refers to the latter].
It is named "the fifteenth.
Now, within this counteractive measure (*pratipakṣa*) as well,
there are likewise fifteen.
Question: Is this not unnecessarily prolix?
Answer: It is not so.
The former was taught for the purpose of providing verification;
the present is taught for the purpose of providing an antidote.
The former was taught with reference to the spontaneous arising of the roots of goodness.
This is now taught for the sake of cultivation;
it is not redundant.
First, it clarifies the many afflictions of those who engage in discursive thought and investigation (*vitarka-vicāra*).
As it is said in the sutras:
for those with an abundance of vitarka and vicāra,
one should instruct them to practice counting the breaths.
Now, since there are three types of the affliction of vitarka and vicāra,
breath serves as their antidote.
This also consists of three points.
First, regarding the practitioner who possesses a sharp mind and engages in vitarka and vicāra while seated in meditation:
When the sharp and discerning mind clings to objects and does not abide for even a single thought-moment,
one should instruct them to practice counting the breaths.
Why is this? Because in the method of counting the breaths,
one binds the mind so that it remains fixed upon the breath.
Breath is the excellent medicine for curing disorder.
If one can proceed from one to ten without losing mindfulness in the interim, [the mind will be stilled].
One will certainly attain entry into meditative concentration and be able to destroy distracted thoughts;
this is the method of counting the breaths.
Within a mind that is settled and discerning,
one counts while maintaining that settled and discerning state;
this can remedy dullness and bring about clarity and sharpness.
Therefore, counting the breath can eliminate the disease of discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) within a clear and sharp mind.
Second, to treat those whose discursive thought is half-clear and half-obscured:
the characteristics of the disease are as previously explained.
Now, as for the method of counteracting this,
one should instruct them to follow the breath,
following its inhalation and exhalation.
Then the mind always relies upon the breath.
Because it relies upon the breath,
when the breath is coarse, the mind is likewise coarse.
The mind is also subtle;
as the subtle breath enters and exits,
one continues to direct the mind toward it as its object.
One is able to break through vitarka and vicāra;
the mind becomes tranquil and luminously discerning,
knowing the inhalation and exhalation of the breath.
Long and short, departing and abiding—
illumination and function are distinct,
capable of shattering dullness and torpor.
Therefore, it is said that one must follow [the breath].
This is to remedy the fault of succumbing to dullness that occurs if one merely counts the breaths.
If one observes only the breath,
there will still be the faults of floating and distraction;
this is not called a skillful antidote.
Regarding the application of vitarka and vicāra within a mind that is drowsy and lethargic:
the characteristics of the arising of vitarka and vicāra are as previously explained.
As for the remedial method,
one should instruct them to observe the breath;
when the breath enters, [observe it].
Contemplate closely from where this breath comes;
through what path it travels in between, and to what place it enters and abides.
The same applies to the breath exhaled from the mouth.
This dharma shall be explained in detail later.
Thus seeking its source,
it emerges without dispersal.
Entering into non-accumulation,
one does not perceive fixed conceptions;
as the luminous mind contemplates and observes, the eye of the mind immediately opens.
It destroys dullness and torpor;
by settling the mind upon the breath,
one can overcome distraction.
Therefore, one uses the observation of the breath (*ānāpānasmṛti*) as an antidote to the maladies of dullness, torpor, and discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
Second, it clarifies the treatment for the prevalent malady of sensual desire,
as stated in the Sūtras.
Regarding those with a predominance of greed,
the teaching of the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) is provided; since there are three types of the disease of desire,
the remedies are likewise intended to be threefold.
First, for those who are excessively attached to external objects,

when illness arises, it originates from attachment to the characteristics of external sensory realms, such as the physical beauty, postures, speech, deportment, and tactile qualities of men and women.
Therefore, the fire of lust blazes unceasingly;
as an antidote, one should be instructed to practice the contemplation of the nine notions (navasaṃjñā).
If one goes to a cemetery to observe the characteristics of a corpse,
one should also carefully contemplate the objects of attraction as they lie prostrate upon the ground.
One contemplates a corpse that is bloated and putrefied,
with pus and blood flowing out,
and excrement and urine.
Just as those insects devour [the corpse],
so too is it with that which I now wear.
"What is there to find attractive?
Having made this observation,
the lustful mind naturally subsides.
Therefore, the nine contemplations (*navasaṃjñā*) can cure the grave illness of lustful attachment to external objects.
The second [set] cures the afflictions of internal and external desire.
The manifestation of these afflictions is as previously described.
If one wishes to treat this,
one should be taught to practice the contemplations of the first liberation (*prathama-vimokṣa*) and so forth,
carefully observing the internal body as impure, decaying, and loathsome.
One should immediately break through attachment to internal objects;
then, as before, one should contemplate the foulness and loathsomeness of external objects, thereby becoming detached from craving for external realms.
This is the first liberation (*vimokṣa*).
By means of this mind of impurity, one contemplates internal and external forms,
thereby being able to destroy the diseases of internal and external attachment and lustful desire.
Regarding those who give rise to craving toward all places:
the signs of the manifestation of this disease of craving are as previously explained.
As for the method of treatment, one should instruct them to practice the contemplation of universal impurity (*mahā-aśubha-bhāvanā*) directed toward all places.
Contemplate all objects—men, women, one's own body, the bodies of others, fields, gardens, houses, clothing, food, drink, and everything that exists in the world—and see them all as impure;
there is not a single place where a mind of craving could arise.
At that time, when one gives rise to a mind of weary detachment toward all things,
then all covetous desires [cease].
There is no further place for it to arise;
this is called the remedy for the disease of desire in all places.
Furthermore, there are three types of the disease of abundant ill-will.
As it is said in the sutras:
for those with an abundance of hatred,
one teaches the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) as the remedy for the disease of anger.
Since there are three types [of afflictions],
their remedies are likewise threefold.
The first clarifies the remedy for those who harbor wrong anger.
Day and night, one should contemplate within the mind the irrational desire to afflict others with evil deeds, which is the manifestation of the arising of anger.

This should be treated as previously explained; one should cause [the practitioner] to cultivate compassion directed toward sentient beings by taking a loved one who has attained happiness as the object.
Entering meditative absorption by means of this,
one sees that while one's own kin obtain happiness,
one causes all enemies and others as well to obtain happiness.
By apprehending the signs of others' happiness,
one is able to give rise to affectionate regard;
this immediately destroys the mind of malice, resentment, and harmful intent toward sentient beings.
Second, to correctly subdue anger:
if one has no anger whatsoever toward other matters, [one is subduing it].
One merely sees others committing evil or violating the precepts,
whereby the symptoms of the arising of the mental affliction of anger manifest,
as fully described previously.
To remedy this, one should practice according to the teachings:
through the contemplation of the dharma-conditioned compassion, one observes that the five aggregates are empty and false,
and thus does not perceive the existence of sentient beings.
How could there be matters of observing or violating precepts, or of right and wrong?
It is simply because one takes the Dharma-joy within all those vows and bestows it upon others.
With a mind of loving-kindness and affection,
one should not inflict further affliction;
thus, both right and wrong are extinguished.
The mind of hatred subsides of its own accord.
This is practicing the compassion based on the conditions of dharmas (*dharmālambana-maitrī*), which can cure the disease of hatred that follows from adherence to principles.
Furthermore, as for those who hate because they engage in disputes regarding all dharmas, [this same practice serves as the remedy].
When the illness arises as previously described,
the remedial method is that one should be instructed to cultivate objectless compassion (*apraṇihitā maitrī*).
Why is this? Because this person, regarding whatever dharma they have attained,
considers it to be correct.
That is to say, one regards others as being not oneself;
one rejoices in those who agree with oneself and feels anger toward those who oppose oneself.
They may give rise to attachments within the four propositions or beyond the four propositions;
or they may further cling to the Middle Way.
In all such cases, there is something upon which they rely.
Therefore, when there is contention and attachment to causal conditions,
thoughts of anger arise.
This is the method for its antidote.
This causes one to cultivate objectless compassion.
When practicing this compassion,
the path of speech is cut off.
The sphere of mental activity ceases;
regarding all phenomena,
one neither recollects nor attends to them.
If there is no recollection,
for what reason would disputes give rise to a mind of anger?
Great compassion is impartial.
It bestows the joy of original purity;
because it is free from the characteristic of harming others,
it is called "loving-kindness" (maitrī), which is able to bestow joy.
It may also be said that when a bodhisattva teaches such a Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings,
it is called "great compassion. One should know that this constitutes the cultivation of unconditioned compassion (*nirālambana-maitrī*).
It serves as the antidote to contention and malice regarding all phenomena.
The fourth clarifies ignorance and manifold afflictions,
as stated in the sūtras.
For those with a preponderance of delusion,
teach the contemplation of causes and conditions. He asks:
The dharma of causes and conditions is profoundly deep in meaning.
How is it that foolish people [fail to understand it]?
He was instructed to contemplate causes and conditions.
He replied:
"As for what is called ignorance,"
This does not mean they are like oxen or sheep; rather, it refers to those who,
though human, intelligent, and of sharp faculties,
fail to attain right wisdom through their analytical deliberations.
To grasp the principle with a distorted mind is called the folly of ignorance;
since this disease of ignorance exists in three forms.
The remedies should also be established as threefold:
first, to treat those who are deluded by the diseases of eternalism and nihilism and who cling through false conceptualization.
Either the view of eternalism arises,
or the view of nihilism arises,
whereby one then destroys the principle of cause and effect.
The characteristics of the illness are as previously explained.
As for the method of remediation,
one should be instructed to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination throughout the three periods of time.
There are two in the past,
eight in the present,
and two in the future.
These are the twelve links of dependent origination.
They are causally conditioned across the three periods of time;
they are neither eternal nor subject to annihilation.
As stated in a verse of the sutra:
"In my true Buddha-dharma, although all things are empty, they are not severed;
their continuity is neither eternal nor subject to annihilation, and thus good and evil deeds are never lost."
If a practitioner can skillfully contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination and does not cling to the views of annihilationism or eternalism,
then the mind of false views will cease.
One may also employ this as an antidote to destroy the delusions of the conventional continuity.
Second, it clarifies the treatment for those in whom the disease of delusion regarding existence and non-existence has arisen.
Erroneous conceptualization,
such as [the notions of] self and non-self,
or the existence and non-existence of the aggregates (skandha), and so forth.
As previously stated,
regarding the establishment of the antidote,
one should be instructed to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination as karmic fruition.
Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination as karmic fruition:
observing the present stage of the kalala is termed ignorance.
Up to birth, old age, death, and so forth—
these are presently constituted by the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements;
all arise from causes and conditions.
At this stage of the kalala, there are three things:
first, life; second, warmth; and third, consciousness.
Therefore, it is called ignorance.
Since this arises from conditions,
it possesses no intrinsic nature.
It cannot be said to exist,
nor can it be said not to exist;
this applies even unto old age and death.
If one knows that it is neither empty nor existent,
one immediately destroys the dualistic views of emptiness and existence;
one should know this to be the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination regarding karmic retribution.
This immediately treats the illness of views regarding existence and non-existence;
now, one may likewise employ this as an antidote to destroy the delusion that clings to causes as being real.
Those who are deluded regarding the nature of the triple world,
if they perceive that the subtle nature can give rise to the myriad phenomena, [will attain realization].
Such wrong reflection is called "reckoning the nature of the world," as explained in detail previously.
The remedial method is to again practice the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination in a single thought-moment. Why is this?
The practitioner deeply contemplates that within a single thought-moment, the twelve are fully present:
the one is not the twelve,
and the twelve are not the one.
Now, when one is discussed in terms of twelve,
and twelve are discussed in terms of one,
one should know that "one" has no fixed nature.
Because there is no fixed singularity,
the nature of the world cannot be apprehended; therefore,
one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination within a single thought-moment.
This contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination within a single thought-moment shatters the deluded ignorance that clings to the nature of the world;
it primarily destroys the views that cling to identity and difference.
Now, one likewise attains the ability to use this to shatter the delusions of mutual dependence and provisional existence.
Fifth, it clarifies that evil karma obstructs the Path and causes many illnesses,
as stated in the Sūtras.
Regarding those who obstruct the Path,
one should instruct them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
Now, since there are three types of such obstructions to the Path, [one must address each accordingly].
The remedies are likewise established as three.
First, to clarify the emergence of obstacles such as depression, dullness, darkness, and obstruction;
the characteristics of the disease of evil karma are as previously explained.
As an antidote, one should be instructed to contemplate any one of the thirty-two marks of a response-body Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*),
or first take up the mark of the white tuft of hair between the Buddha’s eyebrows and contemplate it with eyes closed.
If the mind is dull and dark,
and one cannot achieve success through remote practice,
one should instead face a beautiful and dignified image.
Single-mindedly grasp the signs and,
taking them as objects, enter meditative concentration.
If [the signs] are not clear, [one should continue to cultivate].
He immediately opened his eyes and observed again,
then closed them once more;
in this manner, he grasped a single sign with clarity.
Successively and universally contemplate the characteristics of all phenomena,
causing the eye of the mind to open and become clear,
thereby immediately shattering the heart of昏睡 (drowsiness) and 沈闇 (deep darkness).
The merit of recollecting the Buddha eliminates karmic obstructions.
A question is asked:
"If one grasps its characteristics with clarity,"
One asks: "Since this can destroy dullness and delusion, why not practice the nine contemplations, such as that of the white bones?
The answer is:
The nine perceptions and the perception of white bones concern only the impure body of birth and death;
because their meaning of eliminating transgressions is inferior, they are not antidotes.
Second, regarding the obstacle of evil thoughts and reflections:
the obstruction arises as previously described.
As an antidote, one should be instructed to recollect the merits of the Buddha.
What is mindfulness?

It is the mind of right mindfulness that takes as its object the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, eighteen unique qualities, and all-knowledge; it is the constant, tranquil, and immovable illumination of the dharma-realm, the manifestation of the form-body everywhere, and the immeasurable, inconceivable merit of benefiting all beings.
When one reflects in this way,
it is itself the antidote. Why is that?
This merit of mindfulness of the Buddha arises from the mental factors produced within the superior wholesome dharmas that serve as its conditions;
it is not born of evil thoughts or reflections.
From conditions, mental factors arise from unwholesome dharmas;
because they are well able to destroy evil,
one should mindfully repay the Buddha.
For example, it is like an ugly person of little wisdom who feels self-contempt and shame when in the company of those who are handsome and of great wisdom.
Evil is likewise:
when one abides in a virtuous mind,
shame and remorse naturally cease.
By virtue of the Buddha’s merit,
within every moment of thought,
all obstacles are extinguished.
Regarding the obstacle of the pressure of the state of the *samadhi* (sandwich):
the signs of the arising of sinful karma are as described above.
As for the remedial method:
One should be taught to recollect the Dharma-Buddha.
The Dharma-Buddha is precisely the equality of the dharma-nature (dharmatā).
Neither arising nor ceasing;
devoid of form or color;
empty, quiescent, and unconditioned.
Within the unconditioned,
since there are no objective realms,
what could possibly be the characteristic of oppression?
Because one knows that the objective sphere is empty,
this is itself the antidote.
If one contemplates the thirty-two marks [of a Great Man], [this is likewise the antidote].
This is not an antidote.
Why? Because even before such a person perceives the signs, they have already been disturbed by the objects of experience.
Furthermore, those who again grasp at signs will for the most part fall under the influence of Māra due to this,
and their minds will become deranged and chaotic.
Now, by contemplating emptiness, one breaks through all objective realms;
to maintain the mind in mindfulness of the Buddha brings immeasurable merit.
This immediately extinguishes grave offenses;
this serves as the antidote,
as can be seen from its meaning.
The brief explanation of the remedies for counteracting [afflictions] is concluded.
Second, regarding the clarification of transformative counteraction,
it is explained in the *Mahāyāna-śāstra* within the section on the "Purity and Impurity of the Wisdom of Concentrated Power" among the elucidations of the ten powers.
That treatise states:
"For a person who possesses lustful desire,
teach the cultivation of a mind of loving-kindness."
One who has much anger should practice the contemplation of impurity; one with much delusion [should practice the contemplation of dependent origination].
When the mind is distracted by thoughts of finitude or infinity,
one is instructed to employ wisdom to discern [the truth].
Among those who have no mind,
he teaches them to collect their minds.
If it is thus, [then...]
This is called "transformative treatment.
If it is not so, it is called "non-transformative treatment."
This serves as a rebuttal to what was stated above.
Now it is clarified that there are two kinds of transformative treatment:
first, the transformation of the illness and the simultaneous transformation of the remedy.
Second, while the illness does not change, the dharma changes.
Now, based on the first of these contemplations,
the meaning of transformative treatment is clarified.
Regarding the aforementioned antidotes for treatment:
for those in whom greed is predominant,
one is instructed to contemplate impurity.
Once the contemplation of the mind is accomplished,
one perceives impurity and develops a sense of weary aversion toward the objects before one.
He then gave rise to a mind of anger.
For example, when the Buddha was in the world,
there were certain bhikṣus.
When practicing the meditation on impurity,
if one succeeds, they may look upon others and wish to harm themselves;
such are the types [of practitioners].
One should instruct them to practice the cultivation of loving-kindness by shifting their focus,
in order to remedy anger;
this is called "remediation through shifting."
This is the simultaneous application of medicine and disease.
One who speaks thus should examine and investigate this matter with subtle discernment.
This still does not accord with the intent of the teaching.
Second, regarding the case where the illness does not change while the medicine changes:
the illness of greed does not change, yet one employs the previously mentioned contemplation of impurity as the medicine.
Cultivate the contemplation of loving-kindness as the remedy.
Question: Regarding the nature of the mind of greed, [how is it treated]?
One perceives the favorable marks of others;
compassion likewise perceives the favorable marks of others.
What is the remedy for this?
The answer is:
The Bodhisattva precepts contain explicit texts stating that all men [are to be regarded as fathers].
All are my fathers;
all women are my mothers.
Yet this bodhisattva does not give rise to compassion;
he engages in unrestrained sexual misconduct and does not avoid his six relations.
Regarding the commission of a *pārājika* offense:
if one contemplates the persons before one— whether male or female— as being like one's father, mother, or child,
then a sense of self-respect and affection will arise.
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can destroy covetousness.
For example, parents never give rise to unrighteous thoughts toward their children.
Furthermore, loving-kindness is defined as bestowing happiness upon others.
Covetousness is unwholesome;
it increases the afflictions of others.
This is not the path to bringing happiness.
Reflecting in this way,
he binds his mind and cultivates loving-kindness.
When the meditative concentration of loving-kindness arises, [he enters it].
One immediately remedies covetousness. Why is this?
The immeasurable mind is a dharma of the form realm.
One should not allow a mind of greed to arise.
Thus, although the illness does not change,
one changes one's perspective to treat it.
Now, by classifying them through the single gateway of impurity,
one can understand that the remaining fourteen gateways of dhyāna all possess the dual sense of transformative cultivation.
Furthermore, there are two types of transformation in contemplation:
first, the transformation of the mind while the object remains untransformed;
second, the simultaneous transformation of both mind and object.
One may clearly discern its meaning by carefully investigating it for oneself.
The third [section], which clarifies non-reversing treatment,
also has two intended meanings.
First, the illness does not shift and the contemplation does not shift;
second, the illness shifts while the contemplation does not shift.
Regarding the first, where the illness does not shift and the contemplation does not shift:
It is like a person with a lustful mind who practices the contemplation of impurity;
yet their lust does not cease,
and they further increase their mental conceptions while performing the contemplation.
There is no need to shift one's observation;
rather, one should further cultivate the visualization of pus, blood, and putrefaction until it is complete for a single person. Do not cease until this is accomplished.
Furthermore, they become many people;
in this manner, even down to a single city or a single village,
they all become impure.
As explained in detail in the *Dhyāna-sūtra*,
one enters into treatments such as the "flowing light of white bones" (*śvetāsthi-prabhā-saṃkrānti*);
because the mind of greed is thereby pacified, it is called the "treatment of non-reversion."
Although this principle exists, if one examines it further, I fear it may still not be the primary intent of the teaching.
Regarding the two illnesses: the observation shifts while the treatment does not shift.
When a practitioner has the affliction of desire,
they apply the contemplation of impurity as an antidote;
yet, as desire subsides, hatred arises.
At that time, without turning away from the contemplation of impurity,
one increases the perception within that very impurity;
thus performing the contemplation of impurity and the visualization of white bones emitting light, one enters meditative absorption.
The mind of anger is naturally eliminated.
This also constitutes two meanings:
first, while the object does not shift, the mind shifts.
Regarding the second [category], when the object does not shift, the mind likewise neither shifts nor does it fail to shift.
The same principle applies to the remaining fourteen pairs of antidotes and their meanings of non-shifting.
The fourth [section] clarifies those that serve as combined antidotes.
This is also found in the *Mahāyāna-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Vehicle), in the section explaining the "eight thoughts of renunciation.
That treatise states:
"As for the Bodhisattva’s gift of Dharma..."
By means of the causes and conditions of the gift of Dharma,
they may either preach the Dharma or manifest supernatural powers.
Or again, they may emit light;
such acts of benefiting and liberating sentient beings are called the gift of Dharma.
Furthermore, one who practices the gift of Dharma should skillfully discern the extent of sentient beings' afflictions;
perhaps they have only a single affliction as their ailment.
Sometimes two are mixed together,
or three are mixed together;
if a single affliction is present, it is treated with a single remedy.
When two factors are combined, it is taught that they are treated by means of two methods;
when three factors are combined, it is taught that they are treated by means of three methods.
This constitutes the characteristic of combined treatment.
When there is one illness, one method of treatment is taught,
as previously explained.
When there are two illnesses, two methods of treatment are taught.
If there is the disease of desire and,
furthermore, the disease of anger,
one should treat them together with the contemplations of impurity and loving-kindness.
Why is this? If one employs only a single dharma,
although it may treat one side in a partial manner, [it will not suffice].
To further increase one side would constitute a fault;
now, these two dharmas are mutually complementary.
Then all illnesses will be cured.
One may practice impurity meditation combined with loving-kindness,
or loving-kindness combined with impurity meditation.
Now, one should act according to the illness,
weighing matters by their underlying meaning,
and combining three or four [factors] as appropriate.
Up to the five categories,
all possess their respective meanings;
they are not explained in full here.

The fourth section clarifies the methods for treating illness.
Once the practitioner has settled the mind to cultivate the Way,

Now, regarding the method of sitting in meditation:
if one can skillfully apply the mind,

They will naturally subside. However,

Although there are many ways in which illness arises, [the following shall be explained].
Briefly stated, there are no more than three types:
first, the symptoms of illness arising from the agitation of the four great elements;
second, illnesses arising from the five viscera.
Third, among the five faculties, there are illnesses.
To briefly explain the illnesses of the four great elements:
it is because the earth element has increased excessively.
Swelling, knots, heaviness, and emaciation of the body—
hundreds and one such ailments arise because of the increase of the water element.
Phlegm and mucus cause distension and fullness;
food is not digested;
there is abdominal pain and diarrhea, and so forth.
One hundred and one ailments arise because the fire element increases: the body is parched,
there is chills and high fever, all the limbs and joints ache, the mouth loses its relish, and the large and small excretions are not passed with ease.
One hundred and one ailments arise because the wind element has increased:
the body becomes suspended in emptiness, trembles, suffers from pain, cramps, vomiting, and labored breathing.
In this way, one hundred and one ailments arise.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"If even one of the great elements is disharmonious..."
There are one hundred and one afflictions of disease;
when the four great elements are out of harmony,
the four hundred and four diseases arise simultaneously, and the maladies of the four great elements manifest.
Each has its own specific appearance;
one should examine them while sitting in meditation or within dreams.
These signs are numerous.
It cannot be recorded in full.
Second, the signs of the illnesses arising from the five viscera are explained.
Regarding those illnesses arising from the heart:
There is frequent physical coldness, fever, dryness of the mouth, and so forth;
this is because the heart governs the mouth.
As for those who suffer from ailments arising from the lungs:
The body frequently experiences distension and fullness, with pain and distress in the four limbs, nasal congestion, and so forth;
this is because the lungs govern the nose.
Those whose afflictions arise from the liver often experience excessive grief, sorrow, lack of joy, lamentation, anxiety, anger, headaches, eye pain, and blurred vision.
Because the liver governs the eyes,

those who contract this disease from the spleen experience a wandering wind throughout their bodies and faces, resulting in a pricking sensation, itching, dizziness, pain, and a loss of appetite for food.
Because the spleen governs the tongue,
those whose illness arises from the kidneys may experience constriction and obstruction in the throat, abdominal distension, and fullness in the ears.
Because the kidneys govern the ears,
the five viscera give rise to many ailments,
each having its own specific signs.

its various signs are numerous and manifold,

Regarding what are called the six kinds of breaths and the twelve kinds of breaths:

Increase cures depletion;
cessation cures increase.

Skillfully employing this breath—

He asked:
"If one applies the mind while sitting in meditation to treat illness, will it necessarily be effective?"
The answer is:
If one possesses ten qualities,
there will be nothing that is not beneficial.
The ten dharmas are:
first, faith;
second, application.
Third, diligence;
fourth, constant abiding within conditions;
fifth, the specific arising of causes and conditions.
Sixth is skillful means;
seventh is long-term practice;
eighth is knowing what to adopt and what to discard.
Ninth, skillfully providing protection;
tenth, recognizing obstructions.
What is meant by faith?
This means having faith that this dharma will certainly be able to cure the illness.
What is meant by "application"?
This means using it at the appropriate times as required.
What is meant by "diligence"?
It is the application of effort with single-minded concentration, without ceasing or grasping.
The attainment of perspiration is the measure of completion.
What is meant by "abiding constantly within the conditions"?
It refers to the subtle mind in every moment of thought.
One should act in accordance with the Dharma without distraction.
What is meant by the arising of specific causes?
The arising of specific causes is as explained above.
What is meant by skillful means?
It refers to the mastery of exhaling, inhaling, directing the mind,
and forming mental images.
One does not lose what is appropriate.
What is meant by "long-term practice"?
It refers to when its application does not immediately yield benefit.
Without reckoning days or months,
one constantly practices without ceasing.
What is meant by "knowing what to adopt and what to discard"?
That is to say, knowing what is beneficial, one exerts effort;
knowing what is detrimental, one abandons it.
Gradually transforming the mind, one takes up that which is wholesome.
What is meant by "knowing how to guard"?
It means being clearly aware of the transgressions and violations that arise from various conditions.
What is meant by "obstructing and warding off"?
That is to say: when one has gained benefit, one does not speak of it to others;
when one has not suffered loss, one does not harbor doubt or slander.
If one relies on these ten dharmas as the means to counteract [the opposing faults], [one shall attain success].
It will certainly be effective.
Next, regarding the fivefold elucidation of the deeds of Māra:
*Māra* is translated in the Qin language as "the Slayer."
Because he robs practitioners of the wealth of their merit and kills the life-force of wisdom, he is named Māra.
What is meant by "the deeds of Māra"?
Just as the Buddha takes it as his task to deliver sentient beings through merit and wisdom and lead them into nirvana.
Māra is likewise;
it is his constant business to destroy the roots of goodness in sentient beings and cause them to wander through the cycle of birth and death.
If one can settle the mind within the gateway of the Way,
then as the Way becomes lofty, demonic influences will flourish;
therefore, it is essential to skillfully recognize the activities of demons.
This current explanation consists of three parts:
first, distinguishing the different types of māra-dharmas;
second, clarifying the manifestations of the arising of māra-activities.
The Three Clarities (traividyā) are the methods for destroying Māra.
First, distinguishing the different magical arts of Māra:
there are four kinds of Māra.
First is the māra of afflictions;
second is the māra of the aggregates, sense bases, and elements;
third is the māra of death.
The fourth is the Māra of the devaputras of the desire realm.
First, regarding the māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*):

this refers to the three poisons, the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), as well as the outflows (*āsrava*), floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), bonds (*bandhana*), hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), vexations (*upāyāsa*), and knots (*grantha*).
All of these are able to destroy the work of the path of cultivation.
As a verse in the Mahāyāna-śāstra says:
"Desire is your first army; sorrow is the second."
Hunger and thirst are the third; contact and craving are the fourth;
sleep is the fifth army; fear is the sixth;
doubt and regret are the seventh; and anger is the eighth.
Gain and offerings, empty fame—these are the first nine; Self-exaltation and contempt for others—the tenth.
Such are the hosts of your army; I shall destroy these various forces of yours with the power of my meditative wisdom, Causing you, who oppress and submerge those who have gone forth, to be defeated.
Having attained the Buddha-way, he delivers all people from the two [categories of] aggregates,
elements, and sense-bases, and from Māra;
for the five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements.
All name-and-form (nāmarūpa) bind sentient beings;
because they obscure the pure roots of goodness, merit, and wisdom of the practitioner,
preventing them from increasing, they are called Māra.
This refers to the aggregates and bases of the desire realm;
it is the same for the aggregates and bases of the form and formless realms as well.
If a practitioner’s mind does not clearly understand them and becomes attached to them, [it is an obstruction].
All are called Māras.
If one can neither accept nor cling to them,
but views them as being like empty space, [one is free].
Being free from obscuration,
one immediately destroys the deeds of Māra.
As for the third, the Māra of death:
All karmic retributions of birth and death,
revolving without ceasing,
are all termed "Māra."

Part Seven, One of Two Parts: Explanation of the Cultivation and Realization of the Dhyāna-pāramitā. The first part of the seventh section, "Explanation of the Cultivation and Realization of the Dhyāna-pāramitā," has already extensively elucidated the internal and external skillful means (*upāya*).
If a practitioner can cultivate with single-minded devotion and fix their mindfulness upon the gates of dhyāna,
there will certainly be signs of realization.
Therefore, the seventh [chapter] extensively clarifies cultivation and realization.
Thus the Sūtra says:
"Those who cultivate my Dharma..."
Realization is known by oneself.
Now, within the explanation of cultivation and realization,
I shall further divide it into four parts.
First, the cultivation and realization of mundane meditative signs;
second, the cultivation and realization of signs that are both mundane and supramundane;
third, the cultivation and realization of supramundane meditative signs.
The fourth is the cultivation and realization of meditative signs that are neither mundane nor supramundane.
Now, for the first [section], the explanation of the cultivation and realization of mundane dhyāna,
there are three parts.
First, the four dhyānas;
second, the four immeasurable minds;
third, the four formless attainments.
Now, to explain further the cultivation and realization of the four dhyānas:
as for the four dhyānas,
the first is the first dhyāna.
Second, the second dhyāna;
third, the third dhyāna;
fourth, the fourth dhyāna.
Now, this treatise discusses the fundamental right concentrations (*maulāḥ samyaksamādhayaḥ*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
it states that there are only four,
though this excludes the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*).
This is not fixed;
for the Sarvāstivādins assert that there is such a thing as the "not-yet-reached stage" (anāgamya-bhūmi).
Including the intermediate dhyāna,
these together with the four dhyānas constitute the six stages of concentration (*ṣaḍ-bhūmi-samādhi*).
This is according to the Dharmaguptakas.
For example, it does not state that there is future dhyāna,
yet it states that there is the desire-realm concentration and the intermediate dhyāna,
thereby establishing six stages of concentration.
If one follows the Mahāyāna as well as the explanations provided by Ghoṣaka, then the preparatory stage (anāgamya),
the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), and the dhyānas of the desire realm are all fully present.
Taking the four dhyānas as the seven stages of concentration,
these are integrated herein;
this is inferred through their underlying meaning.
Now, speaking according to the orthodox system of dhyāna,
there are only four [stages] discussed.
First is the explanation of the cultivation and realization of the first dhyāna.
As stated in a verse of the Sūtra:
"Free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, possessing applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra),
born of seclusion, with joy and bliss— such a person enters the first dhyāna."
Having already attained freedom from the fire of lust, one then obtains the cool samādhi;
like a person suffering from great heat entering a cold pool and finding joy,
or like a poor man finding a treasure trove, his heart is moved by the awakening of great delight.
Discrimination is contemplation; entering the first dhyāna is likewise so.
In this verse, the Buddha fully elucidates the characteristics of cultivating and realizing the first dhyāna;
however, its meaning is difficult to perceive.
Now, this shall be analyzed.
Within the explanation of the first dhyāna,
it is divided into three distinct parts.
First, the explanation of the name;
second, the clarification of cultivation;
third, the clarification of the characteristics of realization.
First, regarding the explanation of the names:
as for what is called "the first dhyāna," *dhyāna* is a name for a collection of factors (*aṅga*).
The practitioner first attains the dharmas of the factors (aṅga) of the forest;
therefore, it is called the First Dhyāna.
Furthermore, dharmas such as vitarka and vicāra are designated as "factors."
When a practitioner cultivates the factors of applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra) of the first dhyāna,
these necessarily arise beforehand;
therefore, applied and sustained thought are said to be the name for the first dhyāna.
Question: If it is said that the first dhyāna is so called because it is attained by arising first,
then the stage of "not-yet-arrived" (*anāgamya*) in the desire realm arises most prior to all others.
Why does it not receive the name of "first dhyāna"?
Answer: The term "dhyāna" refers to a forest of meritorious qualities;
[the stages] such as the "not-yet-arrived" (anāgamya) of the desire realm do not possess these.
As long as the dharmas consisting of the factors and branches have not yet arisen,
even if one has previously generated the aspiration,
it is not called the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, in the Mahāyāna,
it is taught that in the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*) and the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
wisdom (*prajñā*) is predominant while meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is scarce.
This place is not blissful;

Furthermore, regarding what is called the first dhyāna,

This is because some people may harbor doubts, saying that there is no concentration within a mind characterized by vitarka and vicāra.

When this dhyāna arises,

Regarding the first point, as for what is called *ānāpāna*:

Third, regarding the different ways of employing the breath:
One teacher instructs that one should bind the mind to the counting of exhalations. Why is this?
Because by counting exhalations, the breath does not become hurried.
The body does not feel bloated;

making it easy to enter samādhi.
There are masters who teach counting the inhalation.
For what reason do they count the inhalation?
First, it is because it is easy to enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*) by following the breath as it is drawn inward.
Second, because external objects are severed;
third, because the thirty-six internal substances are easily perceived;
fourth, because the physical strength is light and vigorous.
Because one pacifies greed and anger through these five internal realities,
there are many such benefits as these; one should thus practice counting the inhalations.
Some teachers teach counting the inhalation and exhalation without fixed rules,

there is no definitive or exclusive method for counting.
According to the practitioner’s mental ease,
they enter meditative concentration without fault by employing the theories of the three masters;
none of them permit counting the inhalation and exhalation at the same time.
Why is this? Because there is a blockage in the breath,
and the illness has arisen within the throat.
It is like a blade of grass:

Because this affliction has arisen;

The second section clarifies the mind that performs the counting,
which is also presented in three parts.
First, it clarifies the mind that performs the counting.
Second, explaining the transformation of conditions;

First, explaining the mind that performs the counting.
With a mind of subtle mindfulness,
one collects the mind and focuses it upon the breath,
counting from one to ten.
Causing the mind not to be distracted is called "counting the breaths.
If the count does not reach ten, it is called "deficient counting."
If one reaches eleven, it is called "increase in number.
However, such numbers of increase and decrease are not the way to attain meditative concentration.
If one proceeds from one to ten,
constantly possessing all ten without the fault of interruption by a single [missing] unit,
it is therefore called the accomplishment of the method of counting.
If, in the interim,
the mind secretly pursues other objects,
the counting of dharmas will become disordered.
Therefore, the meaning of mental awareness as distraction is predominant.
If one were to count by means of "one," then "one" would be without interval.
If there are other conditions,
one will not be aware of it at that time;
therefore, one should attend only to a single breath.
If one cannot eliminate the distraction,
and if it exceeds ten [moments],
another dharma arises.
When a single mind takes two objects as its conditions,

Now, as for counting the breaths,
one should simply focus the mind subtly on the breath and keep count;

If the breath is excessive, the vital energy becomes full;
the abdomen distends and the body feels strained,

Regarding the second type of turning toward the object:
first, one counts the breaths and perceives the breath as subtle.
One should then set aside counting the breaths and simply follow the breath as it flows in and out spontaneously.
If the mind desires stillness,

If the mind becomes dark or agitated, it should then be stilled and illuminated, and form should be brought to rest.
If the mind becomes restless, one should immediately relinquish contemplation and return to counting and following-and-stopping.
Therefore, this is called "returning," whereby the mind no longer wanders or scatters.
Because one concentrates the spirit and quiets discursive thoughts, it is called "purity.
