Therefore, it is said that "special victory" (*viśeṣa-viśeṣa*) refers to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) that is both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*).
When these are compared vertically to the various dhyānas of the three realms,
the meaning of each individual contemplation of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) becomes evident.
The Sequential Dharma-Gate of the Śīla-Pāramitā,
Scroll Seven The Sequential Dharma-Gate of the Śīla-Pāramitā,
Scroll Eight Spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty
The disciple Fa Shen records:

The disciple Guan Ding has revised this seventh section on the cultivation and realization of the Dhyāna-pāramitā, part four. Regarding the cultivation and realization of the "Comprehensive Illumination Contemplation" (Tongming Guan), I shall now distinguish the general meaning of this dhyāna into three parts.
First, the explanation of the names;
second, the discernment of the stages and positions;
third, the clarification of cultivation and realization.

First, regarding the explanation of the name: as for why this dhyāna is called the "Contemplation of Penetrating Clarity" (tongming guan), the method of this contemplation originates from the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* (*Daji jing*), which contains no other specific title for it; it was practiced by various Chan masters of the Northern regions.
Having attained this dhyāna and wishing to transmit it to others, he did not know its name;
yet, while intending to establish them in fundamental dhyāna, the characteristics of the dharmas were vastly different, as if they were facing the sixteen special victories (ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa).
Thus, the names and their referents would be entirely unrelated;
if they were applied, the methods for the practices of the *vimokṣas* (liberations) and *abhibhvāyatanas* (bases of mastery) would be categorically distinct,
such that neither their progression nor their regression would correspond.
For this reason, various masters have separately designated it by the name "Samantaprabhāsa-vipaśyanā-dhyāna" (The Meditation of Universal Illumination).
Some say that this designation appears in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
What is called "pervasive" (sāmānya) refers to the fact that from the very beginning of cultivation, one pervasively contemplates three things.
When contemplating the breath, one simultaneously illuminates both form and mind;
when contemplating form, and so on up to the mind, it is likewise.
This dharma is luminous and pure, capable of opening the eye of the mind and removing all obscurations.
Because one attains penetration through one and reaches mastery through three, seeing without obstruction, it is called "Universal Clarity" (abhiññā).
Furthermore, by skillfully cultivating this dhyāna, one will certainly be able to give rise to the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) and the three types of clear knowledge (trividyā).
In the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, it is stated that when a bhikṣu practicing the Dharma cultivates this dhyāna, if he wishes to attain supernormal powers (*abhijñā*),
he is able to do so immediately. What is here called "supernormal power" refers specifically to the attainment of the six supernormal powers.
"Clarity" (vidyā) refers to that which can produce the three types of supernormal knowledge (*tisro vidyāḥ*);
because the effect is spoken of within the cause, it is called "penetrating clear observation."
Question: Other dhyānas are also capable of producing the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) and the three types of clear knowledge (trividyā).
Why is it that only this dhyāna is specifically described as "the supernormal powers and clear knowledge"?
The answer is:
Other dhyānas possess the quality of giving rise to supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and clear knowledges (*vidyā*), but this dhyāna is not like them;
because it is sharp and swift, it is called "supernatural power and clear knowledge."
Question: As in the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, there is also a distinct explanation for the meaning of this term "dhyāna.
Thus, the sūtra says:
"That which is called dhyāna is so named because it is swift."
Swift, very swift, abiding, great abiding, tranquility, contemplation, cessation, and penetration—this is called dhyāna.
Why, then, are these names established separately now?
The answer is:
Although that sutra contains this explanation, its meaning remains obscure;
since the names used are still general and lack specific designations, the name "Universal Clarity" (Tongming) is further established. Second, the clarification of the successive stages:
This dhyāna has no separate stages;
it is established as having stages based on the four fundamental dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).

However, within each individual dhyāna, there are further superior methods of supramundane meditative concentration that can give rise to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) states, as well as the three knowledges (*vidyā*) and six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), which are swift and sharp.

Furthermore, because one enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling by means of the extinction of all mental factors at the final moment of consciousness in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
it is not the same as the fundamental state of obscure realization which involves clinging to grasping and lacks the functional capacity of spiritual wisdom.
Therefore, although the sequence and stages are the same as those of the fundamental [dhyāna], the insight (*vipaśyanā*) is distinct;
fearing that people might misunderstand this, separate names were established.
Although the names differ, there is no discrepancy in the sequence and stages.
Question: If this dhyāna can lead to entry into the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti),
how does it differ from the nine successive attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpattayaḥ)?
Answer: When cultivating this concentration, because the moments of mind are uninterrupted,
it may also be described as the nine successive concentrations.
However, this ultimately does not constitute the complete attainment of the nine successive attainments (*anupūrva-samāpatti*).
This matter will naturally become clear below.
If one compares it with the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Chengshi lun), its explanation of the nine attainments and eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) also constitutes completeness.
Third, the explanation of cultivation and realization.
Since this dhyāna has no distinct stages or positions,
its cultivation and realization are explained here by reference to the stages and positions of the fundamental [dhyānas].
First, to clarify the characteristics of the cultivation and realization of the first dhyāna, as explained in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*:
that which is called the "first dhyāna" is also termed "endowment" (*samanvāgama*) and is also termed "separation" (*viveka*).
"Detachment" refers to being free from the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*).
"Endowment" refers to possessing the five factors (*pañca-aṅga*).
The five factors are initial application (*vitarka*), sustained application (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), and concentration (*samādhi*).
What is awakening? To awaken to the mind as it truly is, to contemplate the great awakening, and to reflect upon the great reflection while observing the nature of the mind—this is called awakening.
What is contemplation? It is to contemplate the activities of the mind and its great activities.
Pervasive mental flexibility is called contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
What is joy (*prīti*)? It is knowing reality as it is, great knowledge, and the movement of the mind reaching the heart; this is called joy.
What is tranquility (*praśrabdhi*)?
It is said that when the mind is at ease, the body is at ease, and one experiences pleasant contact, this is called "ease" (*praśrabdhi*).
What is "concentration" (*samādhi*)?
It is said that when the mind abides, abides greatly, is not distracted from its object, is without error, and is without inversion—this is called "concentration."
This is a brief explanation of the cultivation and realization of the first dhyāna as presented in that sutra, clarifying its general characteristics.
When one examines the five factors elucidated in this textual passage, they differ significantly from those explained in other sutras and treatises.
Therefore, it must be explained separately; first, we shall explain "like the mind.
"Like the mind" refers to the arising of the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) prior to the first dhyāna, which is also called the stage of "not yet arrived" (*anāgamya-bhūmi*).
However, realization does not arise in isolation; it must necessarily depend upon cultivation.
How does the practitioner cultivate?
From the very beginning of settling the mind, one contemplates that the three factors—breath, form, and mind—are all devoid of conceptual discrimination.
One who contemplates these three matters must first contemplate the path of the breath.
How does one contemplate the breath?
It means sitting in meditative stillness with a concentrated mind and harmonizing the flow of the breath.
With single-minded attention, observe clearly how the perception of breath enters and exits throughout the entire body.
If the wisdom-mind is clear and sharp,
one will immediately perceive that as the breath enters, it does not accumulate, and as it exits, it does not disperse.
Coming, there is no path by which it passes; going, there is no ground upon which it treads.
Although one clearly perceives the breath entering and exiting throughout the body, it is like the wind in space, whose nature is non-existent.
This is a brief explanation of contemplating the breath as being like the characteristics of the mind.
Next, regarding the practitioner who contemplates form as being like [the mind]:
having already understood that the breath depends upon the body and that there is no breath apart from the body.
One should then contemplate the physical form with clarity: such a form was originally non-existent;
it is entirely the result of the karmic attraction of delusive thoughts from previous lives, and exists now because the four great elements and derived matter enclose empty space.
The body is a mere provisional designation.

Contemplate with single-minded attention that the six parts, such as the head, along with the thirty-six substances and the four great elements and four subtle elements, are each individually not the body.
These four subtle and four great elements are likewise each unreal; they do not even exist of themselves.
How can the six parts of the body and the thirty-six constituent substances give rise to a physical form when no color or substance of the body can be apprehended?
At that time, when the mind is free from discrimination, one immediately penetrates the suchness of form.
Next, one contemplates the mind as the practitioner does.
It should be known that because of the existence of the mind,
there is bodily form that comes and goes, moves and shifts.
If this mind did not exist, who would discern form?
From what cause does form arise?
Contemplate this mind with truth: it exists by depending on conditions;
its arising and ceasing are so rapid that no place of abiding is seen, nor is there any characteristic mark.
There are only names; since names are also empty, one who realizes this is one whose mind accords with suchness (*tathatā*).
If one does not perceive the distinctions between the three natures, that is called a mind that accords with suchness.
Furthermore, when the practitioner contemplates the breath,
upon no longer perceiving the breath, they immediately realize that both form and mind are empty and quiescent. Why is this?
Because these three factors are inseparable,
so too are form and mind. If one does not obtain these three things— form, mind, and [the third factor]— then [they do not exist].
Thus, one does not apprehend any dharma.
Why is this? Because it arises from the conjunction of these three factors.
They are able to give rise to all the aggregates, bases, and elements, as well as the various sufferings and afflictions.
Through wholesome and unwholesome karmic actions, one wanders through the five realms of existence in an unceasing cycle of transmigration.
If one realizes that these three matters are non-arising, then all phenomena are from the beginning empty and quiescent.
This is a brief explanation of the characteristics of the cultivation of the mind-as-it-is.
Second, the characteristics of realization are clarified;
this also fully possesses the characteristics of realizing the stage of "not-yet-reached" (*anāgamya*) within the desire realm.
The practitioner observes the three natures as described above and finds that none of them can be apprehended.
Their mind spontaneously abides in *tathatā* (suchness) of its own accord;
this state in which the mind is utterly dissolved and luminously pure is called the "concentration of the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*).
Following this meditative concentration, the mind relies upon the *tathatā* (suchness) of phenomena;
the mind dissolves into the concentration and becomes conjoined with suchness.
In accordance with the Dharma, it sustains the mind, and the mind remains concentrated and unmoving.

When the distinct characteristics of the three dharmas—the body, the breath, and the mind—have completely vanished and are no longer perceived, it is for a time like empty space; therefore, it is called "like the mind.
This is precisely the stage of the "unreached" (*anāgamya*) within the Universal Clarity (*sāmānyaprajñā*).
Next, I shall explain the signs of the arising of the first dhyāna as previously cited in the sūtras; this should fully explain the five factors (*pañcāṅga*) that serve as the marks of realization.
Now, first relying on the awakening factors (*bodhyaṅga*) as the basis, the meaning of "awakening" (*bodhi*) is established.
The explanation of the remaining four factors follows from what has been seen.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "Awakening and great awakening.

As for "awakening," it is awakening to fundamental dhyāna; because one awakens to the signs of contact and arousal, it is called "awakening. This matter is as previously explained, differing only in degree of intensity.
The Great Awakened One suddenly experienced a clear opening of his mind and eyes.
Clearly perceiving the manifestation of the three matters is called "Great Awakening.
This is a peripheral explanation and not the primary intent.
Furthermore, we shall now differentiate the meanings of "awakening" (*bodhi*) and "great awakening" (*mahābodhi*).

What is called "awakening" is the awakening to the characteristics of the mundane world; "great awakening" is the transcending of the mundane world. This is explained in terms of the two truths: the conventional and the ultimate.
The meaning of "with outflows" (sāsrava) and "without outflows" (anāsrava) is also intended here.
Now, to clarify, there are three kinds of the mundane world (*loka*).
First is the fundamental world, which refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) that constitute the primary retribution for a single lifetime.
The mundane world of two meanings refers to the knowledge that the fundamental dharma is related in principle to all external phenomena.
The mundane world of three matters refers to the time when one develops the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), seeing all categories of sentient beings and all worldly affairs.
Since there are three types of the mundane,
the supramundane, as contrasted with the mundane,
is likewise threefold. Why is this so?
The faculties of sentient beings vary—being inferior, middling, or superior, and sharp or dull—and are thus unequal.
Therefore, although they equally realize this realm of the first dhyāna, there are in fact differences in its depth.
Consequently, it is necessary to distinguish the different ways of realizing the first dhyāna by means of three points.
First, regarding the fundamental mundane and supramundane [teachings],
there are two points for explaining how the five factors of clear awareness and great awareness constitute the characteristics of the first dhyāna.
First, the characteristics of the arising of the first dhyāna are clarified;
second, the distinctions between the five factors of the awakening of Great Awakening are explained.
First, the characteristics of the arising of the first dhyāna are clarified.
This constitutes three distinct stages of intention:
first, the initial arousal [of the thought of enlightenment].
Second. Third, regarding the first:
the practitioner who manifests the initial signs.
When entering the first dhyāna,
one suddenly and clearly perceives that the ninety-nine thousand pores of one's own body are empty and porous, and that the breath enters and exits through all these pores.
Although the mind’s eye clearly sees the breath entering and exiting throughout the entire body, [the practitioner remains undisturbed].
Entering without accumulation and emerging without dispersal, coming without a path traversed and going without a place stepped upon,
one then clearly perceives each of the thirty-six internal constituents within the body with distinct clarity.
The thirty-six items are:

hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, thin skin, thick skin, muscle, sinew, bone, marrow, spleen, kidneys, heart, liver, lungs, small intestine, large intestine, stomach, bladder, gallbladder, feces, urine, filth, sweat, tears, nasal mucus, saliva, pus, blood, vessels, yellow phlegm, white phlegm, rheum, fat, grease, brain, and membranes.
Of these thirty-six items, ten are external objects and twenty-six are internal objects;
twenty-two are earth-based objects.
The fourteenth is the element of water.
Having clearly perceived the characteristics of wind, water, and earth,
one further perceives that all things have their own heat, and the characteristic of fire as it boils and cooks them becomes clearly manifest.
Contemplate these four great elements as being like four venomous snakes dwelling together in a single basket;
the nature of each of these four venomous snakes is distinct,
just as a butcher divides a cow into four portions of meat.
Observing minutely that each of the four elements is unrelated to the others,
the practitioner likewise experiences a great shock of awakening.
Furthermore, the practitioner does not merely see the thirty-six components of the body as an impure and loathsome conglomeration of the four elements.
One also perceives five kinds of impure signs.
What are these five?
First, seeing the impurity of the ten external objects, a mind of revulsion arises.
This is called the impurity of specific characteristics.
Second, one observes the twenty-six internal substances within the body, which are inherently impure by nature.
This is called impurity of intrinsic nature.
Third, one personally realizes that this body, from the time of the *kalala*, is formed with the union of the parents' semen and blood as its seed;
this is called impurity of the seed.
Fourth, while this body is in the womb, it dwells between the two organs of digestion—the raw and the cooked;
this is called impurity of the place of birth.
Fifth, after this body has died and been cast away in a cemetery, it decays and becomes foul-smelling and putrid.
This is called ultimate impurity.
One should know that from beginning to end this body is composed of the impure; there is not a single thing in it to be delighted in, for it is utterly loathsome.
Being blind, I have hitherto neglected this foul, putrid body and created the karma of birth and death through attachment to it.
Only now, after immeasurable kalpas, have I begun to awaken to this.
My heart is filled with both sorrow and joy.
The five kinds of impurity are explained in detail in the Mahāyāna-śāstra.
Furthermore, one perceives that within the concentrated mind, consciousness conditions various objects, ceasinglessly from moment to moment;
the mental factors (caitta-dharma) arise in succession,
and the characteristics of what is contemplated differ and are not uniform.
This is called the sign of the initial realization of the first dhyāna.
Next, the signs of intermediate realization are explained:

as the practitioner dwells within this meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the awareness gradually deepens, and they perceive that the breath subsequently gives rise to various distinct signs of respiration within the five viscera.
That which is called blue, yellow, red, white, black, and so forth, varies according to the colors of the internal organs.
When it emerges through the pores or enters through the sense roots, its color-forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) likewise differ.
Thus, the distinctions among these olfactory characteristics (*gandha-lakṣaṇa*) are not uniform.
Furthermore, one sees that this body consists of thin skin, thick skin, membranes, and flesh,
each having ninety-nine layers;
there are three hundred and sixty large and small bones, along with the marrow.
Each has ninety-eight layers.
Within this mass of flesh and bone dwell various worms,
each having four heads, four mouths, and ninety-nine tails.
Such physical forms are not of a single kind;
even the sounds and speech involved in coming and going, entering and exiting, are all fully perceived.
There are only four parts to the brain.
It consists of fourteen layers.
Within the body, the five viscera are layered one over another like lotus flowers; their pores are hollow and sparse, allowing for internal and external communication.
Each layer likewise contains ninety-nine strata, and within the spaces between these various substances, there are eighty types of parasites.
While dwelling within, they cause one another to act;
when the practitioner’s mind is calm and subtle, they may also hear the sounds of the speech of various insects within that concentration,
and sometimes, by means of this, they give rise to the samādhi of understanding the languages of sentient beings.
Among the various channels within the body, the heart channel is primary.
Furthermore, from within the heart channel, the channels of the four great elements arise;
for each of these four great elements, there are ten channels.
Within each of the ten channels, there are further nine channels each, totaling four hundred channels.
From head to foot, these four hundred and four channels all contain wind and blood that flow and circulate within one another.
Within the blood of these vessels, there are also various subtle worms that dwell within them.
In this way, the practitioner understands that the body, both internally and externally, is unreal, just like a plantain tree.

Furthermore, one observes that when the mental factors follow their respective objects, there are always distinctions among the four mental aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.
This is the third sign realized after [the initial stage].
As the practitioner’s samādhi and wisdom become increasingly deep, pure, bright, and sharp.
Furthermore, one sees that the inhalations and exhalations are harmonized and unified into a single mark, like a vessel of lapis lazuli that is neither blue, yellow, red, nor white.
One also perceives that the entry and exit of the breath are impermanent, and that their arising and ceasing are entirely empty and quiescent.
Furthermore, one observes that the characteristics of the body are in a state of constant flux, characterized by impermanence and successive replacement. Why is this so?
When food and drink—the external four great elements—enter the abdomen and nourish the body, the new four great elements are thereby produced.
One should know that the old body perishes accordingly;
just as when new leaves grow on grasses and trees, the old leaves fall away,
so too it is with the body.
Fools, failing to understand, claim this is out of attachment to the body.

The wise, within samādhi, realize that the characteristics of this body are subject to impermanence, undergoing constant flux with arising and ceasing at every moment; it is empty and lacks intrinsic nature, and its form cannot be apprehended.
Furthermore, at the very moment each thought arises, there are sixty kṣaṇas of arising and ceasing.
Some say that six hundred kṣaṇas of arising and ceasing pass with such rapidity.
Emptiness is without intrinsic nature, and the mind cannot be apprehended.
Second, the explanation establishing the characteristics of the five factors of vitarka and vicāra consists of five parts.
First, regarding the explanation of the factor of awakening (bodhyaṅga), the Sūtra says concerning the factor of awakening:
"Awakening, great awakening, contemplation, great contemplation, and great contemplation—these five phrases clarify the characteristics of awakening.
Now, first, I shall explain the two phrases: 'awakening' and 'great awakening.'"
This distinction between the two types of awakening arises from the differentiation between mundane and supramundane spheres.
The mundane sphere is precisely that which possesses distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
The supramundane realm is precisely the characteristic of suchness (*tathatā*).
This suchness, when differentiated, is another name for the distinction between the two truths: the ultimate and the conventional.
Now, this can be easily seen by way of the varying depths of the contemplative gateways (*vipaśyanā-mukha*).
Now, this shall be explained in detail according to the Mahāyāna.
The treatise states:
"There are three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior."
Just as there are three kinds of "difference" (*anyathā*), so too should the "great awakening" (*mahābodhi*) be threefold.

The intent of the treatise is that the conceptual differentiation of conventional designations is called "difference," while the conceptual differentiation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as being of the same essence is called "lower suchness" (*adharatathatā*).
The distinction of the earth element from the other three elements is called "difference.
Their shared state of impermanence, arising, and ceasing without distinction is called "suchness.
This impermanent arising and ceasing is itself termed "difference."
Arising and ceasing are themselves emptiness; there is no difference from the aforementioned "superior" [level].
Now, based on dhyāna, the characteristics of the shallow and deep stages of the gate of contemplation are clarified through the categories of inferior, middling, and superior.
First, the characteristics of the inferior level of awakening are explained.
To perceive the inhalation and exhalation of breath as being distinct from one another in their various colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—is called "awakening.
To perceive that all these breaths are of one and the same wind-element (vāyu-mahābhūta) without difference is called "Great Awakening."
Next, the discernment of the thirty-six constituent elements as distinct is called "discernment" (saṃjñā).
The discernment that the other three great elements have no difference between them is called "great discernment" (mahā-saṃjñā).
The discernment that the mental factors (caitasika) are not one is called "discernment."
These same four states of mind, being without distinction, are called Great Awakening.
Second, to clarify those of middling awakening:
the cessation of this wind is called Awakening.
To realize that the arising and ceasing of respiration is impermanent is called Great Awakening.
To realize each of the other three great elements as distinct is called Awakening.
To realize that they are all equally impermanent and that their arising and ceasing are no different is called Great Awakening.
To awaken to the four minds, recognizing their differences as distinct, is called "awakening"; to realize that impermanence and arising-and-ceasing are not different is called "Great Awakening.
Third, this clarifies the superior grade of awakening.
Regarding the realization that the breath is impermanent because it is distinct:
this breath is impermanent because it is transformed by the eight characteristics (*aṣṭalakṣaṇa*).
What are these eight characteristics?
1. Arising; 2. Abiding;
3. Change.
4. Cessation of cessation;
5. Arising of arising;
6. Abiding of abiding.
Seventh is change;
eighth is cessation.
These eight kinds of characteristics, wherein the substance of phenomena undergoes transformation and differs from one another rather than being identical, are termed "cognition" (*buddhi*).
To realize that the breath is fundamentally empty and quiescent, devoid of the distinctions of the eight characteristics, is called Great Awakening.
To realize that the other three great elements each possess distinct differences of the eight characteristics is called Awakening.
To realize that the other three great elements are fundamentally empty and quiescent from the beginning, devoid of the distinctions of the eight characteristics, is called Great Awakening.
The mind of awakening, as it is transformed and differentiated by the eight characteristics, is designated as "awakening" because it is not one.
The mind of awakening is originally empty and quiescent; being free from the distinctions of the eight characteristics, it is called "Great Awakening. Why is this so?
If the mind were identical to the eight characteristics,
and the eight characteristics were identical to the mind, then the remaining characteristics would be destroyed. Why is this so?
Now, the cessation of form is also these eight characteristics;

the eight characteristics are also the cessation of form. Since the eight characteristics and the cessation of form are not different, the three things—cessation, form, and mind—should likewise not be different.
If that were so, when one speaks of "mind," one would necessarily be speaking of the color of the breath;
yet in reality this is not the case, for it would destroy the characteristics of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*),
just as if someone were to call for fire and water were to arrive instead.
The same applies here to the claim that the mind is invariably identical with the cessation of form.
Furthermore, if the mind were separate from the eight characteristics, such that there could be a mind apart from the eight characteristics,
then the mind would not be the eight characteristics, and the eight characteristics would not be the mind.
If the mind were devoid of the eight characteristics, then the mind would exist only as a name without characteristics.
A phenomenon that lacks characteristics cannot be called "mind.
If the eight characteristics were separate from the mind, then those eight characteristics would have no basis for transition.
Then they cannot be called the eight signs.
Because the eight signs have nothing that is signified,
if one seeks them with such careful scrutiny, the mind and the eight signs are fundamentally non-existent from the beginning.

Furthermore, because it does not rely on the nature of other-existence (parabhāva) and its nature is like space, being without the characteristics of unity or difference, it is called Great Enlightenment (mahābodhi).
One should likewise analyze each preceding cessation of form in this same manner.
This is a brief explanation of the characteristics of superior awakening and great awakening.
Next, the two phrases "contemplation" and "great contemplation" are explained;
these likewise refer back to the aforementioned awakening and great awakening.
Why is this so? Because the initial mind that awakens to the characteristics of the ultimate and the conventional is called "Awakening" and "Great Awakening";
the subsequent mind that repeatedly contemplates and observes is called "Contemplation" and "Great Contemplation."
"Small awakening" refers to what is spoken of after [small] contemplation (*vitarka*), and "great awakening" refers to what is spoken of after great contemplation (*vicāra*).
This meaning is easy to perceive and need not be explained at length.
Next, regarding the explanation of "observing the nature of the mind": this refers to turning back to observe the mind that is capable of great contemplation (*vicāra*).
Why is this so? Although a practitioner may be able to discern the objects before them, if they cannot turn back to realize the observing mind, they will not encounter the true Path.
Now, one must immediately reflect back upon the observing mind itself.

Does it arise from a mind of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), or does it arise from a mind not of contemplation? If it arises from a mind of contemplation, or if it arises from a mind not of contemplation, both positions entail faults.
One should know that the mind of contemplation is ultimately empty and quiescent. This concludes the fivefold explanation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
The second explanation concerns the contemplation of the factors (*aṅga*).
The Sūtra says:
"If one contemplates the movements of the mind, whether they are great, pervasive, or according to one's inclination."
"Contemplating the mind" refers to the aforementioned contemplation of the nature of the mind.
Regarding "practicing the Great Practice," for a Śrāvaka, the Four Noble Truths constitute the Great Practice;
when contemplating the mind, one possesses the correct contemplation of the Four Noble Truths.
Why is this so? Because if a person does not understand the mind,
ignorance leads them to fail to comprehend and thus create various karmic fetters.
This is called the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Through the causal conditions of the Truth of Origination, one will inevitably bring about the fruit of suffering, namely name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), in the future;
this is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
If one contemplates the nature of the mind, it is itself the perfection of precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
Practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is called the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
If there is the right path, then afflictions do not arise in the present.
The cessation of future bitter fruits is called the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya).
This is termed the Great Practice of the Śrāvaka.
If a pratyekabuddha takes the twelve links of dependent origination as their great practice,
a bodhisattva enters directly into non-arising;
through right path and right contemplation, they realize the tranquil samādhi of lapis lazuli.
Seeing the Buddhas within the pores of the skin signifies entering the stage of a Bodhisattva;
this briefly clarifies the characteristics of the path of the great practice of the three vehicles.
As for the universal practitioner (*vyāpaka-caryā*), their contemplative practice has not yet become sharp.
These also involve contemplating the Four Truths by means of the mind;
this is called "Great Practice.
Now, as the contemplation of the Path becomes somewhat sharp, one is able to traverse all conditions universally.
Because one contemplates the Four Truths through the sixteen modes of observation, it is called "universal" (sarvatraga).
Regarding "according to one's will":
if it is universal, even while within meditative concentration, one is able to perceive all conditions.
When emerging from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one contemplates the dissociated (*viprayukta*).
Now, "according to one's will" means that, in accordance with one's intention, one contemplates all phenomena during both entering and emerging from concentration;
this occurs spontaneously and naturally without depending on deliberate mental application (*manasikāra*), and is thus called "according to one's will."
This is a brief explanation of the characteristics of the factor of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Third, the elucidation of the factor of joy (*prīti*).
As for the factor of joy:
The Sūtra says:
"To truly know the great mind, the moving mind, and the ultimate mind—this is called joy.
Regarding "truly knowing":
This is precisely the contemplation of the Four Truths regarding the nature of the mind as described above.
"Great wisdom" refers to the aforementioned practice of contemplation;
if the mind dwells with careful discernment upon its internal object, it is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) because of this knowing.
Therefore, it is said that knowing in accordance with reality is true knowledge.
If one attains sudden enlightenment and knows in accord with principle, giving rise to joy in the mind, it is called "great knowledge.
As for "the movement of the mind reaching the ultimate mind":
Having attained the joy of the Dharma, the mind is stirred;
yet if one follows after this joy, it becomes a perversion.
Now, realizing that this joy is non-existent, one attains the very nature of joy; because one attains the very nature of joy, it is called the "Ultimate Mind."
This is called joy.
Fourth is the clear exposition of the factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*).
As for the factor of tranquility:
The Sūtra says:
"If the body is at ease, the mind is at ease, and one experiences ease, experiencing a pleasant contact—
this is called 'ease'."
Regarding "peace of body":
because one thoroughly understands the nature of the body,
one is not moved by bodily karma and thus attains peace of body.
Therefore, it is called peace of body.
As for peace of mind,
it is because one thoroughly realizes the nature of the mind.
Not being moved by mental karma, one attains peace of mind;
therefore, it is called "peace of mind.
One who experiences this peace—
The mind capable of observation is called "feeling" (vedanā).
Because it knows that feeling is not [inherently] feeling and thereby severs all feelings,
it is called "bliss" (sukha).
Therefore, it is said that "one experiences pleasure through contact with pleasant sensations.
This refers to the accomplishment of two kinds of pleasant phenomena— mundane and supramundane—
and because these pleasant phenomena confront the mind, one experiences pleasure.
Regarding the fifth point, the clarification of the branches,
the Sūtra states:
"If the mind abides in the great abiding, it is not distracted from its object, is without error, and is free from inversion."
This is called concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding "the mind abides":
it is called "abiding" because the mind dwells in the dharmas of worldly concentration, being maintained without distraction.
"Greatly abiding" means that by dwelling in the samādhi of true thusness (tathatā), one maintains the mind so that it does not scatter.
"Not being distracted by conditions" means...
Although one dwells in a single mind,
the discernment of worldly phenomena remains undisturbed;
this is what is meant by being "unerring."
Erroneous names are false delusions;
because one clearly realizes True Suchness (tathatā), false grasping does not arise,
and thus it is said that there is no error.
Regarding "non-perverted":
if the mind grasps at worldly characteristics with partiality,
it will follow the view of existence and sink into the cycle of birth and death.

If one does not attain liberation because the mind is biased toward grasping at "suchness," one will follow the view of emptiness, destroy the causes and effects of the world, and fail to cultivate wholesome dharmas;
this is a most terrifying state.
The practitioner who skillfully masters the ultimate and conventional truths and remains free from these two types of wrong livelihood is said to be non-perverted.
Furthermore, if a person of the Two Vehicles attains this mind, they destroy the four inversions.
It is called "non-inverted.
If a bodhisattva attains this single-mindedness and is able to destroy the eight inversions,
it is called "non-inverted."

When the practitioner first attains the accomplishment of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), they realize that the body and breath are insubstantial, like a plantain tree; now, they abide in this accomplishment of the factor of concentration (*samādhi-aṅga*) of one-pointedness of mind.
Once the mind has become tranquil, it subsequently subsides into a state of subtle stillness;
one then perceives that the characteristics of the body and breath are unreal, like a mass of foam.

This briefly clarifies the signs of the practitioner of inferior capacity realizing the supernormal clarity (*abhijñā*) of the first dhyāna. Second, the explanation of the meaning according to the mundane clarity.
Next, regarding the characteristics of the practitioner of faculties advancing to realize the five branches of the first faculty, there are two parts:
first, the explicit explanation of the characteristics of worldly phenomena;
second, the explanation that establishes the meaning of awakening.
Regarding the first explanation of the meaning, "the world" is intended in two senses:
first, to clarify the world as external objects;
second, to clarify the world as internal objects.
Now, to explain the external meaning, the mundane world is further divided into three points:
first, to correctly clarify the causal conditions of the fundamental mundane world;
second, to clarify the relationship between the fundamental [world] and the external world.
The Threefold Vidyā governs the royal path with rectitude.
First, the Śākya-awakened one realized the fundamental meaning of how the world arises through causes and conditions.
When the practitioner first attains the first dhyāna, they have already witnessed and realized this fundamental world.
At that time, whether one has already seen the Path or has not yet seen it,
one now desires to deeply understand from what cause this fundamental worldly retribution of a single lifetime arises.

At that time, within the samādhi, with the internal wisdom of the mind becoming clear and sharp, one contemplates minutely the thirty-six internal substances, the four great elements, and the five aggregates within the body.
By means of the power of vows, one knows the mind’s aspirations; one knows for what causes and conditions this body exists.
Because of the power of samādhi, wisdom, merit, and roots of goodness, one immediately awakens to and knows it.
Thus, this body and life are entirely due to the karmic power of the five precepts from previous lives.
Sustained by this power through the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it neither ceases nor perishes.

At the moment of the parents' union, the karmic power transforms consciousness, which then conceives of the two drops of semen and blood from the parents—each as large as a bean—as its own, and takes rebirth within them.
At that time, there is the full presence of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*),
and the consciousness-mind (*vijñānacitta*).
Consciousness resides therein, possessing the nature of the five sensory consciousnesses.
After seven days, it transforms like thin curd or congealed butter;
subsequently, it gradually grows as large as a chicken egg yolk.
Through the causal conditions of karmic power, this single body undergoes transformation, and first, the five viscera are established within it to accommodate the five consciousnesses.
At that time, one immediately realizes that the power of the precept against killing has transformed this body internally;
next, it becomes the liver,
upon which the *hun* soul depends.
By the power of the precept against stealing, this body is transformed internally into the kidneys, and the will (*chih*) relies upon them.
By the power of the precept against sexual misconduct, this body is transformed internally into the lungs, and the *po* spirit relies upon them.
By the power of the precept against false speech, this body is transformed internally into the spleen, upon which the intellect (manas) relies.
By the power of the precept against drinking intoxicants, it is transformed internally into the heart, upon which the spirit (vijñāna) relies.
These five spirits—hun, zhi, po, yi, and shen—are simply alternative names for the five consciousnesses.
Once the palaces of the five viscera have been established, the spirits and consciousnesses then have a place to dwell.

Once there is a place of dwelling and entrustment, one must provide for its sustenance; furthermore, the karmic power of the five precepts transforms within the body to form the six palaces (fu) of spirit and qi.
These palaces nourish the five viscera as well as the entire body.
The "palace" (fu) refers to the gallbladder being the palace of the liver;
it stores water so that its qi may harmonize with and moisten the liver.
The small intestine is the palace of the heart.
The heart is red, and the small intestine is also red.
The heart is the seat of blood and qi;
the small intestine likewise conduits blood and qi.
The Master [Qi] moistens the heart and enters the entire body;
therefore, the large intestine is the腑 (fu) of the lungs.
The lungs are white, and the large intestine is also white.
The Master of Killing [the Metal phase] benefits the lungs and completes the transformation of the entire body.
The stomach is the palace of the spleen;
as the stomach is yellow, the spleen is also yellow.
The stomach also moves, and the yellow *jiān* (intermediate space) penetrates the channels; the qi of the spleen enters the four limbs.
The bladder is the palace of the kidneys;
since the kidneys are black, the bladder is also black.
It penetrates dampness to moisten the kidneys and benefits the small intestine and bowels; thus, although the Triple Burner is combined as a single organ system,
each part has its own specific functions.
The upper burner governs the passage of the clear and warm qi of the fluids;
the middle burner governs the passage of the qi of the blood vessels and the spirit;
the lower burner governs the passage of the substances of the feces.
The triple burner governs the benefit of the upper and lower [parts of the body].
The spirits of the five viscera separately preside over the six腑 (fu).
The qi of the six腑 forms the spirits of the five officials.
This primarily explains the principle of the single body.
The organs and viscera support one another to produce seven bodies;
the kidneys produce two bodies.
First, the bones; second, the marrow.
The kidneys belong to the element water; because there are pebbles and sand within water, this is precisely the meaning of "bones."
The liver has two components: one is muscle and the other is intestine.
The liver is wood;
wood is the muscle of earth.
Therefore, sinews and intestines arise from it.
The heart produces blood vessels; the color of the heart is red.
It belongs to the blood to communicate the divine spirit (*śenqi*); its way is spontaneous (*ziran*).
The spleen produces the skin and flesh; the spleen is associated with Earth, and the skin and flesh are likewise Earth.
The lungs are produced from the skin because the lungs are situated above all the other viscera, and the skin is likewise at the top of the body.
These are the five viscera that can produce the seven bodies, also called the seven branches.
The lung is the Grand Minister; it resides above and below, abandoning all that is unrighteous. The liver is the Marshal;
its heart is benevolent and it resides in the center, receiving all varieties [of flavors]. The spleen... [is the Minister of Works; it resides in the center, receiving all varieties of flavors].
Within this interval, the five flavors are balanced;
the kidneys are situated below, surging against the four qi to promote growth.
The seven constituent parts form the body: the bones serve as pillars, the marrow provides lubrication, and the tendons act as seams.
The vessels circulate through it, the blood moistens it, the flesh envelops it, and the skin covers it.
By these causes and conditions, there comes to be the body with its major parts: head, torso, hands, and feet.
The remaining bones became teeth;
the remaining flesh became the tongue;
and the remaining sinews became the nails.
The remaining blood becomes hair;
the remaining skin becomes the ears;
and the consciousness-spirit dwells within.
Through the causal conditions of the power of the precepts, the five *kalala* (embryonic stages) open and expand;
the form derived from the four great elements becomes pure and transforms into the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*).
Thus, when confronting sensory objects, one relies upon these faculties.
Through consciousness, one perceives the causal conditions of the five colors, whereby mental consciousness arises.
When sensory objects cease, consciousness returns to the five viscera.
Thus, for the duration of a single lifetime, the retribution of the four great elements, the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen realms is fully accomplished.
This is a brief explanation of the causal basis for the meaning of the mundane world as the fundamental fruit of retribution throughout a single lifetime.
It is asked:
If it is said that consciousness emerges from within and, abiding among the five sense organs, distinguishes the five objects of perception; [how is this so?]
How does this differ from the tenets of the non-Buddhists?
The answer is as stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:
Without abandoning the eightfold wrong path, one enters the eightfold right path.
It is also said:
"The sixty-two views are the lineage of the Tathāgata."
What is the meaning of these words?
All such points originate from the *Tiwai jing* (Tiwei jing), which clarifies that [this work] was not composed by a human being.
If one does not understand this point, it shall naturally become clear further below.
The second explanation concerns the relationship between the internal world and external lands.
When a practitioner, through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom, and the knowledge of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*), contemplates the body with clear observation:
One immediately knows that this body possesses all phenomena and worldly affairs that emulate heaven and earth. Why is this?
Because the features of this body—the head being rounded—resemble heaven.
The feet constitute the earth element;
internally, there is the space element.

That which is hollow and empty is the stomach; that which is warm is the heat element; that which is firm and strong in spring and summer is the back; and that which is so in autumn and winter is likewise [the earth element].
The dharma of the bodies of the four seasons consists of the four great seasonal nodes and twelve dharmas for the twelve months;
the minor nodes consist of three hundred and sixty dharmas corresponding to the three hundred and sixty days.
The dharma of the breath exhaled from the nose and mouth is like the wind and air within mountains, marshes, streams, and valleys.
The eyes are the sun and moon; the opening and closing of the eyes are day and night; the hair is the constellations;
the eyebrows are the Northern Dipper;
and the veins are the rivers.
The bones become jade and stone;
the skin and flesh become the earth and soil;
the body hair becomes the groves and forests; the five viscera within become the five stars in the heavens.
In the laws of the earth, they are the Five Peaks; in the laws of Yin and Yang, they are the Five Elements; in the laws of the world, they are the Five Truths;
internally, they are the Five Spirits. Cultivated, they become the Five Virtues;
as messengers, they are the Eight Trigrams; and in the administration of punishment, they are the Five Punishments.
The principal organs become the five officials, which ascend as the five clouds and transform into the five dragons.
The heart is the Vermilion Bird;
the kidneys are the Black Warrior.
The liver is the Azure Dragon;
the lungs are the White Tiger;
the spleen is the Gouchen.
These five kinds of sentient beings encompass all the birds and beasts of the world, which are entirely included within them;
they also constitute the five musical notes,
namely, gong, shang, jue, zhi, and yu.
All the myriad people are contained within it;
in relation to the written classics, it constitutes the Five Classics,
and all books and histories emerge from this source.
If it concerns craftsmanship,
it refers to the five sciences and the six arts;
all technical skills are contained therein.
One should know that although this body is small, its significance is related to heaven and earth.
Thus, what is called the "body" is not merely the world of the five aggregates;
it is also the world of the realm.
Third, the explanation of how the Dharma-king within the body governs with righteousness:
through the power of the wisdom of aspiration within samādhi,
the practitioner further becomes aware of that which is within the body.
Because the mind is the great king— superior in righteousness and benevolent in conduct—
it dwells within a hundredfold enclosure;
when it goes forth, it is attended by its officials and retinues in front, behind, to the left, and to the right.
The lungs are the Minister of War;
the liver is the Minister of Instruction;
the spleen is the Minister of Works.
The kidneys are like a great ocean, within which dwells a divine tortoise.
It breathes in the primal qi, circulating the winds to bring forth rain and penetrating the vital energy throughout the four limbs.
These four limbs are the children of the people.
On the left is the Lord of Destiny;
on the right is the Lord of Records.
They are charged with recording the life-spans of human beings.
The Lord of the Central Taiyi is likewise the main pillar of the person.
He is the Great General of Heaven, the Excellency and King,
presiding over the twelve thousand great deities within the body.
The Grand Unity (Taiyi) has eight messengers, which are the Eight Trigrams (Bagua).
Together they constitute the Nine Ministers.
The Triple Burner (Sanjiao) and the Gate of Original Qi (Guanyuan) serve as the Left Altar of the Soil and the Right Altar of the Grain, presiding over rebels and thieves.
The upper burner (shàngjiāo) is where qi circulates; it enters the head to serve as the ancestral temple.
Therein, the sovereign governs and transforms.
If the mind practices the Right Dharma and the multitudes below all follow, then governance will be upright, pure, and peaceful.
Therefore, the five viscera are harmonized and the six repositories are unobstructed and comfortable.
The four elements are at peace and free from all ailments and afflictions, ensuring a full lifespan.
If the mind practices what is not the Dharma, then the various officials will rise in rebellion.
Because they harm one another,
the four great elements become unbalanced and the sense faculties grow dark and obstructed;
thus, harboring this affliction, they reach their end.
This is entirely due to practicing unwholesome dharmas with the mind.
As the Sūtra says:
"When the soul is lost, one immediately becomes deranged."
To lose one's spirit leads to madness;
to lose one's mind leads to delusion;
to lose one's will leads to forgetfulness.
If one loses consciousness, one dies.
One should know that the establishment of the Way of Kings and the governance and transformation of the realm externally are all methods pertaining to the interior of the body.
Such meanings are fully explained as they appear in the *Tiwei jing* (Sūtra of Trapuṣa).
The second section clarifies the meaning related to the internal world.
All that has been explained above is related to external objects. Why is this so?

Before the Buddha appeared in the world, various seers (*ṛṣi*), worldly scholars, and others also understood this dharma as the correspondence between names and meanings; therefore, it is said that the former refers to the meaning of the external world.
Although these seers possessed worldly wisdom and eloquence and were able to penetrate the nature of the world, [they did not realize its ultimate truth].
If one abides in this discrimination, it ultimately remains a mental activity outside of principle; one has not yet seen reality.
Within the Buddha-dharma, such a person is not called a sage.
They remain a worldling (*pṛthagjana*) cycling through the three realms and twenty-five states of existence, having not yet emerged from birth and death.
If one transforms sentient beings, they are called an "old physician" and are also called a "worldly physician.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
When treated by worldly physicians, once cured, the illness recurs; however,
when treated by the Tathāgata, once cured, it does not recur,
as will be explained below.
Now, regarding what is called the "internal worldly meaning":

this refers to the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world to extensively explain the characteristics of the names and meanings of all doctrinal gates (*śāsana-mukha*) in order to transform sentient beings.
Within the concentrated mind, the practitioner intends to understand the characteristics of the primary subjects and their counterparts within these Buddha-dharma doctrinal gates.
By the power of the roots of goodness of samādhi and wisdom, one immediately becomes aware. How is this known?
It is as previously explained: the meaning of the five precepts taught by the Buddha corresponds to the five viscera.
If the four great elements, the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen realms, the four noble truths, and the twelve links of dependent origination are all within the human body,
then one immediately understands that the meaning of these four great elements is established as a counterpoint.
Regarding the five viscera: wind corresponds to the liver;
fire to the heart;
water to the kidneys; earth to the lungs and spleen.
If one hears the names of the five aggregates (skandhas), one immediately realizes that they correspond to the five internal organs of the body:
form corresponds to the liver,
and consciousness corresponds to the spleen.
Perception corresponds to the heart;
sensation corresponds to the kidneys;
mental formations correspond to the lungs.
Although the names do not follow their numerical order, their meanings are interrelated.
If one hears of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*),
one will likewise immediately know how they correspond to the five internal viscera.
The meaning of the ten bases (*āyatana*) and fifteen elements (*dhātu*) can be understood from this alone.
Now, the two bases and three elements shall be analyzed:
all five consciousnesses constitute the mind base (*manāyatana*) and the mind element (*manodhātu*).
The five external sense objects and the internal mental object (dharmadhātu) constitute the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
This constitutes the interrelation of the twenty-three elements (dhātus).
As for the element of mental consciousness (manovijñānadhātu), it takes the initial arising of the five sensory consciousnesses as its basis.
When mental objects (dharmas) are encountered externally, the consciousness that arises is called the consciousness element (vijñānadhātu).
If one hears that the five faculties also correspond internally to the five viscera,
the faculty of sorrow corresponds to the liver.
The faculty of suffering corresponds to the heart;
the faculty of joy corresponds to the lungs;
the faculty of pleasure corresponds to the kidneys; and the faculty of equanimity corresponds to the spleen.
The five faculties possess all three realms as their causal conditions.
Why is this? Because the faculty of grief corresponds to the desire realm.
The faculty of suffering corresponds to the first dhyāna;
the faculty of joy corresponds to the second dhyāna;
the faculty of pleasure corresponds to the third dhyāna.
The faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) associated with the four dhyānas up to the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) is termed "dhyāna accompanied by equanimity.
One should know that the three realms (*tridhātu*) likewise constitute five viscera, as their meanings are interrelated.
Upon hearing this teaching on the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*), one also realizes that this meaning relates to the five viscera.
Why is this so? Because the desire realm possesses the five faculties,
and these five faculties correspond to the five viscera.
The five viscera govern the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The four great elements correspond to the four modes of birth (*yoni*).
Most beings born from eggs are of the nature of the wind element (*vāyu-mahābhūta*), for their bodies are capable of lightness and elevation.
Most moisture-born beings are of the nature of the water element, because they are born from moisture.
Most womb-born beings belong to the nature of the earth element, because their bodies are heavy and dull.

All beings born by transformation predominantly belong to the nature of the fire element; for while the substance of fire does not exist [prior to birth], it suddenly appears, and they also possess radiance.
Thus, the Tathāgata manifests in order to transform those within the three realms and the four modes of birth.
The teaching of the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the Six Perfections—
know that these three dharmas are like divine elixirs as medicinal remedies, taught specifically to counteract the five viscera, the five faculties, and the aggregates of sentient beings.
Why is this so? As the Buddha taught the meaning of the four truths within a single mind,
one should know that the truth of origination (samudaya-satya) corresponds to the liver because it belongs to the stage of initial birth.
The Truth of Suffering corresponds to the heart, for its fruit is accomplishment;
the Truth of the Path corresponds to the lungs and metal, for it is able to sever and cut;
the Truth of Cessation corresponds to the kidneys and the law of winter storage, for that which already existed returns to non-existence.
Because the One Mind has already opened the way to the Four Noble Truths through the spleen,
it should be understood that the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination and the Six Pāramitās are likewise categorized in this manner.
These three treasuries of Dharma comprehensively encompass all the teaching gates of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, if a practitioner,
with a clear and sharp mind, contemplates the characteristics of the body with discernment,
they will immediately awaken to the names and meanings of all Buddha-dharmas.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra states:
"One who clearly understands this body is one who penetrates all things."
This explains the characteristics of the relationship between the internal meaning and the worldly meaning;
since the intent lies in the profound and subtle, it shall not be described unless one has attained realization.
Second, the explanation that establishes the meaning of the five branches of awakening:
This also has three meanings:
first, descending;
second, ascending.
Third, the threefold ascent.
First, we shall explain the three meanings of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
First, regarding "inferior awakening" and "great awakening": [...]* *Note: The original text contains an ellipsis indicating that the full passage has been truncated.*
Within a tranquil mind, the practitioner fully perceives the characteristics of the two kinds of worlds—internal and external—as previously described.
By discerning that names and referents are distinct, one recognizes them as having the characteristic of separation; therefore, this is called the "world of perceived meaning."
Because it awakens to the meanings of worldly phenomena, it is called "Awakening" (*bodhi*).
A "Great Awakening" (*mahābodhi*) is the awakening that all external names and meanings, though distinct, lack substantial reality and depend solely upon the five viscera.

For example, based on the liver, one explains the precept against killing, the planet Jupiter (*Sakrā*), Mount Tai, the Azure Emperor (*Qīngdì*), the wooden soul (*mùhún*), visual consciousness, benevolence, the *Mao* and *Jiǎo* sections of the *Shī*, the nature of the Earth-trigram (*Zhèn*), and so forth—all such dharmas.
These dharmas are not different from the liver;
the meaning of the liver is not different from the precept of non-killing and so forth.
Because they are thusness, they are called the Great Awakening.
The realization that all other phenomena are like the four internal organs is also thus.
Second, to clarify the realization of great realization:
the practitioner realizes that although the liver is like the precept against killing and so forth, it is likewise for all phenomena.
The liver is not the lungs, spleen, heart, kidneys, or any other such phenomena;
to clearly understand these distinctions is called awakening.
One awakens to the fact that all phenomena, such as the liver, are no different in their impermanence, arising, and ceasing.
The impermanence of the four internal organs and all such phenomena is called Great Awakening (mahābodhi).
Third, to further clarify the distinction between Superior Awakening and Great Awakening:
when a practitioner realizes that the liver and other phenomena possess eight distinct characteristics, this is termed Awakening (bodhi).
To realize that these organs, such as the liver and so forth, are fundamentally empty and quiescent, devoid of any distinct characteristics, is called "Great Awakening" (Mahābodhi).
Thus one discriminates and awakens to the characteristics of Great Awakening, as well as those of the mundane and supramundane.
Although this is the same as what preceded it, there are also differences;
these will naturally become apparent through deep reflection.
Next, the explanation of "reflection" and "great reflection": [text follows].
The meaning and categories regarding the nature of the mind are as previously explained.
This, then, briefly clarifies the characteristics of the factor of awakening of *vitarka* (initial application) within the first *dhyāna* according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The remaining factors—joy (*prīti*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and so forth—should likewise be analyzed one by one in this same manner.
Third, regarding the explanation of the mundane world (*loka*):
this refers to the time when one attains the first *dhyāna* and acquires the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*),
whereby one perceives the phenomena of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) with perfect clarity and distinctness.

It is like beholding an *āmala* fruit within the palm of one's hand; this refers to directly perceiving various phenomena, which differs from the aforementioned method of inferring and discerning worldly affairs through analogical reasoning based on their underlying principles.
Now, regarding the clarification of the mundane world (*loka*), there are two points:
first, correctly perceiving the characteristics of the mundane world;
second, explaining and establishing the meaning of the five factors of *vitarka* and *vicāra*.
Now, regarding the first matter, the characteristics of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*):
because practitioners of superior faculties possess the sharpness of merit and wisdom,
they attain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) upon realizing the first dhyāna due to two causes and conditions.
The first is spontaneous arising;

the second is attained through cultivation. Regarding spontaneous arising: when such a person enters the first dhyāna, they deeply contemplate the three fundamental worldly matters of the mundane realm and are thus able to penetrate the characteristics of the mundane world of meaning.
When awakening to the meaning of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*),
one’s samādhi and wisdom become increasingly profound and sharp, and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) immediately arise;
furthermore, one attains the accomplishment of the eye of derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) produced by the purified four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
By means of this mind of pure form, the eye-powers see all forms and phenomena throughout the ten directions with perfect clarity;
the ability to discern them without confusion is called the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*).
The remaining supernormal powers—the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and the power of the body—are likewise so.

Because they have attained the five supernormal powers, they clearly perceive the distinctions and differences among the realms of form and mind throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time; they see that the various types of sentient beings and the appearances of their lands each differ in every particular.
This is what constitutes the world of those with divergent views.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"By deeply cultivating meditative concentration, one attains the five supernormal powers."
Second, regarding those who cultivate the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and perceive worldly phenomena:
as stated in the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*,
a bhikṣu practicing the Dharma attains the first dhyāna.

Having entered meditative concentration and desiring to attain the supernormal power of the body, he fixes his mind on the tip of the nose and contemplates the inhalation and exhalation of the breath.
He clearly perceives the inhalation and exhalation through ninety-nine thousand pores;
he sees that the body is entirely empty, and even the four great elements are likewise so.
Having contemplated in this way, one becomes detached from the signs of form and attains the supernormal power of the body;
even so it is for the four dhyānas. How does a *dharmānusārin* bhikṣu attain the supernormal power of the eye?
If there is a bhikṣu who attains the first dhyāna and,
observing the inhalation and exhalation of the breath,
truly perceives form; having perceived form, he reflects as follows:
Just as I see all forms of the three periods of time,
I can see them at will whenever I desire;
this is likewise true even up to the fourth dhyāna.
"How does a Dharma-practicing bhikṣu attain the supernormal power of the divine ear?
Kauṇḍinya, if there is a bhikṣu who has attained the first dhyāna..."
Observing the sequence of the inhalation and exhalation of the breath, and even up to the fourth dhyāna, is likewise so.
How does a bhikṣu who practices according to the Dharma attain the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others?
If there is a bhikṣu who observes the inhalation and exhalation of the breath...
When one attains the first dhyāna, one cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā;
this is called the knowledge of others' minds. It is likewise for the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
How does a bhikṣu who practices according to the Dharma attain the knowledge of past lives?
Kauṇḍinya, if there is a bhikṣu who contemplates the inhalation and exhalation of breath and attains the first dhyāna,
he immediately acquires the supernormal power of the divine eye.

Having attained the supernormal power of the divine eye, he observes the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates from the initial stage of *kalala* up to the first existence, and so on, even up to the fourth dhyāna;
it is likewise for all others. Having thus attained the five supernormal powers, he proceeds.

One is then able to see all the various characteristics and differences of the types of beings—both noble and ordinary, across the nine realms—in the lands of the ten directions and three periods of time.
This is called the attainment of supernatural powers through cultivation, whereby one penetrates worldly phenomena without obstruction.
This is the second [section], explaining and establishing the meaning of the five factors of *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought).
Now, first, *vitarka* is explained;
it is also treated according to three meanings, as follows.
Among these two,
there are three superior ones;
those who awaken below and those who awaken greatly.
By means of the supernormal power of the divine eye, one perceives all forms clearly and distinguishes the various categories of sentient beings;
because the differences in their lands and the diversity of their names are manifold, this is called "Awakening."
The Great Awakened One realizes that all things in the world are merely provisional designations;
by contemplating the four great elements with discernment, he perceives no distinctions or differences within the world.
Because it is perfectly clear and distinct, it is called "Great Awakening" (*mahābodhi*).
The same applies to the other four [types of awakening].
Second, the section clarifying the sequence of the various types of awakening leading to Great Awakening.
Using the supernormal power of the divine eye, one perceives that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their material forms have distinct natures; therefore, this is called "Awakening" (*jue*).
Knowing that the four great elements are impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing, and that their nature is without differentiation, is therefore called "Great Awakening" (*da jue*).
The same applies to the other four supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Third, regarding the explanation of the superior awakening and great awakening:
by means of the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*), one clearly perceives that the phenomena of impermanence differ according to their eight aspects (*aṣṭalakṣaṇa*).
This is called awakening (*bodhi*).

Because one awakens to the fact that the dharmas of the eight characteristics are fundamentally empty and quiescent, being of a single characteristic which is no-characteristic, it is called Great Awakening (*mahābodhi*).
The other four [perfections] are likewise.
This is a brief explanation of how, by employing the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), one perceives the phenomena of the world and the characteristics of awakening and great awakening.
One contemplates and reflects upon the nature of the mind;
the characteristics of accomplishing the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*) are as previously described.
The remaining factors of the contemplation— joy, tranquility, concentration, and so forth— should likewise be analyzed one by one in this manner.
The practitioner should know that it is because the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas attain this dhyāna that they rely upon meditative concentration.
Because they have attained indestructible liberation, unimpeded liberation, the three knowledges, and the six supernormal powers,
it is called the contemplation of penetration and clarity.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dhyāna,
One immediately attains the great unimpeded dhāraṇī;
this is likewise true for the four dhyānas up to the fourth.
Next, the second dhyāna is explained.
From this point downward, up to the meditative gate of the cessation-attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the teachings become increasingly profound and subtle.
Since the phenomena and characteristics are manifold, it would be impossible to explain them all in detail; therefore, I shall now separately extract the scriptural passages.
This is merely a brief explanation of the correct meaning.
Regarding what is called the second dhyāna,
the Sūtra says:
The second dhyāna is also called "separation" and is also called "endowment. As for separation,
it is the same as being separated from the five hindrances.
"Endowed" means being fully possessed of three factors, namely:
joy, tranquility, and stability.
The commentary states:
After the initial mind of the first dhyāna, the practitioner becomes weary of the agitation and distraction caused by the *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) of that stage.
He collects his mind in meditative concentration and does not admit these discursive thoughts.
Furthermore, he knows that the higher stages are unreal, and through the contemplation of the truth (*satya*), he observes the cessation of the three natures of body, speech, and mind.
When the mind focuses single-mindedly on internal observation and contemplation, these are extinguished,
and one gives rise to the samādhi of inner purity and great joy.
Within this concentration, one perceives the body as being like a bubble, possessing the practices of the second dhyāna.
Next, the third dhyāna is explained.
The Sūtra says:
"The third dhyāna is also called 'detachment' (viveka)."
"Name" also refers to "possession.
"Free from" means being equally free from the five hindrances;
"possessing" means being fully endowed with the five factors.
This refers to mindfulness, equanimity, wisdom, and meditative concentration.
The commentary states:
Following the second dhyāna, the practitioner becomes weary of the agitation and distraction caused by great joy; he collects his mind and does not accept it.
Furthermore, knowing that the higher stages are not yet truly realized, one collects the mind and contemplates with discernment.
As joy in the Dharma subsides, physical bliss arises;
immediately within this concentration, one perceives the body as being like a cloud, thus accomplishing the practice of the third dhyāna.
Next, the characteristics of the four dhyānas are explained.
The Sūtra says:
"The four dhyānas are also called 'separation' (viveka)."
It is also called "endowed.
As for "detached," it means being equally detached from the five hindrances.
"Endowed with" means being fully possessed of four factors,
namely: mindfulness, equanimity, neither-pain-nor-pleasure, and meditative concentration.
The commentary states:
After the third dhyāna, the practitioner’s mind becomes weary of the dharma of bliss and does not accept it with single-mindedness.

Furthermore, knowing that the fourth dhyāna is not the ultimate truth, he contemplates the three natures; thereupon, his samādhi and wisdom suddenly become clear and pure, arising together with equanimity (*upekṣā*).

The mind does not rely on the wholesome nor does it attach to the unwholesome; abiding precisely within that state, one perceives the body as a reflection while possessing the practice of the four dhyānas.
Next, the station of infinite space (ākāśāyatana) is explained.
The Sūtra says:
"Contemplating the body with revulsion,
one becomes detached from the signs of the body and from all tactile sensations of joy and pleasure."
Discerning the characteristics of form and becoming detached from the aggregate of form,
one contemplates the sphere of infinite space with a single mind;
this is called a bhikṣu attaining the concentration of the sphere of infinite space.
The commentary states:
This may be understood in two senses.
First, as a general observation spanning both above and below.
Second, regarding those that pertain only to their own level and above:
as for those that apply throughout both the lower and upper levels, the Sūtra states:
"By contemplating the body, one becomes weary of it and detaches from the characteristics of the body."
One deeply understands that the faults and transgressions of the body in the desire realm are not merely one;
the constituent parts of the body are all unobtainable.
The three types of contact—such as the body and so forth—are contrasted with the first, second, and third dhyānas.
Regarding "discerning visible forms":
this refers to discerning the distinct differences between the material bodies of the desire realm up to those of the four dhyānas.
One also knows that the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) is unreal and has not yet transcended material phenomena (*rūpadharma*).
The transcendence of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the contemplation of the sphere of infinite space are both as previously described.
Within the fundamental dhyāna (*mauladhyāna*), the three kinds of material phenomena are extinguished, and it corresponds with empty space.
Regarding both [explanations] as being interpreted in terms of their own respective stages:
