"contemplating the body with revulsion and distancing oneself from the characteristics of the body" means one feels revulsion toward the shadow-like form that obscures the mind.
One observes that even these reflected forms are unobtainable.
Regarding the three types of contact associated with the body and so forth, they have already ceased prior to the faculty of distinct joy (*prīti-indriya*).
This refers to the arising of contact from form in the fourth dhyāna, which gives rise to the mind's three types of contact.
One who discriminates the characteristics of form discerns that the joy and bliss of the four dhyānas, as well as forms like shadows, are all deceptive.
One distances oneself from the aggregate of form and contemplates the immeasurable sphere of space.
It is no different from what was previously explained.
Next, to clarify the characteristics of the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*),
the Sūtra says:
If there is a bhikṣu who cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā, observing the mind, intellect,
and consciousness, he knows for himself that this body does not undergo the three types of feeling.
Because one has attained detachment from these three kinds of sensation,
this is called a bhikṣu who has attained the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*).
Explanation:
Regarding "the mind following the intention":
"mind" refers to the equanimity that takes emptiness as its object, entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana-samādhi*) by way of the three natures.
The practitioner employs samādhi to encompass wisdom.

Although one knows that the three natures are not real, in order to avoid the difficulty of [falling into] nihilism, one focuses the mind on consciousness and thus enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
To know for oneself that this body does not undergo the three types of feeling is [the practice of the sphere of nothingness].
Although the fourfold categorization of form is absent in the sphere of infinite space, it still undergoes the latter three categories;

however, when one enters meditative absorption in the sphere of infinite consciousness by taking consciousness as the object, one is completely detached from the fourfold categorization of the realm of form.
All four types of feeling belong to consciousness.
Therefore, it is said that one knows for oneself that this body does not undergo the three feelings;
this may also be stated as not undergoing the three feelings of suffering, pleasure, and so forth.
Having already attained the detachment from these three kinds of feeling, it is called the mark of the concentration on the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*).
Next, to clarify the mark of the concentration on the sphere of limited consciousness (*parīttavijñānāyatana-samādhi*),
the Sūtra says:
If there is a bhikṣu who contemplates the emptiness of the three periods of time,
knowing that all conditioned phenomena arise and cease, and that the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness also arise and cease;
having made this contemplation, he then sequentially contemplates consciousness.
This consciousness of mine is neither consciousness nor non-consciousness.
If it were non-consciousness, it would be called quiescence;
how then could I seek to sever this consciousness?
This is called attaining the concentration of the sphere of limited consciousness (*parīttābhijñāna*).
The commentary explains:
"Contemplating that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) throughout the three periods of time are empty, and that they both arise and cease."
One deeply contemplates that the mental factors of one’s own stage, as well as those of the higher and lower stages, all possess the characteristics of conditioned phenomena— deceptive and unreal.
To contemplate consciousness in succession means to contemplate both the sphere of consciousness and consciousness itself.
That which is neither consciousness nor non-consciousness is the thorough understanding that all phenomena are unapprehendable.
That which is non-consciousness is called quiescence.
"How shall I now seek to sever this consciousness? Thus,
he applied the skillful means for the cessation of consciousness by focusing on non-conscious phenomena,
entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of limited consciousness (*parittābhijñāna*).
Next, to clarify the perception of non-existence:
the Sūtra states,
"If there is a bhikṣu who possesses the perception of non-existence."
He reflects thus:
"This perception of mine is suffering, it is an outflow, it is a sore, it is an abscess, it is not tranquility.
If I could abandon such a perception as well as the perception of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
This is called tranquility.
If there is a bhikṣu who is able to sever such [states of] neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he is said to have attained the door of liberation of non-perception. Why is this?
A bhikṣu practicing the Dharma reflects thus:
"Whether there is the perception of feeling,
or the perception of consciousness."
Whether it be the perception of contact, the perception of emptiness,
or the perception of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
all such as these are termed coarse perceptions.
If I now cultivate the samādhi of non-perception, I shall be able to permanently sever such perceptions as these;
therefore, I regard the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as a state of tranquility.
Having seen this, he enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Having neither grasped nor clung, he immediately shatters ignorance.
Having shattered ignorance, he is said to have attained the fruit of arhatship.
The commentary states:
That which is not associated with mental perception is the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
It is characterized by suffering, outflows (*āsrava*), and so forth.
This is precisely the contemplation of the faults and transgressions of the attainment of non-perception.
If I can sever such states of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
this is called tranquility.
"Neither-perception" refers to the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
As for "neither-non-perception," one has already perceived the faults of the higher stage and should eliminate them.
It is "tranquil" because it transcends the attainment of non-perception.
One attains the tranquility of nirvana.
If there is a bhikṣu who can sever such non-perception and attain the door of liberation of non-ideation, [he shall likewise do so].
All concentrations within the three realms are termed "perception" (saṃjñā).
Now, by severing this perception, one attains the samādhi of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samādhi);
therein, one is able to destroy ignorance and give rise to the untainted (anāsrava) state within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
One attains the fruit of Arhatship and realizes Nirvana.
Regarding the passage "If a Dharma-practicing bhikṣu has [abandoned] sensation and perception," and so forth, this is a re-explanation of the meaning stated above;
the significance is clear.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states that the first three types of meditative absorption are abandoned by both paths,
whereas the final fourth absorption can never be abandoned by the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
Although ordinary beings may be free from coarse afflictions in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), [they remain bound by subtle ones].
It also possesses ten kinds of subtle phenomena;
because it lacks coarse afflictions,
all ordinary worldlings take this to be nirvana.
The detailed explanation is as given in the sutra.
The commentary states:

This clarifies that the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) of ordinary beings and others cannot give rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*) [knowledge] within the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The subsequent sutra states:
"Kauṇḍinya, if a bhikṣu cultivates the noble path..."
Regarding the passage, "One who feels weary of and detaches from the four dhyānas and the four spheres of emptiness contemplates the path adorned by cessation," the commentary explains:
this clarifies that through a general contemplation of perception (*saṃjñā*), one subsequently enters into cessation (*nirodha*).
This meaning shall be explained in detail below in the section on the liberations (*vimokṣa*).
When a practitioner enters this dharma-gate, they do not take the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) as a realization;
rather, they fulfill all Buddha-dharmas through great compassion and skillful means (*upāya*).
Arising in the six supernormal powers to deliver and liberate sentient beings—
this explains the Mahāyāna according to one dharma-gate.
*The Sequential Dharma-Gate of Explaining the Dhyānapāramitā*, Scroll Eight.
The Sequential Dharma-Gate of the Explanation of the Dhyāna-Pāramitā, Scroll Nine.
Spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty;
recorded by his disciple Fashen.

The Disciple’s Consecration: A Revised Commentary on the Śramaṇa-pāramitā-sūtra, Section Seven: The Cultivation and Realization of the Five Sciences; Part Five: The Cultivation and Realization of Untainted Dhyāna (Anāsrava-dhyāna).
Now, it is explained that there are two kinds of untainted dhyāna.
The first is the untainted [wisdom] that acts as an antidote;
the second is the untainted [wisdom] that takes principle as its object.
Thus, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* says:
There are two kinds of practice:
first, the practice of wisdom;
second, the practice of conduct.
The "practitioner of practice" refers to the nine notions of repulsiveness (*navasaṃjñā*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), and other such antidotes that are untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because they give rise to practice by taking phenomena as objects, they serve as antidotes to destroy all afflictions.
The "practice of practice" refers to untainted practice (*anāsrava-caryā*).
Second, the "practice of wisdom" refers to the Four Noble Truths.
Because the correct contemplation of the emptiness of the twelve links of dependent origination cuts off delusions by means of principle,
it is called the "wisdom-practice" and "outflow-free practice.
This first preceding explanation corresponds to the antidote for outflows.
This is explained according to nine types of dharma-gates:
first, the nine perceptions;
second, the eight recollections.
The thirty perceptions,
the four and eight liberations,
the five and eight bases of mastery, and the ten all-encompassing bases.
7. The nine successive attainments;
8. The lion’s bound-fleet samādhi;
9. The leap-over samādhi.
Now, these nine types of dhyāna are collectively explained as antidotes to the outflows (anāsrava).
Furthermore, the meanings regarding their sequential order and degrees of depth are all as previously stated in the first fascicle.
Now, within these nine types of dharma-gates,
there are two kinds of untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*) that serve as antidotes:
first, the path that destroys phenomena.
Second is the path that does not destroy the Dharma.
That which destroys the Dharma consists of the nine notions, the eight recollections, and the ten notions.
One should skillfully cultivate these three.
If one gives rise to true outflow-free [wisdom],
one immediately becomes an Arhat of the "Destructible Dharma" type.
Second is the path of the "Indestructible Dharma."
That is to say, the liberations, the bases of mastery, the bases of totality, the nine successive attainments, the lion’s stretch, the leap-over samādhis, and so forth.
Having perfected these meditations,
he gives rise to true outflow-free wisdom and becomes an unshakable Dharma Great Arhat.
Now, we provide a general explanation of the three types of dharma-gates within the first [section],
the Contemplation on the Destruction of Dharmas (*dharmavibhavadarśana*). As for why these three dharma-gates are called the "Contemplation on the Destruction of Dharmas":
The practitioner’s mind grows weary of the six desires, regarding them as if they were enemies or thieves;
therefore, one cultivates the nine contemplations as an antidote.
When performing this visualization, although the six desires are destroyed, much fear arises.
If one cultivates the eight kinds of right mindfulness, fear will be eliminated.
Once the mind’s craving has thinned and there is no longer any dread,
at that time, if one wishes to sever the fetters of the three realms, one should diligently cultivate the ten perceptions.
When one accomplishes the ten perceptions,
one immediately slays the thieves of the fetters and becomes an arhat.
This person has already destroyed and extinguished the bodily characteristics of the desire realm.
Because they are unable to fully perfect the contemplation of the three realms, nor to cultivate and refine the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*) and the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*),
they are called "corrupters of the Dharma. [The questioner] asks:
What is the difference between the nine perceptions and the ten perceptions?
The answer is:
there are both differences and non-differences.
As for the differences: the nine perceptions are like binding a thief;
the ten perceptions are like killing a thief.
The nine perceptions are for beginners.
The ten perceptions constitute the accomplishment;
the nine perceptions constitute the cause;
the ten perceptions constitute the fruit.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"There are two gates to the nectar of immortality.
The first is the gate of the contemplation of impurity."
Second is the gateway of ānāpāna.
As for "not being different," it means that by skillfully cultivating the nine perceptions (navasaṃjñā),
one is thereby fully endowed with the ten perceptions (daśasaṃjñā).
This meaning shall be clarified below.
First, regarding the explanation of the nine contemplations (navasaṃjñā): the first is the contemplation of bloating (vyādhmātaka-saṃjñā).
2. The perception of a bloated corpse;
3. The perception of a blood-smeared corpse;
4. The perception of a festering corpse.
5. The perception of a livid corpse;
6. The perception of being devoured;
7. The perception of a scattered corpse.
The eight contemplations on bones and the ninth contemplation on burning—
these nine types of dharma-gates are collectively termed "contemplations" (saṃjñā).
It is able to transform the mind and transform perception; that is to say, it is able to transform the inverted perception of purity within the impure.
Therefore, it is called "perception" (*saṃjñā*).
Now, the nine perceptions will be explained.
This is immediately expanded into four points:
first, clarifying cultivation and realization;
second, clarifying the application of antidotes.
The Dharma subsumed by the three vidyās;
the path leading to liberation through the four vidyās;
and the practitioner who cultivates and realizes them through the one vidyā.
The practitioner should first maintain the purity of the precepts so that the mind feels no regret and easily receives the methods of contemplation.
This can destroy the thieves of afflictions such as sensual desire;
therefore, at this time, one should first [do so].

Observe when a person first dies: speech and conversation cease, the breath exhaled does not return, and suddenly they have died; the vital energy is extinguished, the body grows cold, and there is no longer any sensation or awareness.
The members of the household are struck with alarm and grief, wailing to heaven and crying out to the earth.
"Having just spoken these words, you have suddenly departed;
this is a great terror from which there is no escape."
For example, it is like the fire at the end of an eon that burns everything without exception.
As a verse says:
"When death arrives, there is no distinction between the poor and the wealthy; for one who has not diligently practiced the wholesome Dharma."
Neither noble nor base, neither old nor young—none are exempt.
There is no prayer that can save, nor any place of deception;
there is no resistance by which one may escape. Of all beings, none are exempt.
The nature of death is defined as the state of eternal separation from those one loves, which all who are born detest.
Although it is known to be loathsome, there is no one who can escape it;
my own body will surely become like this before long.
I am no different from wood or stone, lacking any discerning knowledge.
I should not now greedily cling to the five desires and fail to perceive the arrival of death, becoming like cattle or sheep.
Although cattle, sheep, birds, and beasts see the dead, they leap, bound, and roar, yet remain unable to awaken to the truth themselves.
Since I have already obtained a human body and am able to distinguish between the beautiful and the ugly,
I ought to seek the nectar-like Dharma of immortality.
As it is said in a verse:
Though the six sense-faculties are fully complete and their wisdom and discernment are clear and sharp,
they do not seek the Way or the Dharma; they receive this body in vain,
for even birds and beasts possess such intelligence, yet they indulge themselves in sensual pleasures.
Yet they do not know the skillful means; having already obtained a human body and cultivated virtuous deeds for the sake of the Way,
they merely indulge themselves and do not know how to practice wholesome conduct— how are they any different from those [other beings]?
Sentient beings in the three evil realms cannot cultivate the karma of the Path;
having now obtained this human body, one should strive for one's own benefit.
Having reflected thus, the practitioner should proceed.

One should then take a person dear to oneself, whether male or female, strip them of their clothes so they lie on the ground in the nude, and contemplate this corpse before one with single-minded samādhi as if it were a dead body; by doing so, the mind becomes deeply startled and fearful, thereby shattering the heart of attachment.
This is a brief explanation of how the perception of death serves as the preliminary practice for the nine perceptions.
Furthermore, there are two types of those who cultivate the nine perceptions:
first, those of sharp faculties.
Second, there are those of dull faculties.
If a person of sharp faculties maintains their mind in contemplation while visualizing signs such as the bloating of a corpse, they will achieve success.

However, if a person of dull faculties cannot achieve success through such mental visualization, they must observe a person who has just died, go to the site of the corpse, grasp these signs, and then fix their mind upon them for cultivation.
Once the signs have become distinct and the mental visualization is perfected, one immediately enters samādhi.
Thereafter, even when separated from the corpse, one sees it according to one's visualization.
First is the visualization of bloating.
The practitioner, observing the corpse by its side, sees it bloated like a leather bag filled with wind, different from its original appearance.
Within this body there is no master; it is only deluded consciousness that drives and controls seeing, hearing, speaking, and so forth.
Having deceived yourself with this, where do you go now?
You see only an empty house and a bloated corpse with its neck held straight.

This body’s form was once seductive, with delicate skin, crimson lips, white teeth, long eyes, a straight nose, a flat forehead, and high eyebrows; such a beautiful body used to delude the hearts of men.
Now, seeing only this bloated corpse, where is its beauty?
The characteristics of male and female can no longer be discerned.
Taking these very signs, one should contemplate them as being like those of the person one loves.
Having thus rebuked himself, he thought: "This mind of desire is a foul-smelling sack of excrement, bloated and loathsome.
How can it be worth craving and clinging to, such that one sinks into it?
I reflect that my own body has not yet escaped this very condition."
The first samādhi of single-mindedness eliminates worldly greed and attachment.
The second is the contemplation of disintegration.
The practitioner further observes a corpse being blown by the wind and scorched by the sun until it becomes increasingly parched, shattered, and lies broken upon the ground.
Broken into six parts, the five viscera are filled with excrement and urine, overflowing with foul impurities;
observing it in this way, that which I wear is not to be cherished or delighted in.
I was deluded by ignorance and deceived by this thin skin that is but a bag of excrement;
like a moth flying into a flame,
I craved its bright appearance while disregarding the calamity of burning my body.
Reflecting thus, "My own body is likewise;
it has not yet escaped this law," one should,
with single-minded samādhi, eliminate worldly craving and attachment.
Third, the visualization of blood-smeared and overflowing [corpses]:
The practitioner further contemplates a corpse that has been destroyed, with pus and blood overflowing everywhere from head to foot, staining it;
it is impure, foul-smelling, putrid, bloated, and unfit for proximity.
When I examine those whom I love with this perspective, there is nothing therein to be cherished or delighted in.
Driven by delusion, I have remained submerged in this defilement and impurity; where could I find anything truly good?

Reflecting that one's own body has not yet escaped this condition, one should single-mindedly enter samādhi and cultivate the four perceptions of putrefaction to eliminate worldly craving and attachment.

The practitioner contemplates a corpse that, over the gradual passage of time, is drenched by wind, heat, and water; from its nine apertures, worms and pus flow forth, and the skin and flesh rot away in every place.
As it flows and pools upon the ground, its stench increases; that which I once cherished—this beautiful countenance—is now thus stupefied.
Now that I see it putrid and rotten, worse than excrement, how can I still harbor attachment?
Reflecting to oneself that one’s own body has not yet escaped this condition, one should single-mindedly enter the samādhi that removes worldly craving and love.
Fifth is the contemplation on the bloated corpse (*vinīlaka-saṃjñā*).

The practitioner further observes that as the pus and blood of the corpse gradually diminish and it is transformed by wind and sun, the skin and flesh become yellowish-red, mottled with dark and bluish-black bruises, and emit a foul odor.
Reflecting on how those I love have further increased my attachment, I consider where the color of the peach blossoms that once deluded me has now gone.
Thinking thus, I realize that my own body has not yet escaped this law; therefore, with single-minded samādhi, I shall eliminate worldly craving and cultivate the six perceptions of repulsiveness.

The practitioner further contemplates a corpse being devoured by maggots and worms, its eyes pecked out by crows, chewed upon by foxes and dogs, and torn apart by tigers and wolves until the body is mangled, dismembered, and fallen apart—so loathsome. He reflects that this very person he once loved was previously possessed of a clean physique, adorned with fine garments, and deluded by her own coquettish charms.
Now seeing its destruction and the total loss of its original characteristics, it is truly loathsome.
I reflect that my own body has not yet escaped this law; therefore, with single-minded samādhi, I shall eliminate worldly greed and craving.
Seventh is the contemplation on dispersion.

The practitioner further contemplates a corpse being torn apart by birds and beasts until its body is fragmented and scattered; it is blown by the wind and scorched by the sun, its tendons severed and its bones separated, with the head and limbs strewn about in confusion.
When one observes those whom I love in this manner, where is their human form?
Reflecting thus upon my own body, I realize it has not yet escaped these phenomena; therefore, with single-minded samādhi, I shall eliminate worldly craving and attachment.
8. Contemplation on the Skeleton.
The practitioner further observes that the skin, flesh, and other parts of the corpse have completely vanished, seeing only white bones.
There are two kinds of bones seen.
First, one sees the sinews still connected;
second, the sinews are exhausted and the bones are separated.
Furthermore, there are two other types.
First, it is defiled by residual blood, fat, and grease;
second, the bones are as white as jade or shells.
When my beloved looks upon it in this way, the skull is terrifying, its hardened appearance more formidable than that of tiles or stones.
The soft and delicate sensations are all suddenly lost.
He reflects to himself: "My own body cannot escape this law. With single-minded samādhi, he eliminates worldly craving and attachment through the nine perceptions of burning.
The practitioner further proceeds to a charnel ground.
There he may see many grasses and trees burning as corpses are consumed; their bellies burst open, fat gushes forth, and the crackling smoke and stench are utterly terrifying.
Or one may see only the white bones being burned, the smoke and flames blazing intensely until the fuel is exhausted and the fire extinguished, leaving the form identical to ash and dust;
even if they were neither burned nor buried, they would likewise return to obliteration.
When one contemplates those whom I love through this perspective, all their physical characteristics are seen to be utterly exhausted—far worse than the edge of a blade.
Their bodies, once bathed, perfumed, adorned with flowers and powders, soft, plump, and delicate, and possessed of a clear, warm complexion, were merely instruments of flattery and deceit.
These things that delude people have now all been worn away; where, indeed, do they exist?

Reflecting thus, [one realizes] that one's own body has not yet escaped this law. Therefore, with single-minded samādhi, one should eliminate worldly greed and craving through the two types of clarity and the nine meditations on repulsiveness as antidotes.
Once the practitioner has mastered the nine perceptions (navasaṃjñā),
they must necessarily increase their contemplation and practice them again until the meditative cultivation becomes mature and sharp;
at whatever time they perform the observation, the mind will immediately correspond with meditative concentration (samādhi).
Maintain your thoughts with a mind free from distraction;
this can destroy the six desires and eliminate worldly craving and attachment.
As for the six desires:
First, desire for physical form;
second, desire for appearance;
third, desire for deportment and gestures.
Fourth, the desire for speech and sounds;
fifth, the desire for fine and smooth textures;
sixth, the desire for human forms.
Within these six desire realms, six kinds of attachment can arise.
Regarding attachment to color, there are those who are stained by attachment to red;
or reddish-white, or yellowish-white, or black, or reddish-black, or blue, or bluish-white, or the color of a peach blossom.
Ignorant fools, seeing such forms, become submerged, deluded, and intoxicated.
If there were someone who desired physical appearance,
they would merely cling to it, for their face was like the full moon.
One cultivates long eyes, high eyebrows, a slender waist, and delicate fingers; such marks of excellence are upright and majestic, and the mind immediately becomes deluded and attached.

As for those who desire dignified demeanor, there are some who become attached to such deportment and gestures—walking with expansive grace, raising the brows, knitting the face, and smiling with full, coquettish charm—whereby they instantly give rise to passionate defilement.

Regarding those with a desire for speech, there are some who love only the sound of words; when they hear eloquent and flowery discourse that accords with their own inclinations and intentions—phrasing that is refined and pure, and songs of praise that move the heart—they are delighted.

Fools of shallow understanding are deluded by this; those who desire smoothness and softness may simply love the suppleness of the body’s form, its plump skin, and its radiant luster, as if it were cotton-wool (tūla).
When cold, it seeks warmth; when hot, it seeks coolness.
It welcomes massage and clothing, and is perfumed with incense.
Yet, submerged in such ordinary delusions, it is thereby brought to peril and ruin.
Regarding "various desires":
there are those who are attached to all five matters.
Regarding "human desires": [they are as follows].
There are those who do not cling to any of these five things;
they only cling to the mark of a person, whether male or female.
Even if they see the aforementioned five things, if they do not obtain the person they love, they still remain unstained by attachment.
If they encounter someone who suits their fancy, they can renounce what the world prizes and suddenly cast away even their very lives.
Thus, the six heavens of the desire realm delude sentient beings life after life,
causing them to sink into birth and death and drown in the three miserable realms.
One cannot attain liberation.
If one can skillfully cultivate the nine perceptions as an antidote to eliminate them,
then the thieves of the six desires will be shattered and dispersed, and one will swiftly realize nirvana.
Why is this? First, the perception of death destroys the two desires for deportment and speech;
next, the perceptions of bloating, disintegration, and being devoured destroy the desire for physical form.

Next, by contemplating the visualization of blood-smeared corpses, the visualization of bluish lividity, and the visualization of festering and putrefaction, one largely eliminates desire for physical form.
Next, by the contemplation of skeletons and the contemplation of burning, one largely eliminates desire for smoothness and softness.

Through these nine visualizations, one eliminates miscellaneous desires as well as the desire for the physical characteristics of the person to whom one is attached. These are consumed [by the meditations].

Through the contemplation of the repulsive, the contemplation of the dismembered, and the contemplation of the bones, one specifically eliminates the perception of a person; because one sees only the remaining, being devoured, scattered, and bleached white bones, and no longer perceives a person within them to whom one could become attached, these nine contemplations are able to destroy the fetters of desire, and thin out both hatred and delusion.
Because the three poisons are attenuated, the mountain of the ninety-eight latent tendencies (anuśaya) all trembles.
Gradually advancing upon the Path, one uses the Vajra-samādhi to shatter the mountain of fetters and attain the path of the Three Vehicles.
Although the nine perceptions are meditations on impurity, they are capable of accomplishing great matters;
they are like a corpse in the great ocean upon which a drowning person can rely to cross over to safety.
Regarding the phenomena subsumed under the three knowledges (*trividyā*):
these nine perceptions of the mind take the body of the desire realm as their object and are subsumed within the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
They are also a small portion of the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
It is either subsumed under the desire realm, or subsumed under the first or second dhyānas.
A person who has not yet abandoned desire and possesses a distracted mind attains that which is bound to the desire realm;
a person who has abandoned desire attains that which belongs to the form realm.
The eight perceptions, beginning with the bloated (*aughata*), are subsumed within the desire realm, the first dhyāna, and the second dhyāna.
The perception of the pure bone (*śaṅkalā*) is subsumed within the desire realm, the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna;
it is absent in the third dhyāna because of the abundance of pleasure (*sukha*) therein.
Regarding the four clarifications on the nine perceptions for entering the Path:
there are two ways to cultivate the nine perceptions.

If one cultivates them by following the specific objects, this can only suppress the fetters of the desire realm; subsequently, one must separately cultivate the ten perceptions to sever the afflictions of views and thought and achieve the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Second, if one skillfully cultivates the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*), one will possess the ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*) as they engage with practice and enter into principle;
thus, it is unnecessary to laboriously cultivate the ten perceptions through other separate gates.
Why is this so? It is as follows:
The practitioner contemplates that at the time of a person's death, their movements and speech cease in an instant;
the body becomes bloated, putrefies, disintegrates, and undergoes various transformations.
This is impermanent.
If one is attached to this body, then at the time of its impermanent destruction, it is suffering.
If it is impermanent, suffering, and lacks autonomy, then it is non-self.
Because it is impure, impermanent, suffering, and non-self,
the world is not to be delighted in or clung to.
One should contemplate the body in this way.
Although food is in the mouth, brain-saliva flows down and mixes with spittle to form flavor;
yet this is no different from vomiting.
Once it has entered the belly, it immediately becomes filth and excrement.
This is precisely the perception of the impurity of food.
By means of these nine perceptions, one contemplates the body as impermanent, subject to change, and perishing moment by moment;
this is the perception of death.
By means of these nine perceptions, one becomes weary of worldly pleasures;
knowing that the severance of afflictions is itself peace and quiescence is precisely the perception of cessation.
By means of these nine perceptions, one obstructs all afflictions; this is precisely the perception of detachment.
Because one grows weary of the world through the nine perceptions, one knows the cessation of the five aggregates.
Furthermore, there is no need to give rise to thoughts of dwelling in safety;
this is precisely the "perception of exhaustion.
If one can thus skillfully cultivate the nine perceptions, one will possess the ten perceptions and sever the afflictions of views and mental outflows.
It should be known that such a person will certainly proceed toward the path of the three vehicles.

Furthermore, it is taught in the Mahāyāna that if one skillfully cultivates the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*), this opens the gateway to the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*);
once the application of mindfulness to the body is opened, it opens the gateways to the [remaining] three applications of mindfulness.
The four foundations of mindfulness open the gateway to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
the thirty-seven factors open the gateway to nirvana.
By entering nirvana, one extinguishes all sorrow and suffering.
Because Bodhisattvas have compassion for sentient beings,
although they are able to enter nirvana through the nine contemplations,
they do not take the realization of the limit of reality as their final attainment.
Why is this? If there were no characteristic of gratification within form, sentient beings would not become attached to form;
if there were no characteristic of detachment within form, they likewise could not attain liberation from form.
Because there is flavor within form, sentient beings become attached to form.
Because there is the characteristic of detachment within form, sentient beings attain liberation from form.
Yet flavor is not identical to detachment, and detachment is not identical to flavor.
Apart from the sphere of flavor there is no sphere of liberation; apart from the sphere of liberation there is no sphere of flavor.
One should know that form itself is neither bondage nor liberation.
At that time, one does not follow saṃsāra, nor does one realize [nirvāṇa].
Nirvana consists solely in the great compassion that takes pity on all sentient beings;
within this contemplation of impurity, one accomplishes all Buddha-dharmas.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
The nine perceptions are themselves the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Next, the dharma-gate of the eight recollections is explained.
As for what are called the eight recollections:
First, mindfulness of the Buddha; second, mindfulness of the Dharma;
third, mindfulness of the Sangha;
fourth, mindfulness of the precepts.
5. Mindfulness of relinquishment;
6. Mindfulness of the devas;
7. Mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation.
The eighth is the recollection of death. These eight are collectively termed "recollections" because,
within a state of single-minded focus, one maintains mindfulness and does not forget them.
This is termed "recollection" (smṛti).
Now, the explanation of the eight recollections shall be divided into three points.
First, to clarify the purpose of the teaching.
Second, the clarification of cultivation and realization; third, the clarification of the signs of entering the Path.
First, regarding the purpose of the teaching:
the disciples of the Buddha, in forest hermitages (*āraṇya*), empty dwellings, among burial mounds, in mountain forests, or in wildernesses.
Having well cultivated the nine contemplations on impurity and feeling revulsion for the body as something external, one reflects:
"How can I continue to follow after this base, impure sack of stinking excrement and urine?"
At that time, he was struck with such sudden terror that the hair on his entire body stood on end;
furthermore, the evil Māra assumed various forms and shapes to come and terrify him,
seeking to cause his path to regress and perish.
For this reason, one practices mindfulness of the Buddha.
Following the nine perceptions, the eight recollections are taught to eliminate fear,
as stated in the sūtras.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you have a mind of fear while in a forest hermitage (āraṇya),
at that time you should recollect the Buddha, and your terror will immediately cease."
If one does not mindfully recollect the Buddha, one should mindfully recollect the Dharma, and fear will be eliminated.
If one does not mindfully recollect the Dharma, one should mindfully recollect the Saṃgha, and fear will be eliminated.
Thus, we know that these three recollections are taught for the purpose of removing fear.
Question: The Sūtra states that the three mindfulnesses serve as the causes and conditions for removing fear; what then is the purpose of the subsequent five mindfulnesses? Answer:
When that bhikṣu personally practices generosity and maintains the precepts, his fear is immediately eliminated. Why is this?
Because if he were to break the precepts, he would fear falling into hell.
If one is stingy and greedy, fearing falling into the realm of hungry ghosts or into poverty, one should reflect:
"I possess these pure precepts and acts of giving."
Then, one rejoices that all the higher deities are the fruit and reward of generosity and the observance of precepts, and thinks:
"I too possess such merit.
For this reason, one recollects the devas.
It can also cause fear such that [the mind] does not arise within the sixteen modes of practice;
when recollecting *ānāpāna*, even the subtle mental awareness is extinguished.
How much more so should one fear coarse discursive thoughts?
One who contemplates death reflects that the body of the five aggregates arises and perishes from moment to moment;
from birth until now, it has always been accompanied by death.
Why, then, do you now fear death?
Although these five forms of mindfulness are not explained individually here,
one should know that they serve to profoundly eliminate all fear.
Why is this? It is difficult to remove fear by recollecting the virtues of others,
whereas it is easy to remove dread by recollecting one's own virtues.
For this reason, they are not explained separately.
Second, it clarifies the cultivation and realization of the eight recollections.
Regarding the recollection of the Buddha: if a practitioner is in an araṇya (forest hermitage),...
If the mind is filled with fear, one should practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
The Buddha is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha,
up to and including Bhagavān.
He is endowed with the ten titles,
the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics,
great loving-kindness and great compassion, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities.
With the immeasurable light of wisdom and supernormal powers, he is able to deliver immeasurable sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
He is my great teacher who protects and delivers all; what should I fear?
If one recollects with single-minded focus, fear is immediately eliminated.
Second, regarding the recollection of the Dharma:
the practitioner should reflect upon this Dharma as follows.
Skillful emergence results in the fruits of this present life, free from all feverish afflictions;
it does not depend on time to reach the excellent destination, but penetrates it with unimpeded mastery.
"Skillful emergence" means skillfully explaining the two truths so that they do not contradict one another.
This Dharma is called "skillful emergence" because it can emerge from the two extremes.
Regarding those who obtain results in the present life: the teachings of all non-Buddhists lack results in the present life;
only within the Buddha-Dharma do causes and conditions arise through successive transformation.
That is to say, because one's observance of the precepts is pure, the mind attains freedom from regret;
because the mind attains freedom from regret, there arises joy in the Dharma;
because joy in the Dharma arises, the mind attains happiness.
Because one attains mental happiness, one is able to collect the mind;
because the mind is collected, one attains knowledge of reality as it is;
because one attains knowledge of reality as it is, one attains disenchantment.
Through the attainment of weary detachment, one attains freedom from desire;
through freedom from desire, one attains liberation;
and as the fruit of liberation, one attains nirvana.
This is called attaining the retribution of the present life.
"Without feverish affliction" means being free from the feverish afflictions of the three poisons and of birth-and-death.
"Not waiting for time" means:
The followers of various non-Buddhist paths must necessarily wait for specific times and seasons to receive their essential teachings.
The Buddha-dharma is not like this; it is, for example, like firewood that ignites immediately upon meeting fire without waiting for a particular time.

Those who reach the "good destination" through the practice of the Buddha-dharma will certainly attain the joyful fruits of the human and celestial realms, as well as the state of nirvana of the three vehicles.
One who attains unimpeded penetration does so by virtue of obtaining the three seals of the Dharma; thus, one attains unimpeded penetration.
When I cultivate such dharmas as these, what should I fear?
By recollecting them with single-mindedness, fear is immediately eliminated.
Regarding the third recollection, the recollection of the Sangha:
the practitioner should recollect the Sangha;
the Sangha is the community of the Buddha’s disciples.
They are endowed with the fivefold Dharma-body.
Within this, there are four pairs and eight classes, totaling twenty-seven individuals,
who are worthy of receiving offerings and reverential service.
The unsurpassed field of merit in the world,
namely, the community of śrāvakas or the community of pratyekabuddhas.
If the Bodhisattva Saṃgha possesses immeasurable wisdom capable of rescuing and liberating sentient beings who are difficult to save and cross over from suffering—
if such a noble assembly is my true companion, what should I fear?
If one recollects with single-mindedness, fear will immediately be eliminated.
Regarding the fourth mindfulness, that of the precepts:
the practitioner should reflect upon these precepts as follows.
The dwelling place that can ward off all evils and provide security consists of two kinds of precepts:
namely, contaminated precepts (*sāsrava-śīla*) and uncontaminated precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*).
Furthermore, there are two other kinds.
First, the morality of restraint;
second, the morality coexistent with meditative concentration.
The morality of restraint can prevent all evils, whereby the body attains tranquility.
The precepts concurrent with meditative concentration can obstruct all afflictions so that the mind attains internal bliss;
the untainted precepts can destroy the root of ignorance and all evils so that one attains the bliss of liberation.
Since I cultivate such dharmas, what should I fear?
If one recollects with single-mindedness, fear will be immediately eliminated.
Regarding the five recollections on relinquishment:
the practitioner should reflect as follows.
There are two kinds of relinquishment:
first, the relinquishment of giving;
second, the relinquishment of all afflictions.
There are two kinds of giving:
first, the giving of material wealth;
second, the giving of the Dharma.
These two kinds of relinquishment are both termed "relinquishment" (*tyāga*).
It is the very root of all wholesome dharmas.
The practitioner reflects: "Since I have possessed this body, I have likewise possessed such merit of relinquishment and giving."
"What should I fear?
By recollecting this with single-minded attention, fear is immediately dispelled.
These are the six recollections of the devas.
The practitioner should reflect that all those gods, from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations,
were born in those places and enjoy long-lasting happiness because of their roots of goodness derived from past morality and generosity.
May the virtuous Dharma protect and mind us, and may it likewise remember us.
There are four kinds of devas:
the first is named "deva."
Second, the Heaven of Birth;
third, the Heaven of Purity;
fourth, the Heaven of Arising from Meaning.
The retributive fruits of such devas are thus pure.
If I possess the merit of precepts and giving,
at the time of death I shall surely be reborn in that place.
What is there to fear?
By recollecting with single-minded attention, terror is immediately dispelled.
The seven recollections on ānāpāna are as follows:
As explained previously in the first section of the sixty special excellences (*viśeṣa*), if the practitioner’s mind becomes startled or terrified, they should immediately regulate the breath;
by taking the inhalation and exhalation as the object of focus and maintaining full awareness, this completes the tenth stage.
One should immediately speak and mindfully recite *ānāpāna*.
When this reaches sixteen cycles, the spirit will depart.
By single-mindedly attending to the breath, fear and terror are immediately eliminated.
Next, one contemplates those who have died.
There are two kinds of death:
first, natural death.
Second is death due to external causes.
These two kinds of death constantly follow this body;
even if another does not kill one, one will still die naturally.
Why should fear arise?
It is like a brave warrior entering the ranks who feels peace of mind and has no dread when facing death.
In this same way, by single-mindedly contemplating death, fear is immediately eliminated.
This is a brief explanation of the eight recollections as antidotes to fear.
The characteristics of these dharmas therein are analyzed in detail according to the Mahāyāna.
Third, regarding the characteristics of the eight recollections as they lead toward the Path:
If, as previously stated, the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding) merely serves as a provisional means to eliminate fear and various obstacles,
it is now clarified that the skillful cultivation of the eight recollections (*aṣṭānusmṛti*) constitutes a specific gateway for entering the Path.
The explanation of the eight recollections as entry into the Path has two meanings:
first, the manner of entering the Path through sequential cultivation;
second, the attainment of entry into the Path through each individual recollection.
Regarding those who enter the Way through sequential cultivation:

a practitioner who seeks liberation from the disease of afflictions should first contemplate the Buddha as one contemplates a king of physicians, and contemplate the Dharma as one contemplates excellent medicine.
Mindfulness of the Sangha is like attending to a patient;
mindfulness of the precepts is like observing dietary prohibitions;
mindfulness of relinquishment is like providing nourishment and care.
Contemplating the heavens is like a physical illness slightly abating;
contemplating ānāpāna causes one to give rise to dhyāna-concentration;
contemplating death leads immediately to the realization of impermanence and the Four Noble Truths.
If the afflictions of the three realms are exhausted, one immediately attains the Noble Path.
Second, regarding the clarification that each and every thought-moment is a method for entering the Path:
mindfulness of the Buddha is precisely the manifestation of entering the Path through the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*.
As it is taught in the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā* and other sūtras,
regarding the mindfulness of the Dharma, the sūtras state:
"That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma."
The Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, the Six Perfections, the Middle Way,
and the True Mark (dharmatā)— all such dharmas as these are methods for entering the Path.
Regarding the mindfulness of the Sangha, it is as explained in such sutras as the Avalokiteśvara Samādhi and the Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha-rāja.
Mindfulness of the precepts is as explained in the ten kinds of precepts mentioned previously.
Mindfulness of giving is as explained in the Mahāyāna regarding the entrance into the characteristics of the path within the *dānapāramitā*.
As for the remaining three mindfulnesses, if one is mindful of the heavens and the ultimate heaven (*paramārthadeva*), one enters the path.
If one contemplates the signs of entering the path through *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing),
it is as fully explained in the section on "Pervasive Clarity" (*sabbaso-ñāṇa*).
Contemplating death is as explained in the section on the meaning of the perception of death (*maraṇasaññā*).
One should know that by practicing even one of these eight recollections, one immediately attains entry into the Way without needing to cultivate the others.
Because Bodhisattvas seek the Buddha-way, they practice these eight recollections with a mind free from dependence or attachment.
Through the gateway of the Dharma for extensively practicing the skillful means of great compassion, one transforms sentient beings.
It should be known that the eight recollections are themselves the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva.
Next, the gateway of the ten objects of contemplation is explained.
The ten perceptions are:
first, the perception of impermanence;
second, the perception of suffering; third, [the perception of non-self].
1. The perception of non-self;
2. The perception of the impurity of the four nutriments;
3. The perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in.
Sixth, the perception of death;
seventh, the perception of impurity;
eighth, the perception of cessation.
Ninth, the perception of detachment;
tenth, the perception of exhaustion.
Now, the explanation of these ten perceptions shall be presented according to three points.
First, the clarification of stages and positions; second, the clarification of cultivation and realization; third, the clarification of the aspiration for the Path.

Regarding what was stated as "stages and positions": [The text continues: First, the clarification of stages and positions. Second, the clarification of cultivation and realization. Third, the clarification of the aspiration for the Path. As for what was stated as "stages and positions":
Among the various dharmas taught in the Buddha's teachings, there are three kinds of paths:
first, the path of seeing;
second, the path of cultivation.
There are three paths of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). Now,
these ten perceptions clarify the stages of practice by means of these three paths.

Why is this? One who destroys the Dharma has already, while on the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*), subdued the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) and proclivities (*anuśaya*) by means of the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*).
What is now cultivated—the three perceptions such as impermanence (*anitya*) and so forth—is the contemplation of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa-vipaśyanā*).
In order to destroy the sixty-two views and various inverted dharmas,
one enters the path of vision (darśanamārga) and attains the first fruit;
next, there are the four perceptions, beginning with the perception of the impurity of food.
This is for those who are stream-enterers (srotāpanna) and once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin) who have entered the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
Because they wish to sever the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni) and realize the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala),
these four kinds of contemplation on distinct characteristics (pṛthak-lakṣaṇa-vastu-pratyavekṣā) are taught to assist in the perfecting of right view (samyagdṛṣṭi).
Having abandoned the afflictions through deliberation,
one subsequently abandons the three perceptions— of detachment, cessation, and so forth—
and as a non-returner (anāgāmin) practicing the path toward arhatship, one cultivates the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga).
These are taught for the purpose of severing and abandoning craving for the realms of form and formlessness, and for realizing arhatship.
It should be understood that the ten perceptions are explained in terms of their sequential stages according to the three paths;
thus, their general meaning can be readily perceived.
Second, the explanation of cultivation and realization:
First, regarding the perception of impermanence,
it is because one accords with the wisdom that contemplates all conditioned phenomena as impermanent.
This is called the perception of impermanence. Why is this?
Because all conditioned phenomena arise and perish moment by moment.
Because they depend on causes and conditions,
and because they do not accumulate,
at the time of their arising, they come from nowhere.
At the time of cessation, there is no place to which it goes;
therefore, it is called impermanent.
Within this, there are two kinds of impermanence.
First, sentient beings are impermanent;
second, the world is impermanent.
Regarding the impermanence of sentient beings:
The practitioner contemplates himself and all sentient beings:
from the stage of the kalala onwards, the arising and ceasing of form and mind undergo transformation and change,
without a moment’s pause, until old age and death.
Why is this so? Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are subject to the three characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing, and thus undergo transformation.

Therefore, one should know that they are impermanent: that which intends to arise is different from what has arisen; that which intends to abide is different from what has abided; and that which intends to cease is different from what has ceased.
Thus, this transformation and impermanence is momentary and swift, without even a moment's pause.
Therefore, one should know that all sentient beings are entirely impermanent.
As for the impermanence of the world:
As the verse says:
"The great earth, its grasses and trees, all perish; Mount Sumeru and the vast oceans likewise crumble and dry up;
The abodes of the devas are all consumed by fire— At that time, where in this world is there permanence?"
Furthermore, as the Buddha taught, there are two kinds of contemplation on impermanence:
first, that with remainder;
second, that without remainder.
When all persons and phenomena have been exhausted, yet only their names remain,
this is called "with remainder" (sopadhiśeṣa).
When both persons and phenomena are completely extinguished, this is called "without remainder" (nirupadhiśeṣa).
Why is this? If one says that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are impermanent by virtue of the three characteristics, [then...]
The three characteristics themselves cannot be apprehended;
how, then, could there be impermanence?
Just as at the time of arising there is no abiding or ceasing, so too, apart from the time of arising, there is no abiding or ceasing.
If cessation and abiding existed at the very moment of arising, then the characteristic of arising would be destroyed;
this is because arising and cessation are mutually contradictory.
If one claims that cessation exists apart from arising, then the meaning of the three characteristics—including abiding—would likewise be destroyed.
If arising is absent, then cessation has nothing to cease;
therefore, one should know that the three characteristics are unattainable.
If these three characteristics do not exist, [then...]
Why is it called impermanence?
If one does not perceive the characteristic of impermanence, one directly perceives the Noble Path;
this is termed the perception of impermanence.
Question: If that is so, why did the Buddha say that impermanence is a noble truth? Answer:
This is for the purpose of counteracting the inversion of clinging to permanence;
herein, one should not seek for reality.
If the mind reckons impermanence as being real, one falls into the view of nihilism.
Furthermore, there is another [type of] perception of impermanence as explained above in the sections on the Special Victories (viśeṣa) and the Universal Clarities (abhijñā).
The "without remainder" [perception of impermanence] shall be explained in detail below in the section on the Practice of Wisdom (prajñācaryā).
It is asked:
Why, at the beginning of the gateway to the noble practice, is the perception of impermanence taught first?
The answer is:
when all ordinary persons have not yet seen the Path, each values their own respective conduct.
Some say that upholding the precepts is paramount;
some say that extensive learning is paramount;
others say that the twelve dhūta practices are paramount.
Some say that meditative concentration (dhyāna) is paramount;
thus, each values their own respective practice and no longer diligently seeks nirvāṇa.
The Buddha said:
"All these merits are factors conducive to the path leading to nirvāṇa;
however, to contemplate all phenomena as impermanent is the true path to nirvāṇa."
For various such causes and conditions,
although all phenomena are empty, one speaks of this as the perception of impermanence.
Second is the perception of suffering.
The practitioner should reflect in this way:
"If all existing phenomena are impermanent and subject to change, they are the perception of suffering. Why is this so?
From the conjunction of the six internal sense bases and the six external objects,
the six types of consciousness arise.
Within these six types of consciousness, three kinds of sensation are produced.
These are the painful feeling, the pleasant feeling, and the neutral feeling.

Within these three kinds of feelings arise birth, aging, sickness, death, separation from what is loved, failure to obtain what is sought, association with what is hated, and the massing of the five aggregates, and so forth.
It is called suffering because it is oppressed by the eight types of suffering.
Furthermore, this sensation of suffering is itself suffering by its very nature;
therefore, it is what all sentient beings do not desire.
Because this pleasant feeling accords with one's desires,
it is cherished by all sentient beings; yet if attachment arises toward it,
its impermanence and decay will immediately cause one to undergo manifold sufferings.
Thereafter, one undergoes the sufferings of the hells, animals, hungry ghosts,
and so forth. Since all such various sufferings arise from the pursuit of pleasure,
one knows that pleasure is itself suffering.
Although neutral sensation (upekṣā-vedanā) is neither perceived as pain nor pleasure within the mind, and is thus neither grasped nor rejected,
in truth it is a great suffering because it is constantly oppressed by impermanence and flux.
When one contemplates in this way, one perceives no mark of happiness within the three realms that could give rise to craving or attachment.
The arising of aversion and fear in the mind is called the perception of suffering.
It is asked:
If that which is impermanent is itself suffering, then...
The Noble Truth of the Path is conditioned and impermanent; it should therefore also be suffering.
The answer is:
although the Noble Truth of the Path is impermanent, it is able to extinguish suffering and prevent the arising of all attachments.
Furthermore, because it is conjoined with various wisdoms such as emptiness and non-self,
it is merely impermanent and not suffering.
Third is the notion of non-self.
The practitioner should reflect deeply: if all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are entirely suffering, then suffering is itself non-self (*anātman*). Why is this so?
The five aggregates of clinging are entirely suffering.
That which is suffering is not autonomous;
that which is not autonomous is without self.
Why is this? If there were a self that possessed sovereignty, it should not be oppressed by suffering;
thus, one knows that suffering is precisely the absence of self.
Furthermore, among the five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements,
because all phenomena arise from conditions and thus lack intrinsic nature,
they are neither identical to nor distinct from the aggregates.
Furthermore, when one seeks our sixteen types of views, none can be found.
Since the self cannot be found, one abandons all attachments to various views, and the mind has nothing to grasp.
One then attains liberation;
this is called the perception of non-self.
This contemplative practice of the three perceptions—impermanence, suffering, and non-self—is profound and subtle.
This shall be explained further in detail below in the exposition of the Truth of Suffering.
It is asked:
"Impermanence, suffering, and non-self."
Is this one matter, or are these three matters?
If it were one matter, one should not speak of three.
If it were three matters, why did the Buddha say that impermanence is itself suffering?
"Suffering is itself non-self.
Answer:
"These three are one and the same thing."
Because one discriminates through the gate of contemplation on the dharmas associated with outflows (*sāsrava*),
there are three kinds of distinctions.
The perception of the mode of impermanence should be the notion of impermanence (*anicca-saññā*).
The perception of asceticism should be the perception of suffering;
the perception of non-self should be the perception of non-self.
Impermanence does not cause one to enter the triple world.
Suffering causes one to know the faults and transgressions of the three realms;
through non-self, one abandons the world.
Furthermore, impermanence gives rise to revulsion.
Suffering gives rise to fear;
selflessness extracts one from it and brings about liberation.
Furthermore, impermanence negates the view of eternalism.
"Suffering" prevents the view that there is nirvāṇa within the world.
"Selflessness" prevents the view that clings to a locus of attachment.
"Impermanence" refers to those things in the world that are mistakenly grasped as permanent dharmas.
That which the world considers a source of pleasure is suffering;
that which the world considers a firm and enduring self is non-self.
Such various distinctions are all explained in detail within the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the perception of the impurity of the four nutriments:
although a practitioner knows that all things are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self,
they may still give rise to craving and attachment toward food and drink.
One should cultivate the perception of the impurity of food as an antidote.
One should contemplate with precision that this food exists solely because of impure causes and conditions;
for instance, meat is produced from semen, blood, and the urinary tract.
This is the dwelling place of pus-worms;
it is formed from the transformation of ghee, milk, curd, and blood,
and is no different from putrid pus.
Rice resembles white worms, and soup is like excrement broth.
All food and drink, when prepared by cooks, become impure with oily dregs and filth.
Once it enters the mouth, the brain produces putrid saliva that flows down in two channels and mingles with the spittle.
Thereafter, it becomes taste.
Its appearance is like vomit;
it enters through the gate of the abdomen, where earth holds it, water rots it, wind moves it, and fire cooks it.
It is like the dregs and turbidity of porridge boiled in a cauldron sinking to the bottom while the clear liquid remains above;
it is like the dregs of fermented wine,
where the turbid portion becomes excrement and the clear portion becomes urine.
The waist has three orifices through which wind blows pus and fluids, causing them to disperse into the hundred vessels.
First, they combine with the blood and coagulate, transforming into flesh;
from this new flesh, fat, marrow, and bone are produced.
By these causes and conditions, the body faculty (kāyendriya) arises;
from the new and old flesh, the five sense faculties (pañcendriya) are produced;
and from these five faculties, the five consciousnesses (pañcavijñāna) arise.
In succession, the mental consciousness arises, discriminates, grasps at signs, and deliberates upon the beautiful and the ugly;
subsequently, various afflictions such as the notions of "I" and "mine," as well as various sinful karmas, arise.
Contemplate food in this way: its beginning, end, causes, and conditions are all various forms of impurity.
Know that the four internal elements and the four external elements are no different;
it is only through the power of the view of self that one forcibly conceives of them as "I."
There is a practitioner who reflects in this way, knowing the faults and evils of food:
"If I become greedily attached to it, I shall fall into hell or among the hungry ghosts where I must swallow glowing iron balls;
or I shall fall among the animals such as pigs and dogs, where I must devour excrement and filth."
Observing food in this manner gives rise to the perception of revulsion.
Because of this revulsion toward food, the five desires also diminish;
this is precisely the perception of the impurity of food.
Regarding the fifth, the perception of the lack of delight in all worlds:
if a practitioner contemplates the worldly flavors of form and desire, kinsmen and relatives, clothing and ornaments, gardens and groves, kingdoms and lands, human affairs, and so forth.
Consequently, the perception of pleasure arises;
because evil thoughts do not cease, they obstruct the path to detachment from desire.
Therefore, the practitioner should, with a profound mind, carefully contemplate the characteristics of the faults and transgressions of the world.
There are two kinds of transgressions:
first, those concerning sentient beings;
second, those concerning the land.
Regarding the faults and transgressions of sentient beings:
all sentient beings are subject to the affliction of the eight sufferings and have nothing upon which they can truly rely or cling.
Furthermore, one observes that sentient beings possess an abundance of craving and desire.
They do not distinguish between the beautiful and the ugly, being like beasts;
because their anger is so heavy, they do not even accept the Buddha’s words, they do not respectfully listen to the Dharma, and they have no fear of the evil realms.
Because their delusion is so great, they do not seek according to principle and fail to recognize the distinction between the honorable and the lowly.
Some are stingy, greedy, arrogant, envious, fierce, perverse, deceitful, treacherous, slanderous, malicious, and devoid of faith; they fail to recognize kindness or righteousness.
Others, due to an abundance of sinful karma, commit the five heinous crimes, show no reverence for the Triple Gem, and treat virtuous people with contempt.
In this world, sentient beings who are virtuous are very few, while those who are corrupt and evil are many.
One should deeply contemplate such faults and transgressions of the afflictions and give rise to weary detachment.
Likewise, one should not cultivate intimacy with such lands.
Regarding transgressions and faults, as it is said in verse:
"In some lands there is much cold; in some lands there is much heat."
There are lands without protection, or lands with much evil,
or lands with much hunger; some lands have much disease,
while others do not cultivate merit— such are places devoid of joy.
The practitioner deeply contemplates that such evil matters in the desire realm contain no place of happiness;
even when the retributions of the upper three realms are destroyed, the sorrow and suffering therein are more intense than those in the lower realm.
It is like falling from a very high place and being shattered and ruined;
as the Sūtra says:
"In the three realms there is no peace."
It is like a house on fire,
filled with manifold sufferings,
and most terrifying.
If one constantly contemplates these signs, one will develop a profound sense of weary detachment (*nirveda*), and sensual perceptions (*tṛṣṇā-saṃjñā*) will not arise.
This is called the perception of the world as unlovely (*lokānabhirati-saṃjñā*).
Sixth is the perception of death (*maraṇa-saṃjñā*).
If the practitioner, while cultivating the various contemplations mentioned above, gives rise to even slight laziness and is unable to swiftly sever the outflows (*āsrava*),
they must at that time deeply cultivate the contemplation of death and the absence of conceptualization.
As the Buddha spoke on the meaning of the perception of death,
a certain bhikṣu bared one shoulder and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I am able to cultivate the perception of death."
The Buddha said,
"How do you practice?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I do not hope to live for even one more year.
The Buddha said,
"You have practiced the contemplation of death while being negligent."
Again, another bhikṣu said,
"I do not expect to live for seven months.
Another bhikṣu said:
"They live for seven days, six days, five days, four days, three days, or two days.
The Buddha said,
"All of you are practicing the contemplation of death while being negligent."
There was a bhikṣu who said,
"From dawn until the mealtime.
Another bhikṣu said:
After the duration of a single meal,
the Buddha said,
"All of you are practicing the contemplation of death with negligence."
A certain bhikṣu bared one shoulder and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I cannot guarantee that my inhalation will follow my exhalation,
nor can I guarantee that my exhalation will follow my inhalation. The Buddha said:
Excellent, excellent!
This is the true cultivation of the perception of death;
this is the true practice of heedfulness.
If one can cultivate the perception of death in this way,
it should be known that such a person has destroyed the thief of indolence,
and all wholesome dharmas will constantly manifest before them.
This is called the cultivation of the perception of death.
As for the seven perceptions of impurity,
they are as previously described in the general clear observation (sāmānyapratyavekṣaṇā).
One contemplates the thirty-six constituents of the body as five kinds of impurity;
this should be explained in detail therein.
[Next are] the eight perceptions of abandonment.
Ninth is the perception of detachment;
tenth is the perception of exhaustion.
Because one relies upon nirvāṇa to sever the afflictions and fetters, it is called the perception of abandonment.
Because one is detached from the fetters and underlying tendencies (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*), it is called the perception of detachment (*vairāgya-saṃjñā*).
Because one exhausts all fetters and underlying tendencies, it is called the perception of exhaustion (*kṣaya-saṃjñā*).
Question:
If that is so, a single perception would suffice;
for what reason are three mentioned?
The answer is:
As with the previous case of the threefold exposition of a single dharma,
impermanence is itself suffering, and suffering is itself non-self.
This perception is likewise:
the perception of cessation is nirvana with remainder;
the perception of exhaustion is nirvana without remainder.
Regarding the two gates of skillful means for the nirvana that transcends conceptualization,
one should know that those who destroy the Dharma accomplish ten conceptions;
it is said that they thereby become arhats who are fully endowed with the two kinds of nirvana.
The nine perceptions and ten perceptions constitute the path for destroying [defilements].
The various classifications of the meaning of the ten perceptions are fully explained as set forth in detail within the Mahāyāna.

Third, regarding the clarification of the characteristics of the paths leading [to liberation], there are three types: first, the path of gradually entering the destruction of phenomena (*dharmakṣaya*), as fully explained previously;
second, the path of non-sequential destruction of phenomena.

From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, one fully cultivates the ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*), severs all fetters (*saṃyojana*), and attains the fruit of arhatship, thereby perfecting the two kinds of nirvāṇa.
Thus says the Mahāyāna.
If, during the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas,
one observes with right wisdom that one is free from all afflictions, this is the perception of detachment (*viveka-saṃjñā*).
To attain the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) and sever the fetters and latent tendencies (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*), this is the perception of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃjñā*).
At the time of entering nirvana, the five aggregates of clinging are extinguished and no longer continue;
this is called the perception of exhaustion. It should be known that from the stage of Dry Wisdom (śuṣka-vipaśyanā) onwards, one speaks of being free from perceptions and so forth.
This differs from what was previously stated regarding the three perceptions, which are collectively placed within the subsequent path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
These three [perceptions] involve entering the path according to one's capacity;
that is, if one cultivates any single perception among the ten perceptions, one will successfully achieve accomplishment.
He is then able to sever the fetters and acquisitions of the three realms and attain arhatship,
realizing the two kinds of nirvāṇa.
Thus, a sutra says:

By skillfully cultivating impermanence, one can sever all craving for sense-desires (*kāmarāga*), craving for form (*rūparāga*), and craving for the formless (*ārūpyarāga*), as well as restlessness, pride, and ignorance; thus the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the three realms are forever exhausted without remainder.
One should know that impermanence itself is the complete entry into the Path and the perception free from affliction.
The nine subsequent perceptions should also be understood in this way,
with each one distinguished according to the characteristics of the path to liberation.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the bodhisattva path, their mind is vast.
Desiring to practice the dharma-medicine of ambrosia for the sake of all sentient beings,
although they know that all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent,
they nevertheless fully accomplish the ten perceptions.
In each and every perception, this bodhisattva enters all dharma-gates in succession,
revolving through them without obstruction, and explains them for the sake of sentient beings.
One should know that these ten perceptions are precisely the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

Regarding the seventh part of the sixth section on the cultivation and realization of the Dhyāna-pāramitā, as expounded by the disciple Guǎngdìng: Following the *pratisaṃvids* (背捨), there are six kinds of dharma-gates.
These are all subsumed within the path of the immovable dharma.
When a śrāvaka of sharp faculties possesses these six dharmas and gives rise to true outflow-free realization,
they immediately become an Arhat of great power who is of the immovable dharma.
Therefore, the Mahāyāna states that an Arhat who does not destroy the dharmas is able to possess the *araṇā-samādhi*, the knowledge of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*), and the *mūrdhan-dhyāna*.
Now, these six types of dharma-gates are divided into four meanings.
This refers to contemplation, refinement, and cultivation.
First, there are the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
These three gateways all belong to the dhyāna of contemplation.
Therefore, the Mahāyāna states:
"The liberations are the initial practice;
the spheres of mastery are the intermediate practice."
The "all-pervasive" (sarvatraga) states are the subsequent practices;
they serve entirely as antidotes to the ignorance, craving, and attachment to purity within the fundamental-flavor dhyāna.
Second, the nine successive attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpattis) constitute the refined dhyāna.
The third, the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*, is precisely the cultivation of meditation (*vāsanā-dhyāna*).
The fourth, the *vyutkrāntaka-samādhi*, is precisely the practice of meditation (*bhāvanā-dhyāna*).
Now, the first, the contemplation of meditation (*vipaśyanā-dhyāna*), is explained as having two meanings.
First, the explanation of the methods for practicing the three stages of contemplative meditation;
second, the clarification of the functions of contemplative meditation.
Regarding the first, the explanation of the methods for the three stages of contemplative practice:
First, an explanation of the liberations (vimokṣa);
second, an explanation of the bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana);
third, an explanation of the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana).
First, I shall explain the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*).
Regarding the eight liberations:
the first liberation is that wherein one possesses the perception of internal forms while externally perceiving forms.
Second, being without internal perception of form while perceiving external forms is the second liberation (*vimokṣa*).
Third, the pure liberation, personally realized by the body, is the third liberation.
Fourth, the liberation of the sphere of infinite space.
The liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness;
the liberation of the sphere of nothingness;
and the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The eighth is the liberation through the cessation of sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā-nirodha-vimokṣa*).
Now, the explanation of this liberation consists of five points.
The first is the explanation of its name.
Second, the clarification of stages and positions;
third, the differentiation of the various methods of contemplation;
fourth, the clarification of cultivation and realization.
Fifth, the characteristics of the paths leading to various destinies.
