First, the explanation of the names: the reason these eight dharma-gates are collectively termed "liberations" (*prātimokṣa*) is that "backing away" (*prati*) refers to turning one's back on the five pure sensual desires, thereby abandoning the mind of attachment.
Therefore, it is called "reversal" (prātikūlya-vairāgya).
As for the "pure and clean five desires," these refer to the coarse and inferior forms,
sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles of the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
To be greedily attached to these dharmas and sink into the three miserable realms is called the impurity of the five desires.
Within the desire realm, the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the fundamental stages of the four dhyānas, and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*),
although one may experience a relish for them, they are all termed the purity of the five desires.
Now, by means of the "reversal" (prātikūlya) and the untainted antidote (anāsrava-pratipakṣa), one breaks through and eliminates [attachment].

Because one feels weary of and detached from the joy and bliss of the fundamental dhyānas of the desire realm, it is said that one is able to turn away from these pure five sensual desires; abandoning this mind of attachment is called "reversal."
Furthermore, many people say that "reversal and abandonment" (*prātipakṣika*) is merely another name for "liberation" (*vimokṣa*).
Now, if we examine this meaning from the perspective of the Mahāyāna, it is not so.
Why is this so? As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"The bodhisattva relies upon the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*) to enter the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpattayaḥ*)."
A person who has realized the fruit of non-returning through bodily witness,
though they have attained the nine successive meditative absorptions,
does not yet receive the designation of being fully endowed with the eight liberations.
Therefore, one should know that the state of wearying detachment from afflictions within the causal stage is called "reversal" (*prātikūlya*).
Later, when one fully contemplates, refines, and cultivates this until true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*) arises and the fetters of the three realms are exhausted,
at that time "reversal" changes its name to "liberation" (*vimokṣa*).
The meaning of such an explanation can be relied upon.
Regarding the second point, the clarification of the successive stages, there are differing interpretations.
If one follows the explanation provided by the Dharmaguptaka school:
The first and second liberations (vimokṣa) are situated in the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
The third, the pure liberation, is situated in the four dhyānas of the form realm (rūpadhātu).
The fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh—these four liberations—are situated in the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti).
The eighth, the liberation through the cessation of feeling and perception (*nirodhasamāpatti-vimokṣa*), transcends the three realms.
According to the explanation of the Sarvāstivādins,
the first two liberations pertain to the desire realm, the first dhyāna, and the second dhyāna.
The third pure liberation exists only in the fourth dhyāna.
It is said that there is much pleasure in the third dhyāna;
furthermore, because it is close to the impure, it is not established as a liberation.
The five lower liberations (*vimokṣa*) clarify that their stages do not differ from those previously described.
Furthermore, other masters state that there are no spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) in the third dhyāna.
In the four dhyānas, there are no *vipaśyanā-mukti* (liberations through contemplation). This differs from what was stated previously;
now it is explained according to the Mahāyāna.
The treatise states:
The first liberation is subsumed under the first dhyāna;
the second liberation is subsumed under the second dhyāna.
It should be understood that these two types of liberation (vimokṣa) reside within the first and second dhyānas.
Because they serve as antidotes to the destruction of the desire realm,
it is said in both cases that one contemplates external forms with a mind of impurity.
The third pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*) is situated within the third dhyāna.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"The pure liberation is called 'pure' because it takes the pure as its object, and because one experiences pleasure pervasively throughout the body."
This is called the realization through direct experience (*kāyasākṣātkriyā*).
Regarding the dharmas of the three realms, if one excludes the third dhyāna, there is no other pleasure that pervades the entire body.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
Within these four dhyānas, there are four bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), each consisting of one "turning away" (parāvṛtti) and one "facing toward" (abhimukha).
One should understand that as one progresses or regresses through these stages with ease,
their position lies within the third and fourth dhyānas.
If one were to universally apply [this] to all [doctrines], it would contradict various treatises.
Now, if one were to fully employ this principle to refute the preceding [arguments] and harmonize the intent of the teachings,
it would become exceedingly convoluted.
The assignment of the five lower liberations (*vimokṣa*) to their respective stages is no different from what was stated previously;
here, I shall explain their sequence according to the interpretation of the latter school.
Regarding the third explanation, the methods of contemplation differ as follows:
If the Dharmaguptakas clarify these eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa),
they take the contemplation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vipaśyanā) as their essence;
if the Sarvāstivādins clarify these renunciations (prātikṣepa), they take the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-vipaśyanā) as their essence.
All of these have the nature of contemplation characterized by aversion.
Now, these eight liberations (aṣṭa-vimokṣa) possess both the contemplation of phenomena and the contemplation of principle;
when they exist as causes, they are termed "liberations."
When the fruition is fulfilled, it is called liberation;
it is also termed "liberation through both.
If one relies exclusively on the explanations of the former two schools:
In this case, both phenomena and principle would be incomplete;
how, then, could one receive the title of "liberated through both"?
Herein, the method of contemplative practice differs from that of the two previous schools.
The differences between shallow and deep levels will naturally become apparent below.
Fourth, the clarification of cultivation and realization:
when a practitioner wishes to cultivate the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*) and the untainted contemplative practices (*anāsrava-bhāvanā*), [they must proceed as follows].
One must strictly uphold the precepts of the five categories, ensuring they are utterly pure.
Furthermore, one should be diligent and courageous, adorning the mind with great vows so that it never falters or sinks,
and thereby be able to accomplish the great task.
Regarding what is called the first liberation (*prathama-vimokṣa*):
not destroying internal or external forms, and not extinguishing the marks of form internally or externally, one contemplates these forms with a mind of impurity; this is called the first liberation.
Why is this? Because sentient beings have two types of conduct:
the conduct of craving and the conduct of views.
Those with a predominance of craving are bound by many fetters of external defilements (*saṃyojana*).
Those with a predominance of views are bound by many internal defilements, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and other views.
For this reason, those with a predominance of craving contemplate the impurity of the external body.
Those with a predominance of views contemplate the impurity and decay of the internal body;
it is now clarified that the practice of contemplation for the liberations (vimokṣa) generally first arises from within.
Once this internal contemplation has been perfected:
Thereafter, one contemplates the external with an impure mind.
How does one contemplate the internal?
The practitioner straightens the body and composes the mind, observing intently the big toe of the foot, visualizing it as being swollen and black like a soybean.
It is also like the appearance of a corn on the foot.
Within a state of meditative stillness, one contemplates this sign until it is formed, and then further visualizes it swelling up to the size of a pear or a bean.
In this manner, one proceeds until seeing the entire foot as large as a chicken egg.
Next, one observes the second, third, fourth, and fifth fingers in the same way.
Next, observing the method for the feet, one again sees them swollen, even unto the soles, heels, ankles, insteps, knees, thighs, and hips, all of which are seen to be swollen.
Next, observe the right foot in the same manner.
Furthermore, one should settle the mind and contemplate with precision:
visualize that the passages for excrement and urine, as well as the waist, spine, abdomen, back, chest, and ribs, are all swollen.
Furthermore, one should settle the mind and observe with clarity that the left shoulder blade, arm, elbow, wrist, palm, and five fingers are all seen to be swollen;
even so for the right shoulder blade.
Furthermore, one should settle the mind and observe with clarity that the neck, head, and jaw are all seen to be swollen.
With his entire body and neck held straight,
he thus observed the body from head to foot and from foot to head,
seeing only its swelling.
A sense of revulsion arises in the mind.
One should further contemplate the decayed, pus-filled, and blood-stained impurity,
as well as the anus and urethra from which worms and pus flow out.
Furthermore, having torn it open, one sees the internal organs and the thirty-six impure substances, putrid and foul-smelling;
a sense of revulsion arises in the mind,
and one regards one's own body as being even worse than a dead dog.
Contemplate the bodies of external loved ones, whether male or female;
they are likewise thus,
and not to be cherished or delighted in.
The detailed exposition is as in the nine perceptions (navasaṃjñā),
with the sole difference that the two perceptions of "scattering" and "burning" are excluded.
When the practitioner cultivates this contemplation, if the afflictions (kleśa) of the desire realm have not yet been stilled, [he should continue].
One should dwell long within this contemplation until the mind of revulsion becomes fully matured.
When one is detached from craving for food, at that time one should advance to the contemplation of white bones.

With a single-minded, tranquil concentration, one should carefully contemplate the space between the eyebrows, imagining the skin and flesh splitting open until one sees white bones as large as fingernails.
It is distinct and clear.
Next, one should mentally tear open the skin and flesh upward;
immediately, the frontal bone and the hairline will be seen.
The bones open with a hollow sound, and one immediately perceives their skeletal form.
One further contemplates the cranial bone, seeing the skin and flesh fall away until the skull-bone is exposed.
Then, one should again fix the mind and proceed from the head downward.
Imagine that the skin and flesh gradually peel away from the body down to the feet;
once the skin and flesh have fallen off, one sees only a skeleton with its joints interlocking, sitting upright and motionless.
At that time, the practitioner, with a concentrated mind, clearly contemplates that these bones arise from causes and conditions:
depending on the metatarsal bones, the tarsal bones are supported;
depending on the tarsal bones, the ankle bones are supported.
Relying on the ankle bone, it supports the shin bone;
relying on the shin bone, it supports the knee bone;
relying on the knee bone, it supports the thigh bone.
Relying on the thigh bones, they support the hip bones; relying on the hip bones, they support the waist bones;
relying on the waist bones, they support the spinal vertebrae;
and relying on the spinal vertebrae, they support the ribs.
Furthermore, the vertebrae support the cervical vertebrae;
depending on the cervical vertebrae, they support the mandible;
and depending on the mandible, they support the teeth.
Above is the skull;
furthermore, by means of the cervical vertebrae,
it supports the clavicles.
Relying on the shoulder bones, they support the arm bones;
relying on the arm bones, they support the wrist bones;
relying on the wrist bones, they support the palm bones.
Relying on the metacarpal bones, one supports the phalanges;
thus, through such successive mutual dependence, there are three hundred and sixty bones.

Contemplating each one with precision, one knows the large and the small, the firm and the soft, all mutually dependent and conventionally designated. Within this, there is no master and no self. What, then, is the view of a self in the body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)?
Inhalation and exhalation are merely wind;
they are neither body nor self.
Contemplating feeling, contemplating the mind, and even contemplating phenomena, one knows them all to be empty and deceptive, without master and without self.
Having performed this contemplation, one immediately destroys the view of self;
pride and the five desires are likewise all eliminated.
At that time, one should again fix the mind and contemplate from head to foot and from foot to head.
Following the body in earnest contemplation, one thoroughly refines the white bones for perhaps hundreds of thousands of times.
When the joints and tendons of the entire skeletal person have been exhausted, the color of the bones becomes like white jade or a conch shell.
Continuing this deep contemplation without ceasing, one then sees a brilliant white light shimmering upon the bones.
Having seen these signs, one should immediately contemplate the space between the eyebrows with clear attention.
While contemplating, if white light is seen blazing forth and all coming toward the practitioner’s mind, one should not grasp at the appearance of the light,
but simply fix the mind on the space between the eyebrows.
If the mind is tranquil and dwells spontaneously in its own state, such that the roots of goodness are brought forth,
one will then see eight-colored light radiate from between the eyebrows, swirling outward and illuminating the ten directions, all of which become entirely bright and pure.
The eight colors are earth, water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, and white.
They illuminate the great earth everywhere; when one perceives the color of the earth, it appears like a pure ground that is yellowish-white.
He sees the color of water as clear water within a deep pool;
he sees the color of fire as the pure flame of smokeless fuel;
he sees the color of wind as a clear breeze free from dust.
Seeing blue, one knows it is Mount Jinguang;
seeing yellow, it is like the *campaka* flower;
seeing red, it is like the morning glow of spring.
One sees a white color like that of jade or snow;
following this appearance of color, there is radiance throughout.
Although one sees the colors with clarity, no substantial form or essence can be apprehended.
This form is transcendent and surpasses anything found in the world.
When this sign arises,
the practitioner’s mind becomes concentrated, peaceful, and filled with immeasurable joy and bliss.
It cannot be fully conveyed by words.
Furthermore, the practitioner should again refine the skeleton from head to foot,
then withdraw the mind once more to contemplate intently at the forehead, fixing the mind upon its object.
Again, one sees eight-colored light rays revolving and emerging.

In this manner, with a concentrated mind, one sequentially contemplates the hairline, the crown of the head, the two ear canals, the brow bones, the eye sockets, the nose, the mouth, the teeth, the jawbone, and the cervical vertebrae.
From top to bottom, throughout the three hundred and sixty bones and joints,
one clearly sees eight-colored light radiating and revolving outward.
The practitioner withdraws the mind and makes it increasingly subtle, moving from head to feet and from feet to head.
Observing this skeleton, one sees it emitting light from its entire body, universally illuminating all things, all of which become bright and pure.
If these are Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, they will all behold the images of the Buddhas within that light.
If the practitioner’s roots of goodness are weak,
they will only perceive the various Buddha-images after reaching the fourth dhyāna.
Once the practitioner has attained this, their radiance shines forth and the joy of their concentrated mind is twice as great as what was previously obtained.
This is called the sign of realizing the first liberation (*prathama-vimokṣa*). Why is that?
Because the internal skeleton has not yet been extinguished.
Therefore, it is called "having the internal appearance of form.
This is because one perceives the eight kinds of external light as well as the impure objects of the desire realm;
hence it is said that one contemplates external forms with an impure mind.
External forms are of two kinds.
Those that are impure, such as the impurities of the desire realm, are impure external forms.
The eight kinds of pure forms are the supramundane forms of the form realm.
Therefore, it is called external form.
Because the practitioner perceives the impurity of both internal and external forms,
they turn away from the mind of the desire realm and find no joy in it.
Because one perceives the eight kinds of pure forms,
one immediately knows that the fundamental first dhyāna is obscured by ignorance, dark, deceptive, unreal, coarse, and inferior; thus,
one is able to relinquish it so that the mind does not become attached.
The treatise states: "To turn one's back on these pure five sensory desires and to abandon the mind of attachment is called 'reversal' (prātikūlya-vairāgya).
Furthermore, as it is taught in the Mahāyāna:"
Regarding the first dhyāna, there is one liberation (vimokṣa).
One should know that this liberation is precisely the untainted (anāsrava) first dhyāna;
if it is the first dhyāna, it necessarily possesses the meaning of the five factors (pañcāṅga).
Now this shall be analyzed:
from the practitioner’s initial practice of the contemplation of impurity up until the luminous appearance of the skeleton-man,
these constitute the signs of the meditative concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*).
Next, gather the mind and settle it in a state of profound stillness between the eyebrows;
this is the sign of the "not-yet-attained stage" (*anāgamya-bhūmi*) of the dhyāna of contemplation.
Eight kinds of light will swirl forth, and one will perceive these eight colors.
Having never seen such things before, his mind was greatly startled and awakened;
this is precisely the characteristic of the awakening factor of contemplation (dhamma-vicaya-sambojjhaṅga).
He discerned that the eight colors were each distinct in their characteristics and were not of this world.
This is the factor of mindfulness (smṛti).
A heart filled with jubilation is the factor of joy (prīti).
The dharma of tranquility gladdens and delights the mind.
This is precisely the factor of joy (*prīti-aṅga*).
Although one perceives this form, there is no inverted perception, and the samādhi is immovable;
this is precisely the factor of one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā-aṅga*).
Now, to briefly distinguish the characteristics of these five factors of the untainted (anāsrava) contemplative dhyāna:
one should know that they differ categorically from the five factors found within the aforementioned fundamental, special, and supernormal (abhijñā) dhyānas.
Regarding the two liberations:
one destroys internal form and eliminates the perception of internal form,
yet does not destroy external form nor eliminate the perception of external form.
To contemplate external forms with this mind of impurity is the second liberation (*prātimokṣa*). Why is this so?
Because in the first liberation, the light emitted by the skeleton has already pervaded everywhere.
Now, because one desires to enter the second dhyāna through internal purity,
one destroys and eliminates the internal skeleton; yet, because the views and afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm have not been severed,
one still contemplates the impure characteristics of the external white bones.
Therefore it is said that one contemplates external forms with this impure mind.
Now, to clarify the cultivation and realization:
at the stage immediately following the first liberation (*vimokṣa*), the practitioner—
Without being disturbed by applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*),
one contemplates the internal body as a skeleton, false and unsubstantial, empty and hollow both internally and externally,
focusing exclusively on the signs of disintegration, decay, and extinction.
When observing in this manner, one gradually sees the skeletal figure become putrid, decay, and crumble like fine dust;
it disperses and vanishes into emptiness so that no internal form is seen.
At that time, one simply withdraws the mind and enters meditative concentration.
Taking external light and impurity as objects, one focuses the mind on the center without grasping at the visualization.
Then, the inner mind suddenly becomes clear and pure; one enters the meditative absorption of *samādhi*, and great joy arises simultaneously.
He immediately beholds eight kinds of light shining forth from the Inner Purity, illuminating the ten directions with an intensity twice that of the previous stage.

Having realized the great joy and radiance of the internal dharma, he knows that the fundamental second dhyāna is deceptive, coarse, and inferior; he feels weary of it, turns away from it, and does not cling to it.
Therefore, it is called "reversal" (prātikūlya-vairāgya) and is also termed the untainted second dhyāna.
Within this state, the four factors are fully present, as can be discerned through investigation.
Regarding the third liberation of the pure, which is realized through bodily witness:
as it is taught in the Mahāyāna,
it is pure because its object-condition is pure.
Because one experiences pleasure with the entire body, it is called "bodily realization. Why is this?
It is because the practitioner wishes to enter these three liberations.
Following the two types of liberation, the subsequent mind no longer engages with the contemplation of external impurity;
all things are utterly destroyed, dispersed, and extinguished without remainder,
nor does it experience great joy or agitation.
Simply collect the mind and contemplate with precision the signs of the eight-colored radiance.
Having grasped these signs, enter into deep samādhi.
Refine these eight colors until they are extremely bright and pure; as the mind abides within the object of focus, it will then suddenly and completely enter meditative absorption.
At the moment concentration arises, it is born together with bliss;
one perceives the eight external colors of light as pure and brilliant,
like the radiant hue of exquisite jewels.
Each, according to their respective perceptions, experiences a brilliant and radiant illumination that pervades all directions.
This external purity of form penetrates outwardly and illuminates the mind;
the mind thus becomes clear and pure, and its joy gradually increases.
Pervading the entire body, the whole frame experiences joy and serenity.
Having realized this dharma, the mind turns away from it and does not delight in or cling to it.
This is a brief explanation of the characteristics of the realization of pure renunciation (*śraddhā-vimukti*).
This is also called the untainted third dhyāna;
herein, the five factors are fully present, and deep reflection can be observed.
This is likewise true for the pure matter of the fourth dhyāna and those that follow.
All are subsumed under the pure liberations (*śubha-vimokṣa*);
they differ only in that [the latter] lacks the pervasive bodily bliss (*sarvakāya-sukha*). Question:
If that is so, since pure matter has been present from the very beginning of the liberations (*vimokṣa*),
why is it only now designated as the "pure liberation"?
The answer is:
Within this, one should apply analysis by means of four meanings:
first, the impure and the non-impure;
second, the impure and the pure.
Third is the pure-impure;
fourth is the pure-pure-impure.
Regarding the impure, it refers to the nature and characteristics of the body consisting of the thirty-six components of the desire realm.
This is already impure.
By the power of the contemplation on impurity,
one further perceives this body as bloated, festering with pus, livid, and foul-smelling.
This is to see further impurity within impurity.
Regarding "impurity that is pure": the white bones are originally of an impure substance;

yet when one contemplates them with a concentrated mind, once the grease and fat have completely vanished, they appear like white jade or mother-of-pearl, radiating a brilliant, shimmering white light.
This, then, is purity within impurity.
Regarding impurity within purity:
although there has been pure radiance since the initial liberations (vimokṣa), [it remains so].
However, this radiance has three kinds of impure causes and conditions.
The first is impurity regarding its source,
meaning it emerges from the skeleton.
Second, that which is illuminated is impure;
this refers to the illumination of external objects.
Third, the substance of the light is impure because it has not yet been refined.
For example, just as gold that has not been refined and whose dross is not yet exhausted will have impure luster and color,
for this reason, although the first dhyāna possesses radiance, it is not called "pure" because its objects of perception are not pure.
Although in the second dhyāna there is no white-bone radiance emerging from internal purity,
it still illuminates external impurity;
yet because it has not been refined and because of the presence of great joy, it is also termed "having purity as its object."
Now, regarding the term "pure-pure": the eightfold radiant light is fundamentally pure matter.
Because it is now further freed from three kinds of impurity on this stage, it is called "pure-pure."
It is also called "pure because its object is pure.
Since it is fully endowed with the meaning of purity,
it is therefore described as the "pure liberation" (śubha-vimokṣa).
Regarding the liberation through the fourfold space:
after the practitioner has already removed the impure colors of their own skin and flesh within the desire realm during the first liberation,
they subsequently extinguish the color of the white bones within their own body during the second liberation.
Having cast aside all external impure forms through the two types of liberation (*vimokṣa*),
there remain only the eight kinds of pure forms;
up to the fourth dhyāna, these eight kinds of forms all abide in dependence upon the mind.
For example, just as illusory forms abide dependent upon the illusory mind, if the mind relinquishes the forms, the forms immediately vanish.
When the single mind takes emptiness as its object and accords with emptiness,
it enters the sphere of infinite space.
This clarifies that the method for the cessation of form differs from the previous one.
The realization of the concentration of the sphere of infinite space is as previously explained.
When a practitioner wishes to enter the liberation of infinite space, they must first enter the meditative concentration of space.
The concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) is the primary gateway to the liberations (*vairāgya*).
Because it turns away from the objects of form (*rūpa-ālambana*) by means of the formless (*ārūpya*),
ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who enter this concentration are termed "formless."
When a disciple of the Buddha enters this meditative absorption, their profound mind is single-mindedly directed and does not turn back;
this is called "renunciation" (prātikṣepa).
What is meant by "profound mind"?
Because of having well-cultivated *śamatha*.
What is meant by "exclusively non-retrogressive"?

It is because within this concentration one has well-cultivated *vipaśyanā* regarding emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and the absence of volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
Being able to relinquish the fundamental mind of attachment, one does not sink back into the cycle of birth and death; therefore, this is called "unwaveringly non-retrogressive.
Furthermore, when a disciple of the Buddha enters the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), there are eight noble lineages of contemplation (*āryavaṃśa*).
By means of the fourfold contemplation of antidotes, such as [viewing] abscesses and so forth,
one is able to feel revulsion toward formless phenomena;
and by means of the fourfold correct contemplation, such as impermanence and so forth.
One immediately destroys the two inversions—of the formless as being either non-existent or real—and gives rise to the untainted [wisdom].

The methods for the contemplative practice of the eight noble lineages are all as previously explained during the cultivation of the consciousness-sphere concentration following the space-sphere concentration.

However, whereas one previously cultivates the eight noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) precisely because one wishes to depart from space, the practitioner now cultivates the eight noble lineages at the very moment they enter the concentration of space.
Although they abide within that concentration, they do not cling to the concentration of space; therefore, it is called "rejection" (prātikūlyavimokṣa).
The fifth is the sphere of consciousness;
the sixth is the sphere of nothingness;
and the seventh is the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
One should likewise analyze each of these individually.
As for the "liberation through the cessation of sensation and perception," it refers to turning away from and ceasing sensation, perception, and all mental states and mental factors.
This is called the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling. Why is this so?
Because the disciples of the Buddhas are weary of and averse to a distracted mind.
Entering meditative absorption, one rests in a state resembling *nirvāṇa* that is firmly established within the body;

therefore, it is called "bodily realization" (*kāyasākṣin*). When a practitioner cultivates this liberation through the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha-vimokṣa*), they must extinguish the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), as well as all mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
What is meant by "extinguishing this"?
Although there are no coarse afflictions within the state of non-perception (asaṃjñika),
it is nonetheless fully endowed with the four aggregates (skandha), two bases (āyatana), three realms (dhātu), and ten types of subtle mental factors (caitta).
That is to say: first, sensation;
second, perception;
third, mental formations.
Fourth, contact;
fifth, volition;
sixth, desire.
7. The liberations; 8.
The recollections; 9.
The meditative concentrations.
The ten wisdoms.
What is feeling? It is so-called "cognitive feeling."
What is perception? It is so-called conceptualization of consciousness.
What are volitional formations?
What is called "practice according to the Dharma"? What is contact?
It is mental contact.
What is volition? It is so-called reflection on the Dharma. What is desire?
What is meant by "understanding" in relation to entering and emerging from meditative concentration?
It refers to the understanding of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
What is meant by "mindfulness"? It refers to mindfulness directed toward samādhi.
What is concentration?
It is the mind abiding in accordance with the Dharma. What is wisdom?
This refers to the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya),
the aggregate of wisdom (prajñāskandha), and those formations dissociated from craving for the formless realm, ignorance, restlessness, pride, and the mind;
when the causes and conditions of the dharma of suffering and its origin are combined, there is the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
In the previous liberation from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
although one knows these things and thus does not cling to that sphere, it is called "liberation" because of this non-clinging;
yet, the various mental factors have not been extinguished.
Now, because the practitioner wishes to enter the liberation (*vimokṣa*) from sensation and perception (*saṃjñāvedayita*),
they must necessarily not grasp at the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

When the mind single-mindedly takes true reality as its object and severs the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, then the aggregate, sense base, and element of neither-perception-nor-non-perception cease.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arising from causes and conditions are extinguished;
feeling (*vedanā*) is extinguished, up to and including wisdom (*prajñā*) being extinguished.
Craving (*tṛṣṇā*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and all other afflictions (*kleśa*) are extinguished.
All mental factors (caitta-dharma) cease,
and all that are not mental factors also cease;
this is called that which is not shared with ordinary persons and is not a worldly phenomenon (loka-dharma).
If one can contemplate in this manner, it is called the cessation of sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā-nirodha*).
This is because by means of the sensation and perception that contemplate reality,
one extinguishes the sensation and perception of non-perception, suffering, and its origination (*duḥkha-samudaya*).
Now, when a practitioner wishes to enter the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha-vimokṣa*),
they must further deeply understand that even the perception and feeling capable of observing reality are not ultimately tranquil.
Thus, they relinquish the meditative concentration, feeling, wisdom, and perception that constitute this capacity for observation.
Because one abandons these two minds of true concentration and wisdom,
it is said that one turns away from the mental factors of feeling and perception;
it is like using a subsequent sound to stop a preceding sound.
Once the preceding sound has ceased, the subsequent sound likewise can be eliminated.
When sensation and perception have ceased, the mind accordingly accords with the dharma of cessation;
this dharma of cessation sustains the mind so that it is tranquil and devoid of any cognitive awareness.
Therefore, it is said that one "bodily realizes the cessation of perception and feeling.
Since there is no mental consciousness within this meditative absorption,
if one wishes to enter or emerge from it, one simply follows the duration of the original vow.
Fifth is the analysis of the characteristics of the paths leading to various destinies.
When a practitioner cultivates the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*) to enter the path, there are three types of differences.
The first is to first use the liberations to destroy the factors that obstruct the path.

Subsequently, one fully cultivates the stages of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) up to the samādhis of transcendence (*vyutkrāntakasamāpatti*), encompassing both the objective reality and the contemplative practice.
Only when these are perfected does one give rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and realize the path of the Three Vehicles.
Second, when one cultivates the eight liberations (aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ), this person becomes weary of and detached from birth and death, desiring to swiftly attain liberation;
at that time, they universally cultivate the true contemplation (bhūta-darśana) that takes the truths as its object.
That is, within the eight liberations (aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ), one gives rise to true outflow-free wisdom (anāsrava) and realizes the path of the three vehicles;
this is also called being fully endowed with the eight liberations.
It should be understood that such a person does not necessarily possess the five lower dharma-gates.
Question: If this is so,
and this person has not yet attained the nine successive concentrations (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti),
how can they already receive the name of one who has attained the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa)?
Answer: This matter should be analyzed through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
First, there are those who possess the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) but do not possess liberation.
There is that which is liberation but not sequential concentration;
there is that which is both sequential concentration and liberation;
and there is that which is neither sequential concentration nor liberation.
Regarding these eight liberations (aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ),
as for the third: if a person’s mind of revulsion toward birth and death is profound,
then at the very moment they realize the first liberation, they will deeply contemplate the principle of the true concentration on the Four Noble Truths, which is untainted (anāsrava).
If one, upon generating [this resolve], immediately enters the Vajra-samādhi on this very stage and realizes the path of the Three Vehicles,
it should be known that such a person likewise does not necessarily possess the aforementioned seven types of liberation (vimokṣa).
The mind of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is like space, without anything to be grasped or abandoned.
By the power of skillful means, they skillfully cultivate the liberations (vimokṣa),
fully accomplishing all Buddha-dharmas and delivering sentient beings.
One should know that these liberations (*vimokṣa*) are themselves the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna.
Next, the dharma-gate of the eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) will be explained.
As for the eight spheres of mastery:
First, having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are few, whether beautiful or ugly;
this is called superior knowledge and superior vision,
the first base of mastery.
Second, having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms, whether beautiful or ugly;
this is called superior knowledge and vision.
This is the second base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Third, with the internal perception of formlessness, one perceives external forms that are limited, whether beautiful or ugly;
this is called superior knowledge and vision.
This is the third base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Fourth: Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms, whether beautiful or ugly;
this is called "superior knowledge and vision.
These are the four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
5. The superior sphere of blue;
6. The superior sphere of yellow;
7. The superior sphere of red.
Regarding the eight white spheres of mastery (*śubha-vimokṣa*), according to the *Mālā-sūtra*, the four great elements are employed as the four spheres of mastery.
Herein, it is explained that these spheres of mastery constitute four points of meaning.
First is the explanation of their names.
Second, the clarification of stages and positions;
third, the discernment of the characteristics of cultivation and realization;
fourth, the clarification of the path of progression.
First, regarding the explanation of the names:
there are two meanings for these eight dharmas that collectively clarify the "bases of mastery" (abhibhvāyatana).
First, whether they be pure or impure.
When one attains this contemplation, the five desires can be overcome at will;
therefore, it is called a "sphere of mastery" (abhibhvāyatana).
Second, one skillfully disciplines the mind of contemplation.
For example, when one rides a horse to strike an enemy, it is not merely that the front ranks are broken;
because one can also skillfully control the horse itself, it is called a "place of victory" (abhibhvāyatana).
This, then, differs from the "liberations" (vimokṣa).
The Sūtra also speaks of the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*). If,
by means of the bases of mastery, one exhausts all afflictions,
then one knows that the false aggregates (*skandha*) and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are all extinguished.
At that time, the "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*) are renamed as the "eight spheres of liberation" (*aṣṭau vimokṣāyatanāni*).
Second, regarding the clarification of their sequential stages: here we shall rely solely on what is taught in the Mahāyāna.
The first two bases of mastery are situated in the first dhyāna.
The third and fourth spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are situated after the second dhyāna,
while the [remaining] four spheres of mastery are situated in the fourth dhyāna.
As for why the spheres of mastery are not established in the third dhyāna:
Because those who delight in many mental states are dull-witted,
the first two dhyānas are close to the desire realm; thus,
the afflictions of the desire realm are difficult to destroy.
Although he dwells in the second dhyāna, he still contemplates impurity to break the fetters of the lower stages.
Since the fourth dhyāna is the ultimate limit among the realms of form (*rūpa*),
the supreme position within the realm of form culminates here.
Since the four formless attainments (ārūpya) are devoid of form,
and because the afflictions associated with the earth element have already been attenuated therein,
the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) are not established within them.

Third, to clarify the reason for the cultivation and realization: regarding the statement "internally perceiving the mark of form, one externally perceives forms that are limited," they are called "limited" because the objects of focus are limited;
since the path of observation has not yet increased, one observes the causes and conditions of what is limited.
One observes that [the mind] is mostly fearful and difficult to restrain;
for example, when a deer is roaming and has not yet been tamed, it is not suitable to let it roam at a great distance.
What is meant by "observing the few"?
The practitioner observes his own body as impure;
he also observes that those he loves are likewise impure, bloated, putrefied, and reduced to white bones,
until his mind feels profound revulsion.
Regarding "whether beautiful or ugly," as explained in the section on the first liberation (*prathama-vimokṣa*):
one observes external forms; they are called "beautiful" because they are the fruit of wholesome karma, and "ugly" because they are the retribution for unwholesome karma.
Furthermore, when a practitioner receives from a teacher the method of contemplation for observing various forms of external impurity,
this is called "ugly form. At times,
the practitioner may recall these things and falsely give rise to the perception of purity.
One contemplates pure form as beautiful.
Furthermore, the practitioner fixes the mind on a single point within his own body and contemplates that there are two kinds of form within the desire realm.
First, it can give rise to lust;
second, it can give rise to anger.
That which gives rise to lust is pure form and is therefore called "beautiful"; that which gives rise to anger is impure form and is therefore called "ugly."
One who possesses supreme knowledge and supreme vision observes that when the mind is thoroughly matured,
it feels no greedy attachment toward beautiful forms and no anger toward ugly forms.
One merely contemplates that form arises from the combination of the causes and conditions of the four great elements,
being as insubstantial as a bubble on water; through wisdom,
one profoundly penetrates the characteristics of the provisional and the real.

When a practitioner dwells within this gateway of impurity, they are able to resist the arrival of lust, anger, and various other fetters and latent tendencies; therefore, it is called a "sphere of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*).
It is "mastery" because it overcomes the afflictions of the perversion that perceives purity within the impure.
Furthermore, regarding beauty and ugliness:
there are two types of contemplation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
The first is seeing the thirty-six impure and foul substances within one's own body and the bodies of others.
This is called the "ugly.
Second, having removed the inner and outer skin, flesh, and five viscera,
one contemplates only the white bones as being like conch shells or snow, even to the point where flowing light shines forth.
This is called "excellent.
When the practitioner perceives impurity, they immediately know it to be false and illusory, and their mind does not fear or sink into despair.
When they perceive pure forms, they know they arise from conditions, and their mind does not become attached or defiled.
This is called superior knowledge and superior vision.
Furthermore, when a practitioner, within a limited range of objects, contemplates the transformation of forms at will with mastery,
and is likewise able to skillfully control the observing mind, it is therefore called a "sphere of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Second, having internal perception of forms, one perceives external forms, whether beautiful or ugly;
this is called "superior knowledge and superior vision.
When the practitioner’s mind has been thus disciplined through contemplation, [they proceed further].
At that time, the practitioner who does not extinguish the internal skeletal person further contemplates external forms extensively within meditative concentration.
That is to say, they carefully observe one corpse, up to ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or even a hundred thousand corpses throughout a single land.
From ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or a hundred thousand lands— even a single Jambudvīpa,
up to a single four-continent world system—
all were seen to be entirely corpses.
When one contemplates a single bloated corpse, one sees all bloated corpses;
this applies likewise to those that are decomposed, blood-stained, festering, putrid, livid, or flayed.
Having thus extensively observed the impurity of corpses, the practitioner’s mind becomes deeply weary and loathsome.
Next, one should carefully contemplate a single corpse,
stripping away the skin and bones until only white bones are seen.
In this manner, one proceeds until all corpses have their skin and flesh removed, and white bones are seen filling the entire world.
This contemplation is explained in detail in the *Dhyāna-sūtra* and should be fully set forth therein.
Once the practitioner has perfected the external contemplation of bones,
Furthermore, one should fix the mind and clearly contemplate the white bones within the body,
refining them until they are as bright and pure as jade or a conch shell.
While contemplating these bones, one sees all the skeletal figures outside.
They all arise and stand in rows facing one another, coming forward with their hands raised.
Within samādhi, the practitioner immediately realizes that these skeletal figures have all come according to his mental visualization.
Since there is no fixed reality,
the mind shall not be startled or terrified;
furthermore, one should silently recite in the mind this rebuke to the skeletal person.
"Ha! You skeletal beings, from where have you come?
When he rebukes them in this manner, all the skeletal beings are seen to fall back to the ground.
This may occur many times over.
When the practitioner deeply contemplates the internal bones, they immediately see light radiating universally throughout the ten directions.
All skeletal figures illuminated by this light likewise become bright and pure.
When this contemplation is perfected, regarding all enemies, relatives, and neutral persons, as well as all that is beautiful or ugly—
His mind is equanimous, free from attachment and aversion.
This is called "superior knowledge and superior vision regarding the beautiful and the ugly.
The meaning of superior knowledge and superior vision regarding the beautiful and the ugly is as explained previously.
Furthermore, when the practitioner abides in this contemplation,
they are able to see a single skeleton person pervading the four continents, such that all are skeleton persons.
This is called "many-returning" (bahudhātukī).
Furthermore, because one again collects the mind and contemplates a single skeleton, it is called "superior knowledge and superior vision" (*abhibhāyatanam*).
Because one can prevail over the five objects of sensory desire and the pure appearances of men and women according to one's will,
it is called a "sphere of mastery" (*abhibhū-āyatana*).
Furthermore, one is able to skillfully discipline the contemplation of the mind;
although one knows that the nature of the observing mind is non-existent,
one freely revolves within conditions to contemplate all objects without any obstruction.
Therefore, they are called "spheres of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*).
This is explained in detail in the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, some teachers say:
If one contemplates only all people as impure white bones, this is called "limited.
If one performs the great contemplation of impurity, this is called "extensive.
As for the great contemplation of impurity:
In order to destroy craving and attachment toward all things,
what is meant by "contemplating all things"?
It refers to contemplating the various categories of domestic animals such as elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep, as well as birds and beasts that fly or walk.
One sees them all as corpses, bloated and swollen.
Furthermore, one contemplates food and drink as being like worms or excrement;
clothing, whether silk or cotton, is like pieces of rotting skin and putrid flesh—foul-smelling and loathsome.
Wealth and precious jewels are like venomous snakes;
in an instant they die, transform, and become foul, putrid, and impure.
Grains and rice are like stinking dead insects.
Houses, fields, gardens, kingdoms, cities, towns, the great earth, mountains, rivers, forests, and marshes—all are utterly decayed and putrid, overflowing with impurities that flow and flood forth.
Even down to the sight of bleached bones strewn about, the entire world is thus impure; it is truly loathsome and a source of deep aversion.
Within samādhi, as the practitioner observes accordingly, they immediately perceive the mastery of turning back;
they are able to shatter all worldly likes and dislikes, love and hatred, greed and sorrow, and afflictions.
Therefore, it is called "having the perception of internal forms while externally perceiving forms—whether beautiful or ugly—with superior knowledge and superior vision.
Question: Since the worldly requisites for life are impure, consisting entirely of skin, flesh, sinews, and bones, [how can one perceive them as such]?
How is it that one sees all things as impure and decaying?
The answer is:
this is the transformation through the power of mind on the path of liberation; it is not a perception of reality.
Why is this? Because all things are not real, yet they are pure.
Due to the power of the perversion of purity, one perceives everything as pure and consequently gives rise to craving and attachment.
Although not everything is entirely impure,
through the power of the wisdom of the contemplation of impurity, one perceives all things as impure.
What fault could there be in thus destroying all afflictions?
For example, when the fires of the kalpa-annihilation blaze forth, all kinds of sentient and insentient beings throughout the entire great earth become flames due to the power of that fire;
so it is now with this impure mind.
When one contemplates all worlds and sees them entirely as impure— just as a person with supernormal powers can transform tiles and stones into gold and jade—
one should know that what inherent nature could there be in phenomena?
That teacher has thus clarified it;
one may rely upon this meaning, principle, and practice of the second *abhibhvāyatana* through deep reflection.
Next, the third and fourth *abhibhvāyatanas* are explained.
The method of practice is no different from what preceded it, except that it differs in that there are no internal forms;
the method for eliminating internal forms was explained previously in the first gate of the two liberations.
Now, because the practitioner wishes to overcome and destroy the afflictions of the desire realm,
they again cultivate these two spheres of mastery within the second dhyāna;
as an antidote, they eliminate and extinguish the fetters and latent tendencies of the lower stages so that none remain.
Furthermore, by means of this profound transformation, one contemplates the path so that it becomes sharp, mature, increasingly clear, firm, and unerring;
thus, one's skillful power becomes ever more excellent.

Next, regarding the explanation of the four superior bases (abhibhvāyatana) of blue, yellow, red, and white: the practitioner does not experience the bliss of the body-attestation of the third dhyāna.
When entering the fourth dhyāna, mindfulness and wisdom are purified, and the four colors become even more radiant, like the luster of exquisite jewels.

Because they surpass the previous colors, they are called "spheres of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*). Furthermore, within the fourth dhyāna, the practitioner uses immovable wisdom to refine these four colors, exercising sovereign mastery over their transformation—turning a small amount into much, and much into a small amount.
Because one sees them whenever one wishes to see them and they cease whenever one wishes for them to cease,
they are called "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Furthermore, while the practitioner is in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), although they perceive these superior forms, their fetters and outflows (*āsrava*) have not yet been severed.
At times, a mind of attachment to phenomena may arise.
To sever this attachment to phenomena, one should contemplate this form with discernment, knowing that it arises from the mind.
Just as a magician contemplates the illusory forms created and knows they arise from the mind, thus not giving rise to attachment.
At this time, the "liberations" (vimokṣa) change their name to "bases of mastery" (abhibhvāyatana).
The fourth section clarifies the characteristics of the path to enlightenment through three points.
The first is that one first uses the bases of mastery to discipline the mind.
Thereafter, they fully cultivate and transcend such dharmas as these,
giving rise to true outflow-free wisdom and realizing the paths of the Three Vehicles.
Second, these eight bases of mastery are fully accomplished and lead to deep penetration into the true contemplation of the Four Noble Truths.
Within the fourth dhyāna, one gives rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*).
Possessing thirty-four moments of mind, one severs the fetters of the three realms and realizes the paths of the three vehicles.
Thirdly, there are practitioners who, upon attaining the first *abhibhvāyatana* and entering the first dhyāna, experience a heavy sense of aversion and fear.
He immediately thought to himself:
"What use have I now for practicing various meditative absorptions? I must simply and swiftly attain nirvana.
Having formed this thought, he then deeply contemplated the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the true reality of the Middle Way at that very spot.
If one gives rise to the untainted [wisdom], one immediately realizes the noble fruits of the three vehicles.
The seven lower spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) should likewise be analyzed in this same manner for each.
Although the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows that all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent, [he does not abandon his compassionate vows].
Out of compassion for all sentient beings,
he deeply cultivates the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana).
Within these spheres of mastery, he gives rise to great supernormal powers (abhijñā).
Subduing the celestial Māras and demons, shattering all heterodox paths, and delivering sentient beings—
know that this state of victory is precisely the Bodhisattva’s Mahāyāna.
Next, the Dharma-gate of the ten universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*) is explained.
The ten universal bases (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*) are:
first, blue; second, yellow; third, red; fourth, white; fifth, earth; sixth, water; seventh, fire; eighth, wind; ninth, space; and tenth, consciousness.
These ten are collectively termed "universal bases" because—
Because each and every form illuminates the ten directions and pervades them entirely,
it is called "all-places" (sarvatraga).
This applies even to space in the same way.
Although the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) and spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) involve the eight types of form,
that which they illuminate is narrow and cannot be universal;
therefore, they do not receive the designation "all" (*sarva*).
Furthermore, in the sūtras, they are sometimes described as the ten *kṛtsnāyatanas*.
Some interpret this by saying that these are simply alternative names for the *sarvatragatā* (all-pervasive bases).
Now it is not so.
Initially, that which is called "one color" universally illuminates the ten directions and is thus named "all-pervasive.
Subsequently, the mind transforms into skillfulness and is able to universally illuminate all things.
Within each of the forms, they mutually penetrate one another without any mutual obstruction;
therefore, the name "all-base" (*kṛtsnāyatana*) is established for their locations.
Now, it is explained that these ten all-bases consist of two intentions.
First, the clarification of stages;
second, the differentiation of cultivation and realization.
Regarding the first, the clarification of stages:
Regarding the ten universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the first eight, which are the universal bases of form, are situated within the fourth dhyāna.
The ninth, the universal base of space, is situated in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśāyatana*).
The tenth, the universal base of consciousness, is situated in the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*).

The reason why the "all-bases" (*sarvataḥ*) are not established within the first three dhyānas is that, when a practitioner first begins training, those three stages contain vitarka, vicāra, prīti, and sukha, which are in motion;
thus, they cannot cause form to be pervasive and remain stable. Furthermore, in the higher station of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), there is no substance that can be expanded.
Nor does one obtain happiness therein. Furthermore,
the Buddha did not speak of a "sphere of nothingness," for because it is immeasurable and boundless, no such sphere is established.
In the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the mind is dull and the perception is difficult to grasp;
because it is vast, it is not established as a "sphere" (āyatana).
Second, the cultivation and realization are explained.
When the practitioner abides in the fourth dhyāna, having attained mastery over superior form,
they should then employ a mind of pure mindfulness to relinquish the seven kinds of color and directly attend to the color blue.
One takes up a small mark of blue light and flame, as large as a blade of grass.
With single-minded focus on the center, one corresponds with that small blue.
One contemplates the mind moving this small blue to universally illuminate the ten directions.
Then one sees light that shines everywhere according to one's mind;
the entire world appears filled with the blue sign, remaining steady and unmoving like a blue world-system.
This is called the "blue universal base" (nīla-kṛtsnāyatana).
The characteristics of the meditative cultivation of the remaining seven *kṛtsnāyatana*s should likewise be distinguished individually in this same manner.

Some teachers state that when cultivating the *kṛtsnāyatana*s, one takes the appearance of grass, leaves, and so forth as the object; because these arise from external forms, their appearance becomes pervasive and universally illuminating.
To speak in such a manner not only deviates from the methods of the contemplation gate (*vipaśyanā-mukha*),
but is also entirely unrelated to what is taught in the Mahāyāna.
Since the practitioner has already accomplished the "all-pervasive base" (*ākāśa-kṛtsnāyatana*) by means of which they wish to enter the all-pervasive base of space.
When entering the liberation of space,
the object of that liberation is narrow; therefore,
it is not yet called a "universal sphere" (kṛtsnāyatana).
Now, because it further extensively encompasses the space of the ten directions,
it is called the "all-pervasive base of space" (ākāśa-kṛtsnāyatana).
One who wishes to enter the "all-pervasive base of consciousness" (vijñāna-kṛtsnāyatana) [should proceed as follows].
One should likewise first enter the liberation of the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana-vimokṣa*).
Within the meditative concentration of consciousness, one extensively contemplates this consciousness,
seeing it pervading the ten directions entirely as consciousness.
Therefore, it is called the "consciousness of all bases.
If a practitioner wishes to cultivate the all-pervading bases (kṛtsnāyatana), once they have attained mastery over them,
they should take these all-pervading bases as the foundation.
Thereafter, one employs skillful observation of the mind upon the blue within all things,
causing the yellow, red, white, and so forth to enter into it without destroying the fundamental characteristic of the blue,
while being able to perceive the other colors fully within that blue color.
This concludes the brief explanation of all the *kṛtsnāyatana*s (totalities) and *abhibhvāyatana*s (spheres of mastery).
It is asked:
Why is the characteristic of the path leading to liberation (*mārga-gati-lakṣaṇa*) not differentiated within the context of all the *kṛtsnāyatana*s?
Answer: In all the Śrāvaka sūtras,
it is frequently stated that "all objects" (sarvatra) are objects of outflow (sāsrava).
However, since the methods for cultivating the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are inferior in their capacity to generate the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state, they are not analyzed here.
If one wishes to analyze them according to the Mahāyāna doctrine:
This is similar to what was explained previously regarding the liberations (*vimokṣa*) and the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Now, the Bodhisattva, desiring to universally accomplish the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and to universally manifest forms,
seeks to fully realize all matters within the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

Since this cultivation pertains to all places, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* also refers to it as the "Pāramitā of All Places. Second, the method for clarifying the function of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) through contemplation is explained.
Once the Buddha’s disciples have attained these three stages of contemplative practice,
if they wish to manifest rare and wondrous events to transform sentient beings and cause their minds to become pure,
they should extensively cultivate all the supernatural powers and spiritual capacities.

These are the so-called six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), fourteen transformations (*caturdaśa vikurvaṇā*), four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvid*), the samādhi of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*), knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), the meditative concentration of the summit (*mūrdhan-dhyāna*), the meditative concentration of mastery (*vaśitā-samādhi*), the refined meditative concentrations (*pariśuddha-dhyāna*), the eighteen transformations (*aṣṭādaśa vikurvaṇā*), and other such great merits.
All should train in these liberations, bases of mastery, and totalities.

Having mastered them through training, one should manifest supernormal transformations so that many sentient beings may behold them with joy, develop faith and submission, and thereby attain liberation.
Next, the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) are explained.
As for the six supernormal powers:
first is the supernormal power of the divine eye (divyacakṣur-abhijñā).
2. The supernormal power of the divine ear; 3.
the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others;
4. the supernormal power of recollecting past lives; 5. the supernormal power of mastery over psychic transformations.
Sixth is the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*).
All these are called "supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*): "spiritual" (*abhi*) refers to the celestial mind, and "power" (*jñā*) is the nature of wisdom.
By means of this innate wisdom, one penetrates and illuminates all phenomena, such as form and mind, without obstruction.
Therefore, they are called "supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*).
Now, following these various dhyānas, the explanation of the six supernormal powers shall be presented in three parts.
First, clarifying that the causes and conditions for attaining the supernormal powers differ.
The second [section] clearly explains the method for cultivating the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);
the third clarifies their transformative functions.
Regarding the first, there are three types of differing causes and conditions for attaining these powers.
The first is that obtained as a karmic reward (*vipākaja*).
For example, those born among the gods or in the pure lands of those with great merit immediately obtain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) as a karmic reward.
The second is that obtained through cultivation (*prāyogika*).
If a person, through mere repentance or by deeply cultivating the aforementioned meditative concentrations,
causes supernatural powers to manifest spontaneously even without employing the specific methods for attaining them.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"By deeply cultivating meditative concentration, one attains the five supernormal powers.
Regarding those attained through the three types of cultivation:
Although the practitioner has realized the various profound meditative concentrations described above,
if they have not severed the obstacles that obstruct the superknowledges (abhijñā), then those superknowledges will ultimately not manifest.
If, while within these meditative concentrations, they further apply the skillful means for attaining the superknowledges, [they will succeed].
The supernormal power of penetrating knowledge that transcends obstacles arises immediately;
it is precisely with reference to this that the meaning is now explained.
Second, the method for cultivating the supernormal powers is clarified.
The explanations found in the sūtras and śāstras vary;
for now, I shall briefly clarify the method for cultivating the supernormal powers by taking the intent of the Mahāyāna.
First, regarding the cultivation of the divine eye power (*divyacakṣurabhijñā*):
The practitioner, with a deeply compassionate mind for all beings,
makes a vow desiring to see the signs of death and rebirth among the sentient beings of the six realms.

At that time, they should abide within the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) of the form realm.
When the cultivation of right mindfulness is complete with four conditions, the supernormal power of the divine eye arises. What are these four?
First, light constantly shines, being no different between day and night.
Second, contemplate the two truths so that all worldly obstructions appear like empty space, devoid of any characteristic of concealment.
Third, with a concentrated mind, first select an easily visible object and take it as the focus of the mind.
Constantly and diligently applying skillful cultivation with the desire to see the object before one;
fourth, within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the production of the four great elements that accomplish the pure eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).
This is called the fulfillment of the harmony of these four conditions.
Consequently, a pure consciousness arises,
whereby one perceives the signs of suffering and joy as sentient beings of the six realms in the ten directions die here and are born there;
as well as forms that are luminous or dark, near or distant, obstructed or unobstructed, coarse or subtle.
To see through to the end without obstruction, with perfect clarity and distinctness—
this is called the supernormal power of the divine eye (divyacakṣus-abhijñā).
Second, to clarify the cultivation of the supernormal power of the divine ear (divyaśrotra-abhijñā).
Once the practitioner has seen forms,
if they wish to hear their sounds, they should,
within meditative concentration, carefully apprehend subtle sounds that can be heard beyond obstructions.
Listen with single-minded attention, for you wish to hear it.
If the mind is clear and sharp, one will produce the pure matter derived from the four great elements that constitutes the faculty of the ear;
thus, one hears all sounds within and beyond obstructions—the voices of suffering, pleasure, sorrow, and joy, and various differing modes of speech throughout the six realms of existence.
This is called the supernormal power of the divine ear.
Regarding the cultivation of the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others among the three knowledges:
once the practitioner has heard the sounds, [he proceeds as follows].
If one wishes to know the matters contemplated within the minds of sentient beings,
one should immediately, while in meditative concentration, observe the signs of joy, anger, fear, and so forth in the person before one;
one will then fully know that these all abide in dependence upon the mind.
Using these signs, one should contemplate the dharmas that are the objects of the mind’s recollection with single-minded intent, wishing to know them.
If the mind is clear and sharp, supernormal powers will arise from this.
To know the thoughts and affairs of sentient beings as soon as they are perceived is called the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (paracittajñāna-abhijñā).
Fourth, the cultivation of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna) is explained.
Once the practitioner has known the minds of others,
if they wish to know their own past lives as well as the deeds performed by themselves and others throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, they should then,
within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), personally recollect their own experiences.
He recollects with single-minded intent all the deeds performed throughout the course of days,
months, and years, even down to the actions committed during the stage of the *kalala*.
Thus he desires to know them through mindfulness.
If the mind is clear and sharp, one immediately develops supernormal powers;

one then personally knows, with perfect clarity and distinctness, the characteristics of the karmic deeds performed throughout one's past lives, from a single lifetime up to hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
Up to the knowledge of the past lives of others is also like this;
this is called the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*).
Fifth, the cultivation of the supernormal power of mastery over the body (*ṛddhi-vidhi-abhijñā*) is explained.
Once the practitioner has known their past lives,
if they wish to attain the supernormal power of bodily transformation,
they should, within samādhi, bind the mind to the space within the body and extinguish coarse and heavy material forms.
Constantly taking up the sign of lightness and emptiness, one generates a mind of great desire and diligence.
With wisdom, one evaluates the power of the mind;
when the mind is capable of lifting the body, one knows for oneself that the power of the mind is already great enough to lift it.
For example, just as a person learning to jump constantly lifts their body lightly,
so too does the body manifest when the contemplation of the mind is perfected.
There are three types of the supernormal power of bodily mastery (*kāya-ṛddhi*).
First, the ability to go;
second, transformation;
third, mastery.
That which is called "being able to arrive" is of four kinds:
first, the body can fly through the air without obstruction, like a bird;
second, one can make the distant near so that one arrives without having traveled.
Third, passing away from here and emerging there;
fourth, being able to reach [the destination] in a single thought-moment.
Second, the transformation of supernormal power (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇā*).
The great can become small and the small can become large;
the one can become many and the many can become one;
all various things can be transformed at will.
Regarding the three types of noble supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*):
within the six external sense objects, one can contemplate impure things that are not normally enjoyed so as to make them pure,
and one can make pure things that are normally enjoyable appear impure.
This is the dharma of mastery.

The supernormal power of the mind (ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna) arises from the cultivation of the stages of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), the bases of totality (kṛtsnāyatana), and the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda).
This is called the supernormal power of bodily manifestation (kāya-ṛddhi-abhijñā).
Because the practitioner has attained this supernormal power of the body at will (*kāya-ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*),
they are able to manifest transformations according to their wishes.
Whether they desire to attain liberation for themselves or to deliver sentient beings, [they can do so].
One must sever the mental afflictions.
At that time, one should cultivate the untainted supernormal powers (*anāsrava-abhijñā*).
The cultivation of these untainted supernormal powers will be explained in detail later in the section on the contemplation of the truths (*satya-vipaśyanā*).
Question:
Are the lower six successive stages of cultivation exactly as previously described?
Answer: Yes.
This explains the sequence according to one specific path.
However, if a practitioner follows what they find most suitable, they may attain it by proceeding through the preceding stages of study;
it is not necessarily the case that all must follow the order previously explained.
Third, regarding the clarification of transformations:
the fourteen types of transformation can give rise to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*),
and by means of these supernormal powers, one is likewise able to manifest transformations.
What are called the fourteen transformations?
First, in the desire realm and the first dhyāna,
one accomplishes two transformations.
First, the transformation of the first dhyāna within the first dhyāna;
second, the transformation of the desire realm from the first dhyāna;
and third, the accomplishment of the three transformations from the second dhyāna.
One who is in the first or second dhyāna creates an emanation in the second dhyāna;
one who is in the second dhyāna creates an emanation in the first dhyāna;
one who is in the third dhyāna creates an emanation in the desire realm.
Third, one achieves four types of transformations through the third dhyāna:
first, transformation within the third dhyāna;
second, transformation within the second dhyāna.
In the first dhyāna of the three dhyānas, there is the transformation of the first dhyāna.
In the fourth dhyāna of the three dhyānas, there is the transformation of the desire realm.
Fourthly, in the fourth dhyāna, one accomplishes the five types of transformations.
1. Transformation from the fourth dhyāna into the fourth dhyāna;
2. Transformation from the fourth dhyāna into the third dhyāna; 3. Transformation from the fourth dhyāna into the second dhyāna;
4. Transformation from the fourth dhyāna into the first dhyāna.
The five [masteries] and the four dhyānas transform within the desire realm;
these constitute the fourteen transformations.
If a person accomplishes these transformations, they possess the eighteen transformations.
The merits of all supernatural powers and contemplative practices are immeasurable and boundless.
These matters are so subtle that how could they ever be fully recorded in writing?
For now, I shall merely list their names in brief.
It is intended to let students know that all supernatural powers and transformations arise from the contemplation of dhyāna.
These various supernatural powers, when present within the mind of a bodhisattva, are called the "perfection of supernatural powers" (ṛddhipāramitā).
Next, the nine successive attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti) will be explained.
As for the nine successive attainments:
one becomes detached from all desires and detached from all evil and unwholesome states.
With directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he enters the first dhyāna.

In this manner, he successively enters the second, third, and fourth dhyānas; the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
These are called the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).
The explanation of the nine successive attainments consists of three parts:
first, the explanation of the names.
Second, clarifying the stages and positions;
third, clarifying cultivation and realization.
First, the explanation of the names.
Now, as for these nine dharmas all being designated as "successive concentrations" (anupūrvavihārasamādhi):
because the aforementioned dharma-gates have not yet matured in terms of contemplative practice,
the mind contains interruptions when entering meditative absorption.
This is not called sequential meditative concentration (*anupūrva-samādhi*).
Since the practitioner has already accomplished the methods of meditative observation,
they can now, through mastery gained by refining them within this state, arise from the mind of the first dhyāna.
Next, one enters the first dhyāna with a continuous stream of mind,
not allowing any other thought—
whether wholesome or defiled— to enter.
Thus, up to the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, these are called the nine successive concentrations (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).
They are also called "refined dhyāna" (*parikarmadhyāna*). Why is this so?
The disciples of the Buddhas, whose minds delight in the untainted (*anāsrava*) and who have previously attained the various flavors of dhyāna,
now wish to remove their impurities by refining them with untainted dhyāna,
making them all pure according to the method of refining gold. [The interlocutor] asks:
Regarding the explanation of the method of refinement within the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*),
what is the difference between this and the method of perfuming meditation (*vāsita-dhyāna*) elucidated by the Abhidharma masters?
The answer is:
there are both similarities and differences.
In that case, one uses the untainted (anāsrava) to refine the tainted (sāsrava).
Now, these are also similar because they refine the contaminated by means of the uncontaminated. That [previous section],
however, merely clarifies the refinement of the four dhyānas for the purpose of preventing regression and transforming the dull into the sharp,
as well as for the sake of present-life happiness and rebirth in the five Pure Abodes.
Only the four dhyānas are refined;
in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there is no method of refinement.
